There crowded upon her all the stories she had been told of Marooners' Rock, so called because evil captains put sailors on it and leave them there to drown. They drown when the tide rises, for then it is submerged.

Of course she should have roused the children at once; not merely because of the unknown that was stalking toward them, but because it was no longer good for them to sleep on a rock grown chilly. But she was a young mother and she did not know this; she thought you simply must stick to your rule about half an hour after the midday meal. So, though fear was upon her, and she longed to hear male voices, she would not waken them. Even when she heard the sound of muffled oars, though her heart was in her mouth, she did not waken them. She stood over them to let them have their sleep out. Was it not brave of Wendy?

It was well for those boys then that there was one among them who could sniff danger even in his sleep. Peter sprang erect, as wide awake at once as a dog, and with one warning cry he roused the others.
He stood motionless, one hand to his ear.

'Pirates!' he cried. The others came closer to him. A strange smile was playing about his face, and Wendy saw it and shuddered. While that smile was on his face no one dared address him; all they could do was to stand ready to obey. The order came sharp and incisive.
'Dive!'
There was a gleam of legs, and instantly the lagoon seemed deserted. Marooners' Rock stood alone in the forbidding waters, as if it were itself marooned.

The boat drew nearer. It was the pirate dinghy, with three figures in her, Smee and Starkey, and the third a captive, no other than Tiger Lily. Her hands and ankles were tied, and she knew what was to be her fate. She was to be left on the rock to perish, an end to one of her race more terrible than death by fire or torture, for is it not written in the book of the tribe that there is no path through water to the happy hunting-ground? Yet her face was impassive; she was the daughter of a chief, she must die as a chief's daughter, it is enough.

They had caught her boarding the pirate ship with a knife in her mouth. No watch was kept on the ship, it being Hook's boast that the wind of his name guarded the ship for a mile around. Now her fate would help to guard it also. One more wail would go the round in that wind by night.
In the gloom that they brought with them the two pirates did not see the rock till they crashed into it.
'Luff, you lubber,' cried an Irish voice that was Smee's; 'here's the rock. Now, then, what we have to do is to hoist the redskin on to it and leave her there to drown.'
It was the work of one brutal moment to land the beautiful girl on the rock; she was too proud to offer a vain resistance.

Quite near the rock, but out of sight, two heads were bobbing up and down, Peter's and Wendy's. Wendy was crying, for it was the first tragedy she had seen. Peter had seen many tragedies, but he had forgotten them all. He was less sorry than Wendy for Tiger Lily: it was two against one that angered him, and he meant to save her. An easy way would have been to wait until the pirates had gone, but he was never one to choose the easy way.
There was almost nothing he could not do, and he now imitated the voice of Hook.
'Ahoy there, you lubbers,' he called. It was a marvellous imitation.
'The captain,' said the pirates, staring at each other in surprise.
'He must be swimming out to us,' Starkey said, when they had looked for him in vain.
'We are putting the redskin on the rock,' Smee called out.
'Set her free,' came the astonishing answer.
'Free!'
'Yes, cut her bonds and let her go.'
'But, captain----'
'At once, d'ye hear,' cried Peter, 'or I'll plunge my hook in you.'
'This is queer,' Smee gasped.
'Better do what the captain orders,' said Starkey nervously.
'Ay, ay,' Smee said, and he cut Tiger Lily's cords. At once like an eel she slid between Starkey's legs into the water.

Of course Wendy was very elated over Peter's cleverness; but she knew that he would be elated also and very likely crow and thus betray himself, so at once her hand went out to cover his mouth. But it was stayed even in the act, for 'Boat ahoy!' rang over the lagoon in Hook's voice, and this time it was not Peter who had spoken.
Peter may have been about to crow, but his face puckered in a whistle of surprise instead.
'Boat ahoy!' again came the cry.
Now Wendy understood. The real Hook was also in the water.

He was swimming to the boat, and as his men showed a light to guide him he had soon reached them. In the light of the lantern Wendy saw his hook grip the boat's side; she saw his evil swarthy face as he rose dripping from the water, and, quaking, she would have liked to swim away, but Peter would not budge. He was tingling with life and also top-heavy with conceit. 'Am I not a wonder, oh, I am a wonder!' he whispered to her; and though she thought so also, she was really glad for the sake of his reputation that no one heard him except herself.
He signed to her to listen.
The two pirates were very curious to know what had brought their captain to them, but he sat with his head on his hook in a position of profound melancholy.
'Captain, is all well?' they asked timidly, but he answered with a hollow moan.
'He sighs,' said Smee.
'He sighs again,' said Starkey.
'And yet a third time he sighs,' said Smee.
'What's up, captain?'
Then at last he spoke passionately.
'The game's up,' he cried, 'those boys have found a mother.'
Affrighted though she was, Wendy swelled with pride.
'O evil day,' cried Starkey.
'What's a mother?' asked the ignorant Smee.
Wendy was so shocked that she exclaimed, 'He doesn't know!' and always after this she felt that if you could have a pet pirate Smee would be her one.
Peter pulled her beneath the water, for Hook had started up, crying, 'What was that?'

'I heard nothing,' said Starkey, raising the lantern over the waters, and as the pirates looked they saw a strange sight. It was the nest I have told you of, floating on the lagoon, and the Never bird was sitting on it.
'See,' said Hook in answer to Smee's question, 'that is a mother. What a lesson. The nest must have fallen into the water, but would the mother desert her eggs? No.'
There was a break in his voice, as if for a moment he recalled innocent days when--but he brushed away this weakness with his hook.
Smee, much impressed, gazed at the bird as the nest was borne past, but the more suspicious Starkey said, 'If she is a mother, perhaps she is hanging about here to help Peter.'
Hook winced. 'Ay,' he said, 'that is the fear that haunts me.'
He was roused from this dejection by Smee's eager voice.
'Captain,' said Smee, 'could we not kidnap these boys' mother and make her our mother?'

'It is a princely scheme,' cried Hook, and at once it took practical shape in his great brain. 'We will seize the children and carry them to the boat: the boys we will make walk the plank, and Wendy shall be our mother.'
Again Wendy forgot herself.
'Never!' she cried, and bobbed.
'What was that?'
But they could see nothing. They thought it must have been but a leaf in the wind. 'Do you agree, my bullies?' asked Hook.
'There is my hand on it,' they both said.
'And there is my hook. Swear.'
'They all swore. By this time they were on the rock, and suddenly Hook remembered Tiger Lily.
'Where is the redskin?' he demanded abruptly.
He had a playful humour at moments, and they thought this was one of the moments.
'That is all right, captain,' Smee answered complacently; 'we let her go.'
'Let her go!' cried Hook.
''Twas your own orders,' the bo'sun faltered.
'You called over the water to us to let her go,' said Starkey.

'Brimstone and gall,' thundered Hook, 'what cozening is here?' His face had gone black with rage, but he saw that they believed their words, and he was startled. 'Lads,' he said, shaking a little, 'I gave no such order.'
'It is passing queer,' Smee said, and they all fidgeted uncomfortably. Hook raised his voice, but there was a quiver in it.
'Spirit that haunts this dark lagoon to-night,' he cried, 'dost hear me?'
Of course Peter should have kept quiet, but of course he did not. He immediately answered in Hook's voice:
'Odds, bobs, hammer and tongs, I hear you.'
In that supreme moment Hook did not blanch, even at the gills, but Smee and Starkey clung to each other in terror.
'Who are you, stranger, speak?' Hook demanded.
'I am James Hook,' replied the voice, 'captain of the _Jolly Roger_.'
'You are not; you are not,' Hook cried hoarsely.
'Brimstone and gall,' the voice retorted, 'say that again, and I'll cast anchor in you.'
Hook tried a more ingratiating manner. 'If you are Hook,' he said almost humbly, 'come tell me, who am I?'
'A codfish,' replied the voice, 'only a codfish.'
'A codfish!' Hook echoed blankly; and it was then, but not till then, that his proud spirit broke. He saw his men draw back from him.
'Have we been captained all this time by a codfish!' they muttered. 'It is lowering to our pride.'

They were his dogs snapping at him, but, tragic figure though he had become, he scarcely heeded them. Against such fearful evidence it was not their belief in him that he needed, it was his own. He felt his ego slipping from him. 'Don't desert me, bully,' he whispered hoarsely to it.
In his dark nature there was a touch of the feminine, as in all the great pirates, and it sometimes gave him intuitions. Suddenly he tried the guessing game.
'Hook,' he called, 'have you another voice?'
Now Peter could never resist a game, and he answered blithely in his own voice, 'I have.'
'And another name?'
'Ay, ay.'
'Vegetable?' asked Hook.
'No.'
'Mineral?'
'No.'
'Animal?'
'Yes.'
'Man?'
'No!' This answer rang out scornfully.
'Boy?'
'Yes.'
'Ordinary boy?'
'No!'
'Wonderful boy?'
To Wendy's pain the answer that rang out this time was 'Yes.'
'Are you in England?'
'No.'
'Are you here?'
'Yes.'
Hook was completely puzzled. 'You ask him some questions,' he said to the others, wiping his damp brow.
Smee reflected. 'I can't think of a thing,' he said regretfully.
'Can't guess, can't guess,' crowed Peter. 'Do you give it up?'
Of course in his pride he was carrying the game too far, and the miscreants saw their chance.
'Yes, yes,' they answered eagerly.
'Well, then,' he cried, 'I am Peter Pan.'
Pan!
In a moment Hook was himself again, and Smee and Starkey were his faithful henchmen.
'Now we have him,' Hook shouted. 'Into the water, Smee. Starkey, mind the boat. Take him dead or alive.'
He leaped as he spoke, and simultaneously came the gay voice of Peter.
'Are you ready, boys?'
'Ay, ay,' from various parts of the lagoon.
'Then lam into the pirates.'

The fight was short and sharp. First to draw blood was John, who gallantly climbed into the boat and held Starkey. There was a fierce struggle, in which the cutlass was torn from the pirate's grasp. He wriggled overboard and John leapt after him. The dinghy drifted away.

Here and there a head bobbed up in the water, and there was a flash of steel followed by a cry or a whoop. In the confusion some struck at their own side. The corkscrew of Smee got Tootles in the fourth rib, but he was himself pinked in turn by Curly. Farther from the rock Starkey was pressing Slightly and the twins hard.
Where all this time was Peter? He was seeking bigger game.
The others were all brave boys, and they must not be blamed for backing from the pirate captain. His iron claw made a circle of dead water round him, from which they fled like affrighted fishes.
But there was one who did not fear him: there was one prepared to enter that circle.

Strangely, it was not in the water that they met. Hook rose to the rock to breathe, and at the same moment Peter scaled it on the opposite side. The rock was slippery as a ball, and they had to crawl rather than climb. Neither knew that the other was coming. Each feeling for a grip met the other's arm: in surprise they raised their heads; their faces were almost touching; so they met.

Some of the greatest heroes have confessed that just before they fell to they had a sinking. Had it been so with Peter at that moment I would admit it. After all, this was the only man that the Sea-Cook had feared. But Peter had no sinking, he had one feeling only, gladness; and he gnashed his pretty teeth with joy. Quick as thought he snatched a knife from Hook's belt and was about to drive it home, when he saw that he was higher up the rock than his foe. It would not have been fighting fair. He gave the pirate a hand to help him up.
It was then that Hook bit him.

Not the pain of this but its unfairness was what dazed Peter. It made him quite helpless. He could only stare, horrified. Every child is affected thus the first time he is treated unfairly. All he thinks he has a right to when he comes to you to be yours is fairness. After you have been unfair to him he will love you again, but he will never afterwards be quite the same boy. No one ever gets over the first unfairness; no one except Peter. He often met it, but he always forgot it. I suppose that was the real difference between him and all the rest.
So when he met it now it was like the first time; and he could just stare, helpless. Twice the iron hand clawed him.

A few minutes afterwards the other boys saw Hook in the water striking wildly for the ship; no elation on his pestilent face now, only white fear, for the crocodile was in dogged pursuit of him. On ordinary occasions the boys would have swum alongside cheering; but now they were uneasy, for they had lost both Peter and Wendy, and were scouring the lagoon for them, calling them by name. They found the dinghy and went home in it, shouting 'Peter, Wendy' as they went, but no answer came save mocking laughter from the mermaids. 'They must be swimming back or flying,' the boys concluded. They were not very anxious, they had such faith in Peter. They chuckled, boylike, because they would be late for bed; and it was all mother Wendy's fault!
When their voices died away there came cold silence over the lagoon, and then a feeble cry.
'Help, help!'

Two small figures were beating against the rock; the girl had fainted and lay on the boy's arm. With a last effort Peter pulled her up the rock and then lay down beside her. Even as he also fainted he saw that the water was rising. He knew that they would soon be drowned, but he could do no more.

As they lay side by side a mermaid caught Wendy by the feet, and began pulling her softly into the water. Peter, feeling her slip from him, woke with a start, and was just in time to draw her back. But he had to tell her the truth.
'We are on the rock, Wendy,' he said, 'but it is growing smaller. Soon the water will be over it.'
She did not understand even now.
'We must go,' she said, almost brightly.
'Yes,' he answered faintly.
'Shall we swim or fly, Peter?'
He had to tell her.
'Do you think you could swim or fly as far as the island, Wendy, without my help?'
She had to admit that she was too tired.
He moaned.
'What is it?' she asked, anxious about him at once.
'I can't help you, Wendy. Hook wounded me. I can neither fly nor swim.'
'Do you mean we shall both be drowned?'
'Look how the water is rising.'

They put their hands over their eyes to shut out the sight. They thought they would soon be no more. As they sat thus something brushed against Peter as light as a kiss, and stayed there, as if saying timidly, 'Can I be of any use?'
It was the tail of a kite, which Michael had made some days before. It had torn itself out of his hand and floated away.
'Michael's kite,' Peter said without interest, but next moment he had seized the tail, and was pulling the kite toward him.
'It lifted Michael off the ground,' he cried; 'why should it not carry you?'
'Both of us!'
'It can't lift two; Michael and Curly tried.'
'Let us draw lots,' Wendy said bravely.

'And you a lady; never.' Already he had tied the tail round her. She clung to him; she refused to go without him; but with a 'Good-bye, Wendy,' he pushed her from the rock; and in a few minutes she was borne out of his sight. Peter was alone on the lagoon.

The rock was very small now; soon it would be submerged. Pale rays of light tiptoed across the waters; and by and by there was to be heard a sound at once the most musical and the most melancholy in the world: the mermaids calling to the moon.

Peter was not quite like other boys; but he was afraid at last. A tremor ran through him, like a shudder passing over the sea; but on the sea one shudder follows another till there are hundreds of them, and Peter felt just the one. Next moment he was standing erect on the rock again, with that smile on his face and a drum beating within him. It was saying, 'To die will be an awfully big adventure.'
translated_paragraphs: 你闭上眼睛，运气好的话，有时候会瞧见一团淡淡的颜色，漂在黑暗里，美得很，还没有个形状。再把眼睛闭紧一点，那团颜色便渐渐有了轮廓，也鲜亮起来，再使一下劲儿就要烧起来了。就在它要烧起来的前一瞬，你看见了那片礁湖。人在大陆上，离礁湖最近也就到这儿了，只有那么快活的一刻。要是能多留一刻，说不定你还能看见浪花，听见美人鱼唱歌。

漫长的夏日里，孩子们常常一整天待在这片潟湖上，大半时候在游泳，在水面漂浮，或是在水里玩美人鱼玩的游戏。千万别因此以为美人鱼跟他们交上了朋友。恰恰相反，温蒂一直觉得遗憾的是，在岛上待了那么久，竟没有一条美人鱼肯对她说句客气话。她轻手轻脚地摸到潟湖边上，常一眼看见好几十条。尤其是放逐岩上，她们最爱躺在那里晒太阳，懒洋洋地梳理头发，看得温蒂直着急。有时她甚至能悄悄游到离她们不到一码的地方，简直像在水里踮着脚尖。可是一被她们瞧见，她们就钻进水底，还多半要用尾巴溅她一身水。那可不是凑巧，是故意的。
她们对男孩们也一视同仁，当然，彼得除外。彼得常在放逐岩上跟她们一聊就是几个钟头，哪条美人鱼出言不逊，他就一屁股坐到她的尾巴上。他还把她们的一把梳子送给了温蒂。

在月相交替的时候观看美人鱼，最叫人念念不忘。那时她们会发出奇异的哀鸣。不过到那时候，潟湖对凡人可很危险。直到我们现在要讲的那个夜晚为止，温蒂从没在月光下见过潟湖。倒不完全是出于害怕，彼得自然会陪她去。更要紧的是，她有条硬规矩，人人都得七点上床。不过雨后天晴的日子，她倒常在湖边。这时候美人鱼会成群结队地浮上来，玩她们的水泡。彩虹映着的水里冒起五颜六色的泡泡，她们把泡泡当球，用尾巴欢欢喜喜地击来击去，设法让它们一直留在彩虹里，直到破掉。球门设在彩虹的两端，只有守门的可以用手。有时湖上有好几百条美人鱼一起打球，那场面十分好看。
可孩子们一露出要加入的意思，就只好自己玩自己的了。美人鱼们立刻消失得无影无踪。不过我们有证据，她们其实偷偷看着这些不速之客，而且也不介意偷师。就是约翰想出了一个顶泡泡的新法子：不用手，改用头。美人鱼的守门员就学去用了。约翰在永无岛上留下的印记，仅此一项。
午饭以后，孩子们躺在一块岩石上休息半个钟头，那情景想必也十分好看。这是温蒂坚持的规矩。哪怕午饭是假装吃的，休息也得来真的。于是他们躺在阳光下，身上闪闪发亮，她就在旁边坐着，一副煞有介事的样子。
故事就发生在这样的一天。大家都待在放逐岩上。岩石比他们那张大床大不了多少，可他们当然都懂得怎样不占地方。这会儿他们正在打瞌睡，至少是闭着眼睛躺着，间或趁温蒂不注意，互相掐上一把。她正忙着缝衣服呢。
就在她缝衣服的时候，潟湖变了。细细的寒颤掠过水面，太阳不见了，影子悄悄爬过水面，湖水凉了下来。光线暗得温蒂再也穿不进针眼。她抬起头看，素来欢笑盈盈的潟湖，竟显得可怕而不友善。
她明白，来的并不是黑夜，而是一种跟黑夜一样黑的东西。不，还要更糟。那东西还没到，只是先叫大海打了个寒战，通报一声：它就要来了。究竟是什么？
她听人讲过的放逐岩的故事，霎时全拥进了心头。那岩石所以叫这个名字，是因为恶毒的船长把水手丢在上面，任由他们淹死。等到涨潮，整块岩石都会没入水中，他们就淹死了。
她当然该马上叫醒孩子们。不光因为一种未知的东西正悄悄朝这边来，也因为岩石已经凉了，让孩子们睡在上面对身体没好处。可她是个年轻妈妈，不懂得这个道理。她只知道，午饭以后休息半个钟头，定下来的规矩就非遵守不可。于是，虽然心里害怕，虽然恨不得听到个男人的声音，她还是没有叫醒他们。就连后来听见被压低的桨声，一颗心都提到了嗓子眼，她也没把他们叫醒。她站在他们身旁，守着他们把这一觉睡足。温蒂可真勇敢，是不是？
幸亏男孩们当中有一个，连睡着了都能嗅出危险。彼得猛地直起身，一下子就像狗一样清醒。他出声示警，一声便把大伙儿都惊醒了。
他一动不动站着，一只手拢在耳边。
“海盗！”他叫道。其余的人都往他身边凑。他的脸上浮出一种奇异的笑，温蒂瞧见，不禁打了个哆嗦。这种笑容还在的时候，谁也不敢同他搭话，只能站定等候命令。命令果然来了，又快又干脆。
“潜下去！”
只见一阵腿脚翻飞，转眼整片潟湖仿佛已没有一个人。那块放逐岩孤零零立在森冷的水中，仿佛它自己也遭人放逐了。
小艇越驶越近。那是海盗的舢板，上面有三个人影。两个是斯密和斯塔基，第三个是个俘虏，正是虎莲公主。她的双手和脚踝都给缚住了，也明白等着自己的是什么。他们要把她丢在岩石上等死。对她的族人来说，这种结局比火烧、拷打至死都可怕。族里的书上不是写着吗，通往幸福猎场的路，没有一条从水中经过。可她的脸上看不出任何波澜。她是酋长的女儿，就得死得像一个酋长的女儿。这就够了。
她是衔着刀子往海盗船上爬时被捉住的。船上并无人站岗。虎克夸口说，单是人们在风里传他的名字，就够把船周围一英里的水面守得严严实实。如今，她的下场也能帮着守船。夜里的风中，又将多出一声哀号，向四面传开。
在两个海盗自己带来的昏暗里，他们一直没瞧见岩石，直到小艇砰地撞了上去。
“把船头迎风打过去，你这旱鸭子！”一个带爱尔兰口音的声音喊道。那是斯密。“岩石在这儿。好了，现在咱们只消把这印第安姑娘吊上去，留她在这儿淹死。”
把这美丽的姑娘搬到岩石上，只用了一瞬，粗暴的一瞬。她太骄傲，不肯作毫无用处的挣扎。
离岩石很近的一处隐蔽地方，有两颗脑袋正在水里一沉一浮，那是彼得和温蒂。温蒂在掉眼泪，因为她头一回亲眼见到这种悲惨事。彼得倒见过许多悲惨事，只是全都忘了。他不像温蒂那样为虎莲公主伤心；惹他生气的是，两个欺负一个。他打算救她。省事的办法是等海盗走了再救，可彼得从来不挑省事的办法。
他几乎没有什么不会干的。这会儿，他学起了虎克的声音。
“喂，那边两个旱鸭子！”他喊道。那声音，学得真是惟妙惟肖。
“船长！”两个海盗惊讶地瞪着对方。
找来找去，没见着人。“想必他是游过来找咱们的。”斯塔基说。
“我们正把那印第安姑娘往岩石上放呢！”斯密大声报告。
“放了她！”回答叫他们大吃一惊。
“放了她！”
“对。割断她的绳子，放她走。”
“可是，船长——”
“马上，听见没有？”彼得叫道，“不然我就拿钩子扎进你的肚皮。”
“这可怪了。”斯密倒抽一口气。
“还是照船长的命令办吧。”斯塔基紧张地说。
“遵命，遵命。”斯密说着，割断了虎莲身上的绳索。她立刻像鳗鱼一样，从斯塔基两腿之间滑进水里。
温蒂当然为彼得的聪明得意极了。可她知道，他本人也会得意极了，多半会学一声雄鸡叫，那就露馅了。她马上伸手去捂他的嘴。可手才伸在半途就停住了。潟湖上传来虎克的嗓音：“船上的人，喂！”这一回，说话的不是彼得。
彼得兴许原本是要啼叫，这下却惊讶地撮起嘴，吹出一声口哨。
“喂，船上的人！”那喊声又来了。
这会儿温蒂明白了。真的虎克也在水里。
他正向小艇游来，手下举起一盏灯引路，不多久他就游到了。借着提灯的光，温蒂看见他的钩子勾住了船舷。他湿淋淋地钻出水来，她看见了那张凶恶、黝黑的脸。她直打哆嗦，恨不得立即游走，彼得却一动也不肯动。他浑身的精神都活蹦乱跳，也给自己的本事陶醉得有点头重脚轻。“我是不是个奇才？哦，我真是个奇才！”他对她悄悄说。她固然也这么想，可替他的名声着想，她可真庆幸除了自己，没人听见这话。
他做了个手势，叫她听。
两个海盗十分好奇，想知道船长来找他们有什么事。可虎克只是坐在那儿，用铁钩托着脑袋，一副忧郁至极的模样。
“船长，一切都好吗？”他们小心翼翼地问。他只回了一声空洞的呻吟。
“他在叹气。”斯密说。
“他又叹气了。”斯塔基说。
“他又叹了第三声。”斯密说。
“出了什么事，船长？”
他这才终于满怀悲愤地开了口。
“咱们完了！”他叫道，“那些男孩找着了一个妈妈。”
温蒂尽管还在害怕，胸口却骄傲得鼓了起来。
“啊，多倒霉的日子！”斯塔基叫道。
“什么叫妈妈？”无知的斯密问。
温蒂吃惊得脱口而出：“他居然不知道！”打这以后，只要她想到人要可以养个海盗当心爱的玩伴，她愿意养的就一直都是斯密。
彼得把她拉进水下，因为虎克已经猛地站起，喝问：“什么声音？”
“我什么也没听见。”斯塔基一面说，一面把灯举到水面上。海盗们往那儿一望，却看见了一件奇景：我告诉过你的那个鸟窝正浮在湖上，永无鸟坐在上面。
“瞧，”虎克回答斯密方才的问题，“那就是个妈妈。好一堂课！窝一定是掉进了水里。可当妈妈的会丢下自己的蛋吗？不会。”
他的声音哽了一下，仿佛在那一瞬，他想起了天真无邪的童年，那时——可他拿钩子一扫，把这点软弱扫开了。
鸟窝漂过，斯密大受触动，目不转睛地望着那只鸟。可是更多疑的斯塔基说：“既然她是个妈妈，没准她守在这里是要帮彼得。”
虎克瑟缩了一下。“对，”他说，“我老是怕这个，怎么也甩不掉。”
是斯密热切的嗓音，把他从沮丧中唤醒。
“船长，”斯密说，“咱们何不把那些男孩的妈妈绑来，让她当咱们的妈妈？”
“好一个王者的计谋！”虎克高叫。这个主意刚一出口，在他的伟大脑袋里就有了可以动手的办法。“咱们抓住那些孩子，全押上船。男孩们撵上跳板走进海里，温蒂则留下来，做咱们的妈妈。”
温蒂又一次忘了该保持安静。
“休想！”她喊了一声，赶快把头一沉。
“什么声音？”
可是他们瞧不见什么。他们想，准不过是一片树叶在风里响。“伙计们，你们同意吗？”虎克问。
“伸手为誓。”两人齐声说。
“我就伸钩为誓。起誓吧。”
于是大家立了誓。这会儿他们已经上了岩石，虎克忽然想起了虎莲公主。
“那印第安姑娘呢？”他冷不丁地问。
他有时候会故意逗人玩。他们以为，这又是那么个时候。
“办妥啦，船长，”斯密得意地答道，“我们放了她。”
“放了她！”虎克叫道。
“那，那是您亲口下的命令。”水手长结结巴巴地说。
“您隔着水面喊，叫我们把她放了。”斯塔基说。
“硫黄加苦胆！”虎克雷鸣般地吼道，“这是玩的什么骗局？”他气得脸都黑了。可一看便知，他们真的相信自己说的话，这可把他吓了一跳。“伙计们，”他说，身子有些发抖，“我可没下过这样的命令。”
“这也太古怪啦。”斯密说。三个人都坐立不安。虎克提高了嗓门，声音却在打颤。
“今夜在这阴暗的潟湖出没的幽灵，”他喊道，“你听得见我吗？”
彼得理该闭口不言。当然，他偏不。他马上用虎克的嗓音回答：
“见鬼，铁锤加铁钳！我听得见你。”
在那千钧一发的时刻，虎克连腮帮子都没白一下。斯密和斯塔基却吓得紧紧抱作一团。
“陌生人，你是谁？说！”虎克喝问。
“我是詹姆斯·虎克，”那声音答道，“快乐罗杰号的船长。”
“你不是！你不是！”虎克嗓音嘶哑地喊。
“硫黄加苦胆！”那声音回敬道，“你再说一遍，我就把锚抛进你肚子里。”
虎克换上了讨好些的口气。“你要是虎克，”他几乎是谦卑地说，“那你告诉我，我是谁？”
“一条鳕鱼，”那声音答道，“只不过一条鳕鱼。”
“鳕鱼！”虎克茫然地重复。直到这时，他那骄傲的精神才垮了下来。他看见手下在往后躲他。
“难道过去这么久，指挥我们的一直是一条鳕鱼！”他们嘟嘟囔囔，“这可大大有损咱们的体面。”
他养的狗也朝他龇起牙来。可尽管他已成了这么个悲剧人物，对他们他几乎全没在意。面对如此可怕的证据，他需要找回的不是手下对他的信心，而是他自己对自己的信心。他感觉到，那个“我”正在从他身上溜走。“老伙计，别丢下我呀。”他用嘶哑的嗓音求它。
他阴沉的天性里，跟所有伟大的海盗一样，还藏着几分女性的心思。这有时会带给他一点直觉。猛然间，他想到试试猜谜游戏。
“虎克，”他大声问，“你还有另一副嗓音吗？”
彼得从来拒绝不了一个游戏，快快活活地用自己的声音回答：“有啊。”
“还有另一个名字吗？”
“是植物吗？”虎克问。
“不是。”
“矿物？”
“不是。”
“动物？”
“成年男人？”
“不！”这一声回答，响得满是轻蔑。
“男孩？”
“普通男孩？”
“了不起的男孩？”
这一回，温蒂听到响亮的回答是“是”，心里真不是滋味。
“你在英格兰吗？”
“不在。”
“你在这儿吗？”
虎克彻底糊涂了。“你们来问他几个问题。”他一边擦着湿漉漉的额头，一边对另外两个人说。
斯密想了想。“我一件也想不出来。”他遗憾地说。
“猜不着，猜不着！”彼得学着雄鸡啼叫，“你们认输了吗？”
当然，他一得意，就叫游戏玩过了头。那几个坏蛋看出了机会。
“是呀，是呀。”他们迫不及待地回答。
“那好，”他大叫，“我就是彼得·潘！”
潘！
一瞬间，虎克又是原来的虎克了，斯密和斯塔基也又是他忠心耿耿的爪牙了。
“这下逮着他了！”虎克高喊，“斯密，下水！斯塔基，看住小艇！活要见人，死要见尸。”
他一面说一面跳，彼得快活的声音也同时响起来。
“男孩们，都准备好了吗？”
“遵命，遵命！”潟湖上好几个方向传来回答。
“那就狠狠揍这些海盗！”
这一仗打得短促而激烈。第一个叫对方见血的是约翰。他勇敢地爬上小艇，牢牢揪住斯塔基。两人搏斗得极凶，海盗的短弯刀都给夺出了手。斯塔基扭脱身，翻入水中。约翰跟着跳了下去。小艇独自漂走了。
水面上，这儿那儿冒起一颗脑袋。一道刀光闪过，随即是一声惨叫，或是一声呐喊。混乱中也有人打到了自己人。斯密的开瓶钻刺中了图图的第四根肋骨。反过来，他自己也挨了卷毛一记轻刺。离岩石远些的地方，斯塔基正把斯莱特利和双胞胎逼得节节退让。
这工夫彼得在哪里？他在找更大的猎物。
旁的孩子都是勇敢的男孩，可也不该为他们躲避海盗船长而责怪他们。他的铁爪在他身边划出了一圈死水。男孩们就像受惊的鱼，飞快地逃离那一圈。
可是有一个人并不怕他，有一个人已经准备好了，要跨进那个圈子。
奇怪的是，他们并没有在水里相遇。虎克游到岩石边，要爬上去喘口气。就在同一刻，彼得从对面往上攀。岩石滑得像个圆球，说是攀登，不如说是在爬行。两人都不知道另一方正在过来。双方伸手各自摸索着借力，却碰到了对方的胳膊。他们惊讶地一抬头，脸几乎贴上了脸。就这样，两人相遇了。
有些最伟大的英雄也承认，临交手之前，心里曾经往下一沉。要是彼得那时候也这样，我会承认的。毕竟，眼前这个可是那位海上大厨唯一害怕的人。可彼得心里一点也没往下沉。此刻他只有一种感觉，就是欢喜。他高兴得把那口漂亮的小牙齿咬得咯咯响。只一眨眼，他已从虎克的腰带上拔出一把刀，正要刺下去，忽然发现自己在岩石上占的位置比敌手高。这样打，不公平。他伸出一只手，就要把海盗拉上来。
虎克就在这时候咬了他一口。

叫彼得怔住的并不是疼，而是这太不公平了。他忽然一点办法也没有了，只能惊骇地瞪着眼看。每个孩子头一回受到不公平的对待，都是这样。当他来到你身边做你的孩子，他以为自己有权得到的，归根结底只有一样，就是公平。你对他不公平，往后他仍会爱你，却再也不能完完全全是从前那个男孩了。没有谁能把头一回受的不公平全然抛在脑后。谁都不能，只有彼得例外。这种事，他常常碰上，却又一回回忘得干干净净。我想，这才是他跟其余所有人真正不同的地方。
所以，这回碰上这种事，对他仍像是头一回。他只能望着，一点办法都没有。那只铁手在他身上连抓了两下。

过了几分钟，别的男孩看见虎克在水里拼命划着，直奔海盗船而去。那张可憎的脸上已没有得意之色，只有一片惨白的恐惧。鳄鱼正在他身后穷追不舍。换个时候，男孩们一定会游在旁边喝彩。如今他们却都心里不安：彼得和温蒂同时不见了。他们游遍了潟湖找他们，高声喊两人的名字。后来他们找着小艇，便乘它回家，一路还喊着“彼得！温蒂！”回答他们的只有美人鱼嘲弄的笑声。“他们准是游回去了，或者飞回去了。”男孩们这样下了结论。其实他们并没有多着急，因为他们对彼得十分有信心。他们还像一般男孩那样偷着乐：这下可以晚点上床啦，而且全要怪温蒂妈妈！
等他们的说话声渐渐远去，潟湖上落下冰冷的沉寂。接着，传来一声微弱的呼喊。
“救命，救命！”
两道小小的身影正被水浪拍在岩石上。女孩昏了过去，躺在男孩的胳膊上。彼得用尽最后一点力气，把她拉上岩石，自己也在她身边躺倒。就在他也要昏过去的那一刻，他看见海水正在上涨。他知道，他们很快就会被淹没，可他已经无能为力。
他们肩并肩躺着的时候，一条美人鱼握住了温蒂的双脚，轻轻把她往水里拉。彼得觉得她正从自己身边滑走，猛地惊醒，赶得恰恰好，及时把她拉了回来。可他不得不把实情告诉她。
“温蒂，我们在岩石上，”他说，“可这块岩石越来越小了。马上水就要漫过去了。”
她这时还没明白。
“我们得走呀。”她说，话里几乎还带着点轻快。
“是呀。”他微弱地答道。
“我们是游走，还是飞走呢，彼得？”
他非得对她说了。
“温蒂，你觉得，不用我帮忙，你能独自游到或是飞到岛上去吗？”
她不得不承认，自己已经太累了。
他呻吟了一声。
“你怎么了？”她立刻为他担起心来。
“我帮不了你，温蒂。虎克弄伤了我。我既不能飞，也不能游。”
“你是说，我们两个都要淹死吗？”
“你看这水，涨得多快。”
他们伸手蒙住眼睛，不愿意再看。他们以为，自己就要不再存在了。他们就这么坐着，忽然，有样东西轻得像一个吻，擦过彼得的身子，停在那里。它仿佛在怯生生地问：“我能帮上什么忙吗？”
那是一只风筝的尾巴。几天以前迈克尔做的风筝，从他手里挣脱出去，飘走了。
“迈克尔的风筝。”彼得说，一点也没提起精神。可就在下一刻，他已抓住尾巴，把风筝往自己跟前拉。
“它能把迈克尔从地上带起来，”他叫道，“为什么不能把你带走呢？”
“带上我们两个人！”
“它托不起两个人。迈克尔跟卷毛试过。”
“那我们抽签吧。”温蒂勇敢地说。
“叫一位女士抽签？决不。”他已把风筝尾巴系在她身上。她紧紧抱住他，不肯撇下他独自走。可彼得说了声“再见，温蒂”，就把她推出岩石。没过几分钟，她就被风筝带出了他的视线。潟湖上只剩彼得一个人。
露出水面的岩石已经很小了，不多久就要整个淹没。淡淡的光蹑着脚尖越过水面。又过了一会儿，世上最动听、也最忧伤的声音传来。那是美人鱼们在向月亮呼唤。
彼得跟别的男孩不太一样。可这回，他到底害怕了。一阵颤抖掠过他全身，像一道寒战掠过海面。可是海上的寒战总是一道接着一道，直到接连有几百道，彼得却只打了这么一个寒战。下一刻，他已再次挺身站在岩石上，脸上带着那个熟悉的笑，心里有面鼓在敲。那鼓声在说：“去死一回，那可是一场天大的冒险。”

source_paragraphs: The last sounds Peter heard before he was quite alone were the mermaids retiring one by one to their bedchambers under the sea. He was too far away to hear their doors shut; but every door in the coral caves where they live rings a tiny bell when it opens or closes (as in all the nicest houses on the mainland), and he heard the bells.

Steadily the waters rose till they were nibbling at his feet; and to pass the time until they made their final gulp, he watched the only thing moving on the lagoon. He thought it was a piece of floating paper, perhaps part of the kite, and wondered idly how long it would take to drift ashore.

Presently he noticed as an odd thing that it was undoubtedly out upon the lagoon with some definite purpose, for it was fighting the tide, and sometimes winning; and when it won, Peter, always sympathetic to the weaker side, could not help clapping; it was such a gallant piece of paper.

It was not really a piece of paper; it was the Never bird, making desperate efforts to reach Peter on her nest. By working her wings, in a way she had learned since the nest fell into the water, she was able to some extent to guide her strange craft, but by the time Peter recognised her she was very exhausted. She had come to save him, to give him her nest, though there were eggs in it. I rather wonder at the bird, for though he had been nice to her, he had also sometimes tormented her. I can suppose only that, like Mrs. Darling and the rest of them, she was melted because he had all his first teeth.

She called out to him what she had come for, and he called out to her what was she doing there; but of course neither of them understood the other's language. In fanciful stories people can talk to the birds freely, and I wish for the moment I could pretend that this was such a story, and say that Peter replied intelligently to the Never bird; but truth is best, and I want to tell only what really happened. Well, not only could they not understand each other, but they forgot their manners.

'I--want--you--to--get--into--the--nest,' the bird called, speaking as slowly and distinctly as possible, 'and--then--you--can--drift--ashore, but--I--am--too--tired--to--bring--it--any--nearer--so--you--must-- try--to--swim--to--it.'
'What are you quacking about?' Peter answered. 'Why don't you let the nest drift as usual?'
'I--want--you--' the bird said, and repeated it all over.
Then Peter tried slow and distinct.
'What--are--you--quacking--about?' and so on.
The Never bird became irritated; they have very short tempers.
'You dunderheaded little jay,' she screamed, 'why don't you do as I tell you?'
Peter felt that she was calling him names, and at a venture he retorted hotly:
'So are you!'
Then rather curiously they both snapped out the same remark:
'Shut up!'
'Shut up!'

Nevertheless the bird was determined to save him if she could, and by one last mighty effort she propelled the nest against the rock. Then up she flew; deserting her eggs, so as to make her meaning clear.

Then at last he understood, and clutched the nest and waved his thanks to the bird as she fluttered overhead. It was not to receive his thanks, however, that she hung there in the sky; it was not even to watch him get into the nest; it was to see what he did with her eggs.

There were two large white eggs, and Peter lifted them up and reflected. The bird covered her face with her wings, so as not to see the last of her eggs; but she could not help peeping between the feathers.

I forget whether I have told you that there was a stave on the rock, driven into it by some buccaneers of long ago to mark the site of buried treasure. The children had discovered the glittering hoard, and when in mischievous mood used to fling showers of moidores, diamonds, pearls and pieces of eight to the gulls, who pounced upon them for food, and then flew away, raging at the scurvy trick that had been played upon them. The stave was still there, and on it Starkey had hung his hat, a deep tarpaulin, watertight, with a broad brim. Peter put the eggs into this hat and set it on the lagoon. It floated beautifully.

The Never bird saw at once what he was up to, and screamed her admiration of him; and, alas, Peter crowed his agreement with her. Then he got into the nest, reared the stave in it as a mast, and hung up his shirt for a sail. At the same moment the bird fluttered down upon the hat and once more sat snugly on her eggs. She drifted in one direction, and he was borne off in another, both cheering.

Of course when Peter landed he beached his barque in a place where the bird would easily find it; but the hat was such a great success that she abandoned the nest. It drifted about till it went to pieces, and often Starkey came to the shore of the lagoon, and with many bitter feelings watched the bird sitting on his hat. As we shall not see her again, it may be worth mentioning here that all Never birds now build in that shape of nest, with a broad brim on which the youngsters take an airing.

Great were the rejoicings when Peter reached the home under the ground almost as soon as Wendy, who had been carried hither and thither by the kite. Every boy had adventures to tell; but perhaps the biggest adventure of all was that they were several hours late for bed. This so inflated them that they did various dodgy things to get staying up still longer, such as demanding bandages; but Wendy, though glorying in having them all home again safe and sound, was scandalised by the lateness of the hour, and cried, 'To bed, to bed,' in a voice that had to be obeyed. Next day, however, she was awfully tender, and gave out bandages to every one; and they played till bed-time at limping about and carrying their arms in slings.
translated_paragraphs: 在彻底只剩彼得一人以前，他最后听见的是美人鱼们一个个退回海底卧室的声音。他离得太远，听不见她们关门。可她们住的珊瑚洞里，每扇门一开一合，总有只小铃轻轻一响，跟大陆上所有最讲究的人家一样。他听见的是那些铃。
水在不紧不慢地上涨，一直涨到开始啃咬他的脚。等它张口把自己囫囵吞下去以前，总得找点什么消磨时间。于是，彼得望着潟湖上唯一动着的一样东西。他以为是片漂浮的纸，也许是风筝的一部分，漫不经心地猜它要漂多久才能到岸。
不一会儿，他却注意到一件怪事：那纸片到湖面上来，显然怀着一个明明白白的目的。它在跟潮水作战，而且有时还会打赢。彼得向来偏向弱小的一方，每逢纸片赢了，便忍不住为它拍手。多么英勇的一张纸呀。
那其实根本不是纸，是永无鸟。她拼了命，要坐着鸟窝赶到彼得跟前。自从鸟窝落水以来，她学会了一种拍翅膀的办法，多少能使这艘古怪的船听她掌舵。可等彼得认出是她，她已累得精疲力竭。她是来救他的，要把鸟窝让给他，尽管里头还有她的蛋。说真的，我还挺佩服这只鸟的。彼得固然待她很好，有时候却也会捉弄她，叫她吃尽苦头。我只能猜，是他那满口一颗也没掉的乳牙，让她跟达林太太和其余那些人一样，见了就心软。
她冲他叫，说明自己的来意；他冲她问，跑来这里干什么。当然，他们谁也听不懂对方的话。在编出来的奇妙故事里，人可以跟鸟随便交谈。我倒希望，眼下也能假装这是那样一个故事，说彼得对永无鸟作了个十分聪明的回答。可还是实话最好。我只想讲真正发生过的事。好吧，他们不但听不懂对方，连礼貌也忘光了。
“我、要、你、爬、进、窝、里、去，”鸟大声叫，她说得尽可能慢，也尽可能清楚，“进、了、窝、你、就、能、漂、上、岸。可、我、太、累、了，不、能、再、把、它、送、得、更、近，你、得、设、法、自、己、游、过、来。”
“你呱呱地吵些什么呀？”彼得答道，“怎么不跟平常一样，让窝自己漂呢？”
“我、要、你……”鸟说着，把那通话从头到尾又讲一遍。
这回轮到彼得试着把话放慢、说清楚了。
“你、在、呱、呱、吵、些、什、么？”等等等等。
永无鸟生气了。这种鸟的脾气向来很急。
“你这只蠢头蠢脑的小松鸦！”她尖声叫道，“你怎么不照我的话去做？”
彼得听出她像是在骂自己，也没弄明白她骂的是什么，就赌一把，火辣辣地回了一句：
“你才是呢！”
接着，颇为奇妙地，他们两个竟同时恶狠狠地说出了同一句话：
“闭嘴！”
“闭嘴！”
尽管如此，那鸟仍打定主意，只要力气使得出，她就要救他。她最后猛使一把劲，把鸟窝推到了岩石边。然后她飞起来，撇下自己的蛋，好叫他看明白她是什么意思。
他终于明白了。他一手抓住鸟窝，朝盘旋在头顶的鸟挥手致谢。可她留在空中，并不是为了领他的谢意，甚至也不是为了看他爬进窝去。她要看他怎样处置她的蛋。
窝里有两个大白蛋。彼得把它们拿起来，想了想。永无鸟用翅膀遮住脸，不忍心看自己的蛋到这儿就完了。可她仍忍不住，从羽毛缝里偷瞧。

我忘了有没有告诉过你，岩石上立着一根木杆。很久以前，有几个海盗把它钉在这里，给埋藏宝藏的地点做记号。孩子们早已发现了那堆闪闪发光的宝物。每逢心血来潮要恶作剧，他们就把葡萄牙金币、钻石、珍珠和八里亚尔银币像下雨一样撒向海鸥。海鸥以为是吃的，一扑下来，发现上了这种可恶的当，又怒气冲冲地飞走。木杆还在那儿。先前斯塔基把帽子挂在上头，那是顶帽筒很深的防水油布帽，帽檐又宽。彼得把两只蛋放进帽子，将帽子推到湖面上。它浮得漂亮极了。
永无鸟立刻看懂了他的用意，尖声叫起来表示钦佩。可叹的是，彼得听了，也学了一声雄鸡鸣，表示自己完全同意。接着，他爬进鸟窝，把木杆立起来当桅杆，脱下衬衫挂在上面作帆。与此同时，鸟拍着翅膀落到帽子上，又安安稳稳地坐在了蛋上。她往一个方向漂，他被风送往另一个方向，两个都欢呼着。
彼得上岸以后，当然把他那艘小船拖到鸟很容易找着的地方。可是那顶帽子实在太好用，她连原先的窝也不要了。鸟窝漂来漂去，最后散了架。斯塔基常常来到潟湖岸边，满心苦涩地望着那只鸟坐在他的帽子上。往后我们不会再遇到她，还是在这里提一句吧。如今，所有的永无鸟都把窝做成那顶帽子的样式，有一圈宽宽的檐，雏鸟们就在檐上透气。

彼得跟温蒂差不多同时回到了地下的家。温蒂先前叫风筝带得东飘西荡，回来也没早他多少。这下可欢腾极了。每个男孩都有冒险可讲；不过，最了不起的冒险，也许是他们过了睡觉时间好几个钟头还没上床。这件事叫他们兴奋得有点得意忘形，纷纷耍起花样想再多待一会儿，譬如非要人来裹绷带。温蒂虽然为大家平平安安重新团聚而满心欢喜，却也为时间如此之晚大为震惊，便用一种非听不可的声音大喊：“上床，上床！”不过第二天她又格外温柔，给每个人都发了绷带。他们或是一瘸一拐地走，或是用吊带挂起一条胳膊，就这么演着玩，直到又该上床为止。

source_paragraphs: One important result of the brush on the lagoon was that it made the redskins their friends. Peter had saved Tiger Lily from a dreadful fate, and now there was nothing she and her braves would not do for him. All night they sat above, keeping watch over the home under the ground and awaiting the big attack by the pirates which obviously could not be much longer delayed. Even by day they hung about, smoking the pipe of peace, and looking almost as if they wanted tit-bits to eat.
They called Peter the Great White Father, prostrating themselves before him; and he liked this tremendously, so that it was not really good for him.
'The great white father,' he would say to them in a very lordly manner, as they grovelled at his feet, 'is glad to see the Piccaninny warriors protecting his wigwam from the pirates.'
'Me Tiger Lily,' that lovely creature would reply. 'Peter Pan save me, me his velly nice friend. Me no let pirates hurt him.'
She was far too pretty to cringe in this way, but Peter thought it his due, and he would answer condescendingly, 'It is good. Peter Pan has spoken.'

Always when he said, 'Peter Pan has spoken,' it meant that they must now shut up, and they accepted it humbly in that spirit; but they were by no means so respectful to the other boys, whom they looked upon as just ordinary braves. They said 'How-do?' to them, and things like that; and what annoyed the boys was that Peter seemed to think this all right.

Secretly Wendy sympathised with them a little, but she was far too loyal a housewife to listen to any complaints against father. 'Father knows best,' she always said, whatever her private opinion must be. Her private opinion was that the redskins should not call her a squaw.

We have now reached the evening that was to be known among them as the Night of Nights, because of its adventures and their upshot. The day, as if quietly gathering its forces, had been almost uneventful, and now the redskins in their blankets were at their posts above, while, below, the children were having their evening meal; all except Peter, who had gone out to get the time. The way you got the time on the island was to find the crocodile, and then stay near him till the clock struck.

This meal happened to be a make-believe tea, and they sat round the board, guzzling in their greed; and really, what with their chatter and recriminations, the noise, as Wendy said, was positively deafening. To be sure, she did not mind noise, but she simply would not have them grabbing things, and then excusing themselves by saying that Tootles had pushed their elbow. There was a fixed rule that they must never hit back at meals, but should refer the matter of dispute to Wendy by raising the right arm politely and saying, 'I complain of so-and-so'; but what usually happened was that they forgot to do this or did it too much.
'Silence,' cried Wendy when for the twentieth time she had told them that they were not all to speak at once. 'Is your calabash empty, Slightly darling?'
'Not quite empty, mummy,' Slightly said, after looking into an imaginary mug.
'He hasn't even begun to drink his milk,' Nibs interposed.
This was telling, and Slightly seized his chance.
'I complain of Nibs,' he cried promptly.
John, however, had held up his hand first.
'Well, John?'
'May I sit in Peter's chair, as he is not here?'
'Sit in father's chair, John!' Wendy was scandalised. 'Certainly not.'
'He is not really our father,' John answered. 'He didn't even know how a father does till I showed him.'
This was grumbling. 'We complain of John,' cried the twins.
Tootles held up his hand. He was so much the humblest of them, indeed he was the only humble one, that Wendy was specially gentle with him.
'I don't suppose,' Tootles said diffidently, 'that I could be father.'
'No, Tootles.'
Once Tootles began, which was not very often, he had a silly way of going on.
'As I can't be father,' he said heavily, 'I don't suppose, Michael, you would let me be baby?'
'No, I won't,' Michael rapped out. He was already in his basket.
'As I can't be baby,' Tootles said, getting heavier and heavier, 'do you think I could be a twin?'
'No, indeed,' replied the twins; 'it's awfully difficult to be a twin.'
'As I can't be anything important,' said Tootles, 'would any of you like to see me do a trick?'
'No,' they all replied.
Then at last he stopped. 'I hadn't really any hope,' he said.
The hateful telling broke out again.
'Slightly is coughing on the table.'
'The twins began with mammee-apples.'
'Curly is taking both tappa rolls and yams.'
'Nibs is speaking with his mouth full.'
'I complain of the twins.'
'I complain of Curly.'
'I complain of Nibs.'
'Oh dear, oh dear,' cried Wendy, 'I'm sure I sometimes think that children are more trouble than they are worth.'
She told them to clear away, and sat down to her work-basket: a heavy load of stockings and every knee with a hole in it as usual.
'Wendy,' remonstrated Michael, 'I'm too big for a cradle.'
'I must have somebody in a cradle,' she said almost tartly, 'and you are the littlest. A cradle is such a nice homely thing to have about a house.'

While she sewed they played around her; such a group of happy faces and dancing limbs lit up by that romantic fire. It had become a very familiar scene this in the home under the ground, but we are looking on it for the last time.
There was a step above, and Wendy, you may be sure, was the first to recognise it.
'Children, I hear your father's step. He likes you to meet him at the door.'
Above, the redskins crouched before Peter.
'Watch well, braves. I have spoken.'
And then, as so often before, the gay children dragged him from his tree. As so often before, but never again.
He had brought nuts for the boys as well as the correct time for Wendy.
'Peter, you just spoil them, you know,' Wendy simpered.
'Ah, old lady,' said Peter, hanging up his gun.
'It was me told him mothers are called old lady,' Michael whispered to Curly.
'I complain of Michael,' said Curly instantly.
The first twin came to Peter. 'Father, we want to dance.'
'Dance away, my little man,' said Peter, who was in high good humour.
'But we want you to dance.'
Peter was really the best dancer among them, but he pretended to be scandalised.
'Me! My old bones would rattle.'
'And mummy too.'
'What,' cried Wendy, 'the mother of such an armful, dance!'
'But on a Saturday night,' Slightly insinuated.

It was not really Saturday night, at least it may have been, for they had long lost count of the days; but always if they wanted to do anything special they said this was Saturday night, and then they did it.
'Of course it is Saturday night, Peter,' Wendy said, relenting.
'People of our figure, Wendy.'
'But it is only among our own progeny.'
'True, true.'
So they were told they could dance, but they must put on their nighties first.

'Ah, old lady,' Peter said aside to Wendy, warming himself by the fire and looking down at her as she sat turning a heel, 'there is nothing more pleasant, of an evening for you and me when the day's toil is over than to rest by the fire with the little ones near by.'
'It is sweet, Peter, isn't it?' Wendy said, frightfully gratified. 'Peter, I think Curly has your nose.'
'Michael takes after you.'
She went to him and put her hand on his shoulder.
'Dear Peter,' she said, 'with such a large family, of course, I have now passed my best, but you don't want to change me, do you?'
'No, Wendy.'
Certainly he did not want a change, but he looked at her uncomfortably; blinking, you know, like one not sure whether he was awake or asleep.
'Peter, what is it?'
'I was just thinking,' he said, a little scared. 'It is only make-believe, isn't it, that I am their father?'
'Oh yes,' Wendy said primly.
'You see,' he continued apologetically, 'it would make me seem so old to be their real father.'
'But they are ours, Peter, yours and mine.'
'But not really, Wendy?' he asked anxiously.
'Not if you don't wish it,' she replied; and she distinctly heard his sigh of relief. 'Peter,' she asked, trying to speak firmly, 'what are your exact feelings for me?'
'Those of a devoted son, Wendy.'
'I thought so,' she said, and went and sat by herself at the extreme end of the room.
'You are so queer,' he said, frankly puzzled, 'and Tiger Lily is just the same. There is something she wants to be to me, but she says it is not my mother.'
'No, indeed, it is not,' Wendy replied with frightful emphasis. Now we know why she was prejudiced against the redskins.
'Then what is it?'
'It isn't for a lady to tell.'
'Oh, very well,' Peter said, a little nettled. 'Perhaps Tinker Bell will tell me.'
'Oh yes, Tinker Bell will tell you,' Wendy retorted scornfully. 'She is an abandoned little creature.'
Here Tink, who was in her boudoir, eavesdropping, squeaked out something impudent.
'She says she glories in being abandoned,' Peter interpreted.
He had a sudden idea. 'Perhaps Tink wants to be my mother?'
'You silly ass!' cried Tinker Bell in a passion.
She had said it so often that Wendy needed no translation.

'I almost agree with her,' Wendy snapped. Fancy Wendy snapping. But she had been much tried, and she little knew what was to happen before the night was out. If she had known she would not have snapped.

None of them knew. Perhaps it was best not to know. Their ignorance gave them one more glad hour; and as it was to be their last hour on the island, let us rejoice that there were sixty glad minutes in it. They sang and danced in their night-gowns. Such a deliciously creepy song it was, in which they pretended to be frightened at their own shadows; little witting that so soon shadows would close in upon them, from whom they would shrink in real fear. So uproariously gay was the dance, and how they buffeted each other on the bed and out of it! It was a pillow fight rather than a dance, and when it was finished, the pillows insisted on one bout more, like partners who know that they may never meet again. The stories they told, before it was time for Wendy's good-night story! Even Slightly tried to tell a story that night, but the beginning was so fearfully dull that it appalled even himself, and he said gloomily:
'Yes, it is a dull beginning. I say, let us pretend that it is the end.'

And then at last they all got into bed for Wendy's story, the story they loved best, the story Peter hated. Usually when she began to tell this story he left the room or put his hands over his ears; and possibly if he had done either of those things this time they might all still be on the island. But to-night he remained on his stool; and we shall see what happened.
translated_paragraphs: 潟湖上那场交锋有一个很重要的结果：印第安人同他们成了朋友。彼得救了虎莲公主，叫她免于可怕的死难。如今，为了他，公主和她的勇士们什么都肯做。他们整夜坐在上面，替地下的家站岗，等候海盗发动一场大进攻。明摆着的，这场进攻不会再拖多久了。就连白天，他们也在附近转悠，抽着和平烟斗，看上去几乎有点像在等人给几口好吃的。
他们称彼得为“伟大的白人父亲”，在他面前伏地行礼。他喜欢得不得了，其实这种喜欢对他可不大好。
他们拜倒在他脚下，他便神气十足地对他们说：“伟大的白人父亲很高兴见到皮卡尼尼部落的勇士们，守着他的帐篷，不让海盗来犯。”
“我，虎莲，”那位漂亮的姑娘答道，“彼得·潘救我，我是他很好很好的朋友。我不让海盗伤他。”
她生得那样美，本不必如此屈身低头。彼得却觉得这是自己理当受的礼遇，便屈尊答道：“很好。彼得·潘的话说完了。”
每逢他说“彼得·潘的话说完了”，就是叫他们现在也得闭嘴。他们谦恭地照这个意思领会了。可他们对其余的男孩就远没这样尊敬。他们只把男孩们当作寻常的勇士，碰面便招呼一声“你好哇”，如此而已。最叫男孩们烦恼的是，彼得看起来还觉得这很应该。
私下里，温蒂有一点同情他们。可她是位太忠于职守的主妇，不肯听人家说爸爸的坏话。“爸爸懂得最多。”不管心里是怎么想的，她总是这么说。她自己心里想的是，这群印第安人不该管她叫“婆娘”。
现在，该讲那个夜晚了。因为那一夜的冒险，还有冒险带来的结果，他们后来都管它叫“夜晚中的夜晚”。整个白天几乎什么也没发生，仿佛是它悄悄积蓄着力量。此刻，上面，印第安勇士们裹着毯子，各守各的岗位。下面，孩子们在吃晚饭。只有彼得不在，他出去对时间了。岛上要知道几点钟，得先找到那条鳄鱼，再待在它身旁，等着钟敲响。
这顿晚茶恰好是装着吃的。他们围着桌子，个个贪吃得狼吞虎咽，嘴里又叽叽喳喳，互相指责。借温蒂的话说，那动静简直能震聋人的耳朵。她倒不怕闹，可她绝不许他们一伸手就抢东西，还要给自己找借口，说是图图碰了他的胳膊肘。吃饭的时候不许还手，这是硬规矩。有了争执，得彬彬有礼地举起右手，向温蒂呈报：“我要告某某的状。”可通常是，他们要么忘了这条规矩，要么又用得太勤。
“安静！”温蒂已经第二十回告诉他们，不许人人同时说话了。“亲爱的斯莱特利，你的葫芦瓢喝空了吗？”
“还没全空，妈妈。”斯莱特利朝一个并不存在的杯子里看了看，说。
“他连牛奶都还没开始喝呢。”尼布斯插嘴道。
这就叫打小报告。斯莱特利抓住了机会。
“我要告尼布斯的状！”他马上叫道。
不过，约翰的手比他先举起来。
“好了，约翰，你有什么事？”
“彼得既然不在，我可以坐他的椅子吗？”
“坐爸爸的椅子，约翰！”温蒂大为震惊，“当然不可以。”
“他又不真是我们的爸爸。”约翰答道，“我没做给他看之前，他连当爸爸要怎么当都不知道。”
这就叫发牢骚。“我们要告约翰的状！”双胞胎叫道。
图图举起手。他远比其他孩子谦逊，事实上只有他一个人懂得谦逊，温蒂待他也就格外温柔。
“我看，”图图很没把握地说，“我大概不能当爸爸吧？”
“不能，图图。”
图图不常开口，可他有个傻习惯：一开了头，就会接着不停说下去。
“既然我不能当爸爸，”他闷闷地说，“那个，迈克尔，我想你大概也不肯让我当小宝宝吧？”
“不，我不肯。”迈克尔马上顶了回去。他已经坐在自己的篮子里了。
“既然我也不能当小宝宝，”图图越说越沉闷，“那你们觉得，我能不能做个双胞胎呢？”
“当然不能，”双胞胎回答，“当双胞胎是难得不得了的。”
“既然要紧的人物我一个也当不上，”图图说，“你们可有谁想看我变个戏法？”
“不想。”大家都答道。
这回他终于住了口。“我本来也没真抱什么希望。”他说。
讨厌的小报告又此起彼伏了。
“斯莱特利朝桌子上咳嗽。”
“双胞胎先吃了曼密苹果。”
“卷毛拿了塔帕卷，又拿山药。”
“尼布斯嘴里塞得满满的还在说话。”
“我要告双胞胎的状。”
“我要告卷毛的状。”
“我要告尼布斯的状。”
“哎呀，老天爷！”温蒂叫道，“有时候我真觉得，养孩子惹的麻烦，比得的好处多得多。”
她吩咐他们收拾桌子，自己到针线篮前坐下。袜子沉甸甸一大堆，跟往常一样，每只袜子的膝盖处都有个洞。
“温蒂，”迈克尔抗议道，“我这么大，不能再睡摇篮了。”
“我总得有个人睡摇篮，”她答得几乎有点不耐烦了，“你是最小的。家里放个摇篮多好，让家更像个家。”
她做针线的工夫，他们在身边玩耍。多快乐的一圈小脸，多少跳个不停的手脚，在那一炉富有诗意的火光里闪动。这已是地下的家里再熟悉不过的情景。可是，我们眼下看见的，却是最后一回。
头顶上面响起脚步声。你尽可料到，头一个认出那脚步声的是温蒂。
“孩子们，我听见爸爸的脚步了。他喜欢你们到门口去接他。”
在上面，印第安勇士们正蹲伏在彼得面前。
“好好守着，勇士们。我的话说完了。”
接着，跟先前不知多少回一样，快活的孩子们把他从树洞里拉了出来。跟先前一样，可往后再也不会有了。
除了给温蒂带回准确的时间，他还给男孩们带回来些坚果。
“彼得呀，你可真要把他们宠坏了。”温蒂抿着嘴笑道。
“啊，老太婆。”彼得说着，把枪挂起来。
“是我教他，管当妈妈的要叫老太婆。”迈克尔悄声对卷毛说。
“我要告迈克尔的状。”卷毛立刻说。
双胞胎中的老大来到彼得跟前。“爸爸，我们想跳舞。”
“跳吧，小家伙。”彼得的兴致正高。
“可我们也想让你跳。”
彼得其实是他们这群人中舞跳得最好的一个，他却装出惊骇的神情。
“我！我这一身老骨头都要咯吱咯吱响了。”
“妈妈也得跳。”
“什么！”温蒂叫道，“我两只胳膊抱满了孩子都抱不过来，当这么多孩子的妈妈，还要跳舞！”
“可今天是星期六晚上呀。”斯莱特利试探着提醒他们。
其实并不是星期六晚上；至少也可能是，他们早就忘记了日子。可他们每逢想做件特别的事，总先说今天是星期六晚上，然后就去做了。
“彼得，今天当然是星期六晚上呀。”温蒂已经心软了。
“可咱们这把年纪，这种体态，温蒂。”
“又只在咱们亲生的儿女面前。”
“那倒是，那倒是。”
于是，他们宣布可以跳舞，不过得先把睡衣换上。
“啊，老太婆，”彼得在炉火前烤着身子，低头看着坐在那里补袜跟的温蒂，悄悄对她说，“一天的辛劳都过去了，傍晚咱们两个在炉火边歇歇，身旁又有小家伙们陪着，再没有比这更舒心的事啦。”
“多美呀，彼得，是不是？”温蒂高兴得不得了。“彼得，我看卷毛的鼻子长得像你。”
“迈克尔长得像你。”
她走到他身旁，把一只手放在他的肩头。
“亲爱的彼得，”她说，“我养了这么一大家子孩子，当然已过了最好的年华。可你不会想把我换掉吧？”
“不会，温蒂。”
他自然没想换掉谁。可他望着她有些不自在。你知道，一个人弄不清自己究竟醒着还是在梦里的时候，眼睛就会那么一眨一眨的。
“彼得，怎么啦？”
“我只是在想，”他说，有点害怕，“我是他们的爸爸，这件事只是装着玩的，对不对？”
“哦，自然啦。”温蒂端端正正地说。
“你瞧，”他带着歉意解释下去，“要是我真是他们的爸爸，我显得该有多老呀。”
“可他们是咱们的呀，彼得，是你和我的孩子。”
“可不是真的，对吧，温蒂？”他着急地问。
“只要你不愿意，就不是真的。”她回答。她清清楚楚地听见，他松了一口气。“彼得，”她极力把声音放平稳，“你对我究竟是什么感情？”
“一个孝顺儿子对妈妈的感情呀，温蒂。”
“我料到了。”她说。她走开去，独自在房间最远的那头坐下。
“你真奇怪，”他实实在在想不通，“虎莲公主也跟你一样。她也想当我的什么人，却偏说她要当的不是我的妈妈。”
“自然不是，的的确确不是。”温蒂咬字咬得厉害。这下我们知道她为什么对印第安人有点成见了。
“那是什么呢？”
“这种话不该由女士来说。”
“哦，那好吧，”彼得有点恼火，“兴许小叮当肯告诉我。”
“哦，当然，小叮当准会告诉你。”温蒂轻蔑地回了他一句，“她这个小东西，一点也不知羞。”
这时，躲在闺房里偷听的叮当尖声回了句无礼的话。
“她说，她还以不知羞为荣呢。”彼得翻译道。
他忽然来了个念头。“叮当，也许你想当我妈妈？”
“你这傻驴！”小叮当气愤地叫道。
这句话她叫得实在太多了，温蒂不用再听翻译。
“我都快要同意她了。”温蒂没好气地说。你想得到吗，温蒂也会没好气！可她实在很受委屈，又一点不知道，这个夜晚结束以前还会发生什么。要是知道，她就不会用这种口气说话了。

他们谁都不知道。也许不知道反倒更好。这份不知情又给了他们一个快乐的钟头。那将是他们在岛上最后的一个钟头，就让我们替他们高兴吧，里面有完整的六十分钟快乐。他们穿着睡衣又唱又跳。他们唱的，是一首又好玩又叫人起鸡皮疙瘩的歌，要装作连自己的影子也怕。哪里知道，再过不久，真会有些黑影围拢来，叫他们真的害怕得直往后缩。那支舞跳得多么热闹，多么快活。床上床下，你推我打！那与其说是跳舞，倒不如说是枕头大战。跳完了，枕头还非要再战一场，活像两个舞伴知道此生也许再也见不到了。还不到温蒂讲睡前故事的时候，他们自己先讲了多少故事！那晚，连斯莱特利都试着讲一个，可他的开头乏味得可怕，连自己也给吓住，只好阴郁地说：
“是的，这开头可真乏味。嗳，要不，咱们索性假装这就是结尾吧。”
到了末了，大家总算都钻进被窝，等温蒂讲她的故事。他们最爱听这个，彼得最恨的也是这个。往常她只要一开始讲，他便走出屋去，或者用两手捂住耳朵。兴许这一回他若也照样做了，他们全都还在岛上呢。可是这天晚上，他坐在自己的凳子上没走。结果如何，我们就要看到了。

source_paragraphs: 'Listen, then,' said Wendy, settling down to her story, with Michael at her feet and seven boys in the bed. 'There was once a gentleman----'
'I had rather he had been a lady,' Curly said.
'I wish he had been a white rat,' said Nibs.
'Quiet,' their mother admonished them. 'There was a lady also, and----'
'O mummy,' cried the first twin, 'you mean that there is a lady also, don't you? She is not dead, is she?'
'Oh no.'
'I am awfully glad she isn't dead,' said Tootles. 'Are you glad, John?'
'Of course I am.'
'Are you glad, Nibs?'
'Rather.'
'Are you glad, Twins?'
'We are just glad.'
'Oh dear,' sighed Wendy.
'Little less noise there,' Peter called out, determined that she should have fair play, however beastly a story it might be in his opinion.
'The gentleman's name,' Wendy continued, 'was Mr. Darling, and her name was Mrs. Darling.'
'I knew them,' John said, to annoy the others.
'I think I knew them,' said Michael rather doubtfully.
'They were married, you know,' explained Wendy, 'and what do you think they had?'
'White rats,' cried Nibs, inspired.
'No.'
'It's awfully puzzling,' said Tootles, who knew the story by heart.
'Quiet, Tootles. They had three descendants.'
'What is descendants?'
'Well, you are one, Twin.
'Do you hear that, John? I am a descendant.'
'Descendants are only children,' said John.
'Oh dear, oh dear,' sighed Wendy. 'Now these three children had a faithful nurse called Nana; but Mr. Darling was angry with her and chained her up in the yard; and so all the children flew away.'
'It's an awfully good story,' said Nibs.
'They flew away,' Wendy continued, 'to the Neverland, where the lost children are.'
'I just thought they did,' Curly broke in excitedly. 'I don't know how it is, but I just thought they did.'
'O Wendy,' cried Tootles, 'was one of the lost children called Tootles?'
'Yes, he was.'
'I am in a story. Hurrah, I am in a story, Nibs.'
'Hush. Now I want you to consider the feelings of the unhappy parents with all their children flown away.'
'Oo!' they all moaned, though they were not really considering the feelings of the unhappy parents one jot.
'Think of the empty beds!'
'Oo!'
'It's awfully sad,' the first twin said cheerfully.
'I don't see how it can have a happy ending,' said the second twin. 'Do you, Nibs?'
'I'm frightfully anxious.'
'If you knew how great is a mother's love,' Wendy told them triumphantly, 'you would have no fear.' She had now come to the part that Peter hated.
'I do like a mother's love,' said Tootles, hitting Nibs with a pillow. 'Do you like a mother's love, Nibs?'
'I do just,' said Nibs, hitting back.
'You see,' Wendy said complacently, 'our heroine knew that the mother would always leave the window open for her children to fly back by; so they stayed away for years and had a lovely time.'
'Did they ever go back?'

'Let us now,' said Wendy, bracing herself for her finest effort, 'take a peep into the future'; and they all gave themselves the twist that makes peeps into the future easier. 'Years have rolled by; and who is this elegant lady of uncertain age alighting at London Station?'
'O Wendy, who is she?' cried Nibs, every bit as excited as if he didn't know.
'Can it be--yes--no--it is--the fair Wendy!'
'Oh!'
'And who are the two noble portly figures accompanying her, now grown to man's estate? Can they be John and Michael? They are!'
'Oh!'

'"See, dear brothers," says Wendy, pointing upwards, '"there is the window still standing open. Ah, now we are rewarded for our sublime faith in a mother's love." So up they flew to their mummy and daddy; and pen cannot describe the happy scene, over which we draw a veil.'

That was the story, and they were as pleased with it as the fair narrator herself. Everything just as it should be, you see. Off we skip like the most heartless things in the world, which is what children are, but so attractive; and we have an entirely selfish time; and then when we have need of special attention we nobly return for it, confident that we shall be embraced instead of smacked.
So great indeed was their faith in a mother's love that they felt they could afford to be callous for a bit longer.
But there was one there who knew better; and when Wendy finished he uttered a hollow groan.
'What is it, Peter?' she cried, running to him, thinking he was ill. She felt him solicitously, lower down than his chest. 'Where is it, Peter?'
'It isn't that kind of pain,' Peter replied darkly.
'Then what kind is it?'
'Wendy, you are wrong about mothers.'
They all gathered round him in affright, so alarming was his agitation; and with a fine candour he told them what he had hitherto concealed.

'Long ago,' he said, 'I thought like you that my mother would always keep the window open for me; so I stayed away for moons and moons and moons, and then flew back; but the window was barred, for mother had forgotten all about me, and there was another little boy sleeping in my bed.'
I am not sure that this was true, but Peter thought it was true; and it scared them.
'Are you sure mothers are like that?'
'Yes.'
So this was the truth about mothers. The toads!
Still it is best to be careful; and no one knows so quickly as a child when he should give in. 'Wendy, let us go home,' cried John and Michael together.
'Yes,' she said, clutching them.
'Not to-night?' asked the lost boys bewildered. They knew in what they called their hearts that one can get on quite well without a mother, and that it is only the mothers who think you can't.
'At once,' Wendy replied resolutely, for the horrible thought had come to her: 'Perhaps mother is in half mourning by this time.'
This dread made her forgetful of what must be Peter's feelings, and she said to him rather sharply, 'Peter, will you make the necessary arrangements?'
'If you wish it,', he replied, as coolly as if she had asked him to pass the nuts.
Not so much as a sorry-to-lose-you between them! If she did not mind the parting, he was going to show her, was Peter, that neither did he.

But of course he cared very much; and he was so full of wrath against grown-ups, who, as usual, were spoiling everything, that as soon as he got inside his tree he breathed intentionally quick short breaths at the rate of about five to a second. He did this because there is a saying in the Neverland that, every time you breathe, a grown-up dies; and Peter was killing them off vindictively as fast as possible.

Then having given the necessary instructions to the redskins he returned to the home, where an unworthy scene had been enacted in his absence. Panic-stricken at the thought of losing Wendy the lost boys had advanced upon her threateningly.
'It will be worse than before she came,' they cried.
'We shan't let her go.'
'Let's keep her prisoner.'
'Ay, chain her up.'
In her extremity an instinct told her to which of them to turn.
'Tootles,' she cried, 'I appeal to you.'
Was it not strange? she appealed to Tootles, quite the silliest one.
Grandly, however, did Tootles respond. For that one moment he dropped his silliness and spoke with dignity.
'I am just Tootles,' he said, 'and nobody minds me. But the first who does not behave to Wendy like an English gentleman I will blood him severely.'

He drew his hanger; and for that instant his sun was at noon. The others held back uneasily. Then Peter returned, and they saw at once that they would get no support from him. He would keep no girl in the Neverland against her will.
'Wendy,' he said, striding up and down, 'I have asked the redskins to guide you through the wood, as flying tires you so.'
'Thank you, Peter.'
'Then,' he continued, in the short sharp voice of one accustomed to be obeyed, 'Tinker Bell will take you across the sea. Wake her, Nibs.'
Nibs had to knock twice before he got an answer, though Tink had really been sitting up in bed listening for some time.
'Who are you? How dare you? Go away,' she cried.
'You are to get up, Tink,' Nibs called, 'and take Wendy on a journey.'

Of course Tink had been delighted to hear that Wendy was going; but she was jolly well determined not to be her courier, and she said so in still more offensive language. Then she pretended to be asleep again.
'She says she won't,' Nibs exclaimed, aghast at such insubordination, whereupon Peter went sternly toward the young lady's chamber.
'Tink,' he rapped out, 'if you don't get up and dress at once I will open the curtains, and then we shall all see you in your _negligee_.'
This made her leap to the floor. 'Who said I wasn't getting up?' she cried.

In the meantime the boys were gazing very forlornly at Wendy, now equipped with John and Michael for the journey. By this time they were dejected, not merely because they were about to lose her, but also because they felt that she was going off to something nice to which they had not been invited. Novelty was beckoning to them as usual.
Crediting them with a nobler feeling Wendy melted.
'Dear ones,' she said, 'if you will all come with me I feel almost sure I can get my father and mother to adopt you.'
The invitation was meant specially for Peter; but each of the boys was thinking exclusively of himself, and at once they jumped with joy.
'But won't they think us rather a handful?' Nibs asked in the middle of his jump.
'Oh no,' said Wendy, rapidly thinking it out, 'it will only mean having a few beds in the drawing-room; they can be hidden behind screens on first Thursdays.'

'Peter, can we go?' they all cried imploringly. They took it for granted that if they went he would go also, but really they scarcely cared. Thus children are ever ready, when novelty knocks, to desert their dearest ones.
'All right,' Peter replied with a bitter smile; and immediately they rushed to get their things.

'And now, Peter,' Wendy said, thinking she had put everything right, 'I am going to give you your medicine before you go.' She loved to give them medicine, and undoubtedly gave them too much. Of course it was only water, but it was out of a calabash, and she always shook the calabash and counted the drops, which gave it a certain medicinal quality. On this occasion, however, she did not give Peter his draught, for just as she had prepared it, she saw a look on his face that made her heart sink.
'Get your things, Peter,' she cried, shaking.
'No,' he answered, pretending indifference, 'I am not going with you, Wendy.'
'Yes, Peter.'
'No.'
To show that her departure would leave him unmoved, he skipped up and down the room, playing gaily on his heartless pipes. She had to run about after him, though it was rather undignified.
'To find your mother,' she coaxed.
Now, if Peter had ever quite had a mother, he no longer missed her. He could do very well without one. He had thought them out, and remembered only their bad points.
'No, no,' he told Wendy decisively; 'perhaps she would say I was old, and I just want always to be a little boy and to have fun.'
'But, Peter----'
'No.'
And so the others had to be told.
'Peter isn't coming.'

Peter not coming! They gazed blankly at him, their sticks over their backs, and on each stick a bundle. Their first thought was that if Peter was not going he had probably changed his mind about letting them go.
But he was far too proud for that. 'If you find your mothers,' he said darkly, 'I hope you will like them.'
The awful cynicism of this made an uncomfortable impression, and most of them began to look rather doubtful. After all, their faces said, were they not noodles to want to go?
'Now then,' cried Peter, 'no fuss, no blubbering; good-bye, Wendy'; and he held out his hand cheerily, quite as if they must really go now, for he had something important to do.
She had to take his hand, as there was no indication that he would prefer a thimble.
'You will remember about changing your flannels, Peter?' she said, lingering over him. She was always so particular about their flannels.
'Yes.'
'And you will take your medicine?'
'Yes.'
That seemed to be everything; and an awkward pause followed. Peter, however, was not the kind that breaks down before people. 'Are you ready, Tinker Bell?' he called out.
'Ay, ay.'
'Then lead the way.'

Tink darted up the nearest tree; but no one followed her, for it was at this moment that the pirates made their dreadful attack upon the redskins. Above, where all had been so still, the air was rent with shrieks and the clash of steel. Below, there was dead silence. Mouths opened and remained open. Wendy fell on her knees, but her arms were extended toward Peter. All arms were extended to him, as if suddenly blown in his direction; they were beseeching him mutely not to desert them. As for Peter, he seized his sword, the same he thought he had slain Barbecue with; and the lust of battle was in his eye.
translated_paragraphs: “那就听好啦。”温蒂安顿下来，开始讲故事。迈克尔在她脚下，七个男孩在床上。“从前有一位先生——”
“我倒宁愿他是位女士。”卷毛说。
“我巴不得他是只小白鼠。”尼布斯说。
“安静，”他们的妈妈告诫道，“也有一位女士的，而且——”
“哦，妈妈，”双胞胎中的老大叫起来，“你是说，现在也还有这么一位女士，对吧？她没死，对不对？”
“哦，没有。”
“她没死，我真是高兴极了，”图图说，“约翰，你高兴吗？”
“我当然高兴。”
“尼布斯，你高兴吗？”
“那还用说。”
“双胞胎，你们高兴吗？”
“我们可高兴啦。”
“唉，老天爷。”温蒂叹了一口气。
“那边少闹一点。”彼得大声说。这故事在他看来哪怕再讨厌，他也要替讲故事的人讨个公道。
“那位先生的名字，”温蒂讲下去，“叫作达林先生。她的名字叫达林太太。”
“我认识他们。”约翰说，存心气气别人。
“我想我也认识他们。”迈克尔说得不太有把握。
“你们知道，他们结了婚，”温蒂解释道，“你们猜，他们有了什么？”
“小白鼠！”尼布斯灵机一动，叫了出来。
“不对。”
“可真难猜呀。”图图说。其实这故事他已经会背了。
“安静，图图。他们有了三个后代。”
“什么叫后代？”
“嗯，双胞胎，你自己就是个后代。”
“约翰，听见没有？我是个后代。”
“后代不就是孩子嘛。”约翰说。
“唉呀，唉呀。”温蒂叹着气，“这三个孩子有个忠心的保姆，叫娜娜。可是达林先生生了她的气，用链子把她拴在院子里。就这样，孩子们全都飞走了。”
“这故事好听极了。”尼布斯说。
“他们飞走了，”温蒂继续讲，“飞到永无岛，飞到走丢的孩子们待的地方。”
“我正猜着他们去了那儿！”卷毛兴奋地插嘴，“说不上为什么，反正我正猜着他们去了。”
“哦，温蒂，”图图叫道，“走丢的孩子里面，有一个是不是叫图图？”
“是呀，是有一个。”
“我在故事里呢。万岁！尼布斯，我在故事里呢！”
“嘘。现在我要你们想想，孩子们全都飞走了，那对不幸的父母心里是什么滋味。”
“呜！”他们一齐哀声叹气，其实谁也没为那对不幸的父母设想哪怕一点点。
“想想那些空床吧！”
“可真凄惨呀！”双胞胎中的老大兴高采烈地说。
“我真不知道这怎么还能有个快活的结尾，”双胞胎中的老二说，“尼布斯，你知道吗？”
“我都担心死啦。”
“要是你们知道母亲的爱有多么深厚，”温蒂得意地告诉他们，“你们就一点都不怕了。”她讲到了彼得最恨的那部分。
“我可喜欢母亲的爱了，”图图拿枕头拍了尼布斯一下，“尼布斯，你喜欢母亲的爱吗？”
“可不是。”尼布斯回拍了一下。
“你们看，”温蒂心满意足地说，“我们的女主人公知道，妈妈一定会给孩子们留着那扇开着的窗，让他们随时都能飞回去。于是，他们在外头一待就是好多年，玩得痛痛快快。”
“他们后来回去过吗？”
“现在咱们就来，”温蒂打起精神，准备使出浑身解数，“瞧一眼未来的情景。”大家约好似的一扭身子，因为要瞧一眼未来，这么一扭就容易多了。“好多年过去了。从伦敦火车站下车的这位女士，举止优雅，年纪却看不出来，她是谁呢？”
“哦，温蒂，她是谁呀？”尼布斯叫道，跟自己完全不知道答案似的兴奋。
“难道是——对——不——确实是——美丽的温蒂！”
“跟着她一起下车的那两位，又是谁？相貌堂堂，仪表不凡，如今都长成了成年男子。会不会是约翰和迈克尔呢？正是他们！”
“‘亲爱的弟弟们，你们瞧，’温蒂抬手往上一指，说，‘窗户还是开着的呀。我们这样一心一意信赖母亲的爱，如今总算得到了回报。’于是他们朝着自己的爸爸妈妈飞上楼去。那份幸福，就是用笔也形容不出。我们还是轻轻落下帷幕吧。”
这就是那个故事。他们和美丽的讲述人一样，听得心满意足。你瞧，一切都如它应有的那样。我们乐颠颠地跑掉，像世界上最没心没肺的东西。孩子们就是这样的，却偏偏那么惹人爱。我们只顾自己，过得快活极了；等到需要有人格外关照的时候，便又高高尚尚地回来领受它，深信等着自己的是拥抱，断不会是一顿打屁股。
他们对母亲的爱当真有这么大的信心，觉得再没心没肺一阵子，自己也是担当得起的。
可在场有个人却知道另一面。温蒂刚一讲完，他就发出一声空洞的呻吟。
“彼得，怎么啦？”她以为他病了，连忙奔到他身边，关切地伸手摸摸他胸口往下的地方。“彼得，哪儿疼？”
“不是那种疼。”彼得阴沉地答道。
“那是什么样的疼？”
“温蒂，关于妈妈的事，你想错了。”
他激动的样子叫人害怕极了，男孩们惊惶地在他身边围了一圈。于是，他十分坦率地说出了从前一直藏在心里的事。
“很久以前，”他说，“我跟你想的一样，以为我的妈妈准会一直给我留着窗子。我便在外头过了一个月亮，又一个月亮，再一个月亮，后来才飞回去。可窗子已经闩上了。妈妈早把我忘得一干二净，我的床上睡着另一个小男孩。”
我说不准这件事是不是真的。可彼得相信它是真的。孩子们都听怕了。
“你拿得准，妈妈们都是那样的吗？”
“拿得准。”
原来妈妈们的真面目是这样。这群癞蛤蟆！
不过凡事还是小心为好。说到什么时候该让步，再没有人比孩子更懂得见机行事的了。“温蒂，咱们回家吧。”约翰和迈克尔一齐叫道。
“好。”她一把抓住他们。
“不会是今晚吧？”走丢的男孩们不知所措地问。他们在那块自称是心的地方深深知道，没有妈妈，一个人照样可以过得很不错；觉得没有妈妈就不行的，只有妈妈们自己。
“现在就走。”温蒂斩钉截铁地回答。一个可怕的念头刚掠过她心头：“也许妈妈现在已过了重孝，换上半孝的衣裳了。”
这种惧意使她忘了彼得心里该是什么感受。她口气有点硬，对他说：“彼得，请你把该安排的事安排一下，好吗？”
“你愿意就好。”他答得很冷淡，仿佛她不过请他递一递坚果。
他们之间，竟连一句“舍不得你走”也没有！要是她对分离满不在乎，他彼得就要让她看看，他也一样不在乎。
他当然在乎，在乎得厉害。大人们跟往常一样，又把一切都搅坏了。他满腔都是对他们的怒火，以至刚一钻进自己的树洞，就故意又浅又急地呼吸起来，每秒钟大约呼五次。因为永无岛有种说法，你每呼吸一回，就有一个大人死去。彼得一心报复，能杀多快，就要多快地杀。
他把该吩咐的事吩咐了印第安人，便回到地下的家。他不在的工夫，家里上演了很不光彩的一幕。想到就要失去温蒂，走丢的男孩们吓慌了，一个个气势汹汹地向她逼近。
“她要是走了，会比她没来以前还糟！”他们叫道。
“不能让她走。”
“把她扣在这里当俘虏。”
“对，用链子拴住。”
在这紧要关头，她本能地知道该向他们当中的谁求助。
“图图，”她叫道，“我向你求救。”
怪不怪？她偏偏向图图求救，他不正是最傻的一个吗？
图图回应她的方式却气派极了。就在那一瞬间，他身上那股傻气消失得干干净净，说出的话庄严有力。
“我只是个图图，”他说，“没人把我当回事。可谁第一个不拿英格兰绅士该有的礼数对待温蒂，我就叫谁狠狠出一回血。”
他拔出佩刀。在那一瞬间，他自己的太阳正高悬在正午。其余的人心里不安，都退了回去。随后彼得回来了，他们一眼看出，休想他帮忙。没有哪个姑娘会因为彼得而违背自己的心愿，被迫留在永无岛。
“温蒂，”他大步来回走着，说，“你飞起来容易累，我已经请印第安人给你们带路，穿过树林。”
“谢谢你，彼得。”
“接着，”他用惯于受人服从的人那种短促、利落的声音说，“小叮当会带你们过海。尼布斯，去叫醒她。”
尼布斯敲了两回才听见应答。其实叮当早就坐在床上听了好一阵子了。
“谁呀？谁许你来的？走开！”她叫道。
“叮当，你得起床啦，”尼布斯在外面喊，“要你陪温蒂出一趟远门。”
叮当听说温蒂要走，自然高兴得不得了；可叫她给温蒂当向导？她才不干呢。这层意思，她用了比这更难听的话来说。说完，她又装睡去了。
“她说她不肯！”尼布斯见她竟敢这样抗命，吓得叫出了声。彼得便板着脸朝那位年轻姑娘的闺房走去。
“叮当，”他厉声道，“你要是不马上起来穿衣裳，我就拉开帘子，叫大伙儿都瞧瞧你只穿睡衣的样子。”
这下她一跃就跳到地板上。“谁说我不起来了？”她喊道。
在这当儿，男孩们正十分凄凉地望着温蒂。她已和约翰、迈克尔一起收拾妥当，准备上路。到了这时候，他们情绪这样低落，不单因为即将失去她，也因为隐约觉得她要到个很美好的地方去，偏偏没邀请他们。新鲜事物照例在向他们招手。
温蒂却把他们的心思往高尚处想，顿时软了心。
“亲爱的孩子们，”她说，“你们要是愿意都跟我来，我几乎敢保证，我能请爸爸妈妈把你们全收养下来。”
这邀请尤其是说给彼得听的。可每个男孩想到的全是他自己，立刻欢喜得跳了起来。
“可他们不会嫌我们这一大伙太难应付吗？”尼布斯还跳在半空就问。
“哦，不会，”温蒂飞快地盘算了一下，说，“也不过就是客厅里得多摆几张床。每个月第一个星期四会客的时候，拿屏风挡住就行了。”
“彼得，我们能去吗？”他们一齐哀求。他们想当然地以为，自己若去，彼得自然也去。可说实话，他们也不大在意。孩子们就是这样，只要新鲜事物一敲门，他们随时准备撇下最亲爱的人。
“好吧。”彼得苦涩地笑了笑。他们立刻奔去收拾东西。
“好啦，彼得，”温蒂以为自己把一切都安排妥了，说，“走以前，我要给你吃药。”她很爱给他们喂药，次数无疑也太多了。当然，那药只是水。但水是从葫芦里倒出来的，她又总会先摇一摇葫芦，再一滴滴数好，叫这水多少有了几分药性。不过这一回，她没把药水给彼得喝。她刚配好它，就看见他脸上有种神情，叫她心里猛然一沉。
“彼得，去收拾东西吧。”她浑身发抖地说。
“不，”他装作满不在乎地答道，“温蒂，我不跟你走了。”
“要的，彼得。”
为了显出她的离去丝毫不能使自己动心，他在房间里蹦来跳去，快活地吹着他那没心没肺的排箫。她只好追着他满屋子跑，尽管这样做实在不大体面。
“去找你妈妈呀。”她哄他。
即便彼得也真的有过一个称得上妈妈的人，他现在也不再想她了。没有妈妈，他照样过得很好。关于妈妈这种人，他前前后后想过一遍，记得的只有她们的坏处。
“不，不，”他斩钉截铁地告诉温蒂，“兴许她会说我老了，而我只想永远当个小男孩，快快活活地玩。”
“可是，彼得——”
于是，只好把这话告诉其余的人。
“彼得不跟我们走。”
彼得不去！他们茫然望着他，每个人的肩上都扛着一根棍子，每根棍子上都挂着一个包袱。他们的第一个念头是，彼得自己不去了，大概也就改了主意，不准他们走了。
可彼得太骄傲，不肯那样做。“要是你们找到了各自的妈妈，”他阴郁地说，“但愿你们到时候会喜欢她们。”
这话冷嘲得厉害，叫人听了浑身不自在。大半男孩的脸上都现出了些迟疑。他们的神情似乎在问，自己竟想要走，难道不是一群傻瓜吗？
“好啦，”彼得嚷道，“别大惊小怪的，也别哭哭啼啼。温蒂，再见！”他快快活活伸出手来，活像他们这会儿真的非走不可，因为他还有要紧事待办。
他既没有半点更想要一枚“顶针”的意思，她也只好把手递给他握了握。
“彼得，你会记得换干净的法兰绒内衣吧？”她留恋地待在他身边，问道。关于他们的绒布内衣，她一向十分在意。
“还有，你会吃药吧？”
好像没什么别的话可讲了，接下来是一阵尴尬的沉默。可彼得并不是个会当着众人的面垮下来的人。“小叮当，好了吗？”他大声唤道。
“好啦，好啦。”
“那么，前头带路。”

叮当飞快地顺着最近那棵树钻了上去。可没有一个人跟上。恰恰在这一刻，海盗向印第安人发动了可怕的袭击。头顶上原先静悄悄的空气里，突然爆开了尖叫和钢刀相击的声音。地底下却一片死寂。他们张开嘴，再也合不住。温蒂双膝跪地，双臂却伸向彼得。所有的胳膊都伸向他，仿佛突然被一阵风齐齐地吹向他的方向。他们无声地恳求他，千万不要撇下他们。至于彼得，他已抓起了剑，就是他自以为曾杀过海上大厨的那把剑，他眼中燃起了求战的光。

sections.title_zh: 第12章　孩子们被抓走了
sections.title_en: CHAPTER XII — THE CHILDREN ARE CARRIED OFF
source_paragraphs: The pirate attack had been a complete surprise: a sure proof that the unscrupulous Hook had conducted it improperly, for to surprise redskins fairly is beyond the wit of the white man.

By all the unwritten laws of savage warfare it is always the redskin who attacks, and with the wiliness of his race he does it just before the dawn, at which time he knows the courage of the whites to be at its lowest ebb. The white men have in the meantime made a rude stockade on the summit of yonder undulating ground, at the foot of which a stream runs; for it is destruction to be too far from water. There they await the onslaught, the inexperienced ones clutching their revolvers and treading on twigs, but the old hands sleeping tranquilly until just before the dawn. Through the long black night the savage scouts wriggle, snake-like, among the grass without stirring a blade. The brushwood closes behind them as silently as sand into which a mole has dived. Not a sound is to be heard, save when they give vent to a wonderful imitation of the lonely call of the coyote. The cry is answered by other braves; and some of them do it even better than the coyotes, who are not very good at it. So the chill hours wear on, and the long suspense is horribly trying to the paleface who has to live through it for the first time; but to the trained hand those ghastly calls and still ghastlier silences are but an intimation of how the night is marching.
That this was the usual procedure was so well known to Hook that in disregarding it he cannot be excused on the plea of ignorance.

The Piccaninnies, on their part, trusted implicitly to his honour, and their whole action of the night stands out in marked contrast to his. They left nothing undone that was consistent with the reputation of their tribe. With that alertness of the senses which is at once the marvel and despair of civilised peoples, they knew that the pirates were on the island from the moment one of them trod on a dry stick; and in an incredibly short space of time the coyote cries began. Every foot of ground between the spot where Hook had landed his forces and the home under the trees was stealthily examined by braves wearing their mocassins with the heels in front. They found only one hillock with a stream at its base, so that Hook had no choice; here he must establish himself and wait for just before the dawn. Everything being thus mapped out with almost diabolical cunning, the main body of the redskins folded their blankets around them, and in the phlegmatic manner that is to them the pearl of manhood squatted above the children's home, awaiting the cold moment when they should deal pale death.

Here dreaming, though wide-awake, of the exquisite tortures to which they were to put him at break of day, those confiding savages were found by the treacherous Hook. From the accounts afterwards supplied by such of the scouts as escaped the carnage, he does not seem even to have paused at the rising ground, though it is certain that in that grey light he must have seen it: no thought of waiting to be attacked appears from first to last to have visited his subtle mind; he would not even hold off till the night was nearly spent; on he pounded with no policy but to fall to. What could the bewildered scouts do, masters as they were of every warlike artifice save this one, but trot helplessly after him, exposing themselves fatally to view, the while they gave pathetic utterance to the coyote cry.

Around the brave Tiger Lily were a dozen of her stoutest warriors, and they suddenly saw the perfidious pirates bearing down upon them. Fell from their eyes then the film through which they had looked at victory. No more would they torture at the stake. For them the happy hunting-grounds now. They knew it; but as their fathers' sons they acquitted themselves. Even then they had time to gather in a phalanx that would have been hard to break had they risen quickly, but this they were forbidden to do by the traditions of their race. It is written that the noble savage must never express surprise in the presence of the white. Thus terrible as the sudden appearance of the pirates must have been to them, they remained stationary for a moment, not a muscle moving; as if the foe had come by invitation. Then, indeed, the tradition gallantly upheld, they seized their weapons, and the air was torn with the warcry; but it was now too late.

It is no part of ours to describe what was a massacre rather than a fight. Thus perished many of the flower of the Piccaninny tribe. Not all unavenged did they die, for with Lean Wolf fell Alf Mason, to disturb the Spanish Main no more; and among others who bit the dust were Geo. Scourie, Chas. Turley, and the Alsatian Foggerty. Turley fell to the tomahawk of the terrible Panther, who ultimately cut a way through the pirates with Tiger Lily and a small remnant of the tribe.

To what extent Hook is to blame for his tactics on this occasion is for the historian to decide. Had he waited on the rising ground till the proper hour he and his men would probably have been butchered; and in judging him it is only fair to take this into account. What he should perhaps have done was to acquaint his opponents that he proposed to follow a new method. On the other hand this, as destroying the element of surprise, would have made his strategy of no avail, so that the whole question is beset with difficulties. One cannot at least withhold a reluctant admiration for the wit that had conceived so bold a scheme, and the fell genius with which it was carried out.

What were his own feelings about himself at that triumphant moment? Fain would his dogs have known, as breathing heavily and wiping their cutlasses, they gathered at a discreet distance from his hook, and squinted through their ferret eyes at this extraordinary man. Elation must have been in his heart, but his face did not reflect it: ever a dark and solitary enigma, he stood aloof from his followers in spirit as in substance.

The night's work was not yet over, for it was not the redskins he had come out to destroy; they were but the bees to be smoked, so that he should get at the honey. It was Pan he wanted, Pan and Wendy and their band, but chiefly Pan.

Peter was such a small boy that one tends to wonder at the man's hatred of him. True he had flung Hook's arm to the crocodile; but even this and the increased insecurity of life to which it led, owing to the crocodile's pertinacity, hardly account for a vindictiveness so relentless and malignant. The truth is that there was a something about Peter which goaded the pirate captain to frenzy. It was not his courage, it was not his engaging appearance, it was not--. There is no beating about the bush, for we know quite well what it was, and have got to tell. It was Peter's cockiness.

This had got on Hook's nerves; it made his iron claw twitch, and at night it disturbed him like an insect. While Peter lived, the tortured man felt that he was a lion in a cage into which a sparrow had come.

The question now was how to get down the trees, or how to get his dogs down? He ran his greedy eyes over them, searching for the thinnest ones. They wriggled uncomfortably, for they knew he would not scruple to ram them down with poles.

In the meantime, what of the boys? We have seen them at the first clang of weapons, turned as it were into stone figures, open-mouthed, all appealing with outstretched arms to Peter; and we return to them as their mouths close, and their arms fall to their sides. The pandemonium above has ceased almost as suddenly as it arose, passed like a fierce gust of wind; but they know that in the passing it has determined their fate.
Which side had won?
The pirates, listening avidly at the mouths of the trees, heard the question put by every boy, and alas, they also heard Peter's answer.
'If the redskins have won,' he said, 'they will beat the tom-tom; it is always their sign of victory.'

Now Smee had found the tom-tom, and was at that moment sitting on it. 'You will never hear the tom-tom again,' he muttered, but inaudibly of course, for strict silence had been enjoined. To his amazement Hook signed to him to beat the tom-tom; and slowly there came to Smee an understanding of the dreadful wickedness of the order. Never, probably, had this simple man admired Hook so much.
Twice Smee beat upon the instrument, and then stopped to listen gleefully.
'The tom-tom,' the miscreants heard Peter cry; 'an Indian victory!'

The doomed children answered with a cheer that was music to the black hearts above, and almost immediately they repeated their goodbyes to Peter. This puzzled the pirates, but all their other feelings were swallowed by a base delight that the enemy were about to come up the trees. They smirked at each other and rubbed their hands. Rapidly and silently Hook gave his orders: one man to each tree, and the others to arrange themselves in a line two yards apart.
translated_paragraphs: 海盗的袭击完全出人意料。这个事实足以证明，不讲规矩的虎克这仗打得不合规矩。白人要是照规矩来，凭他的本事，可休想打印第安人一个措手不及。

照这种战争一切不成文的规矩，向来该由印第安人进攻。他们精于谋略，总会选在破晓前，因为知道白人的勇气到那时已落到了最低处。与此同时，白人应在那边起伏的高地顶上筑起一座简陋的木栅寨，坡脚得有溪流经过；离水源太远，简直是自取灭亡。他们在那儿等候进攻。没经验的紧攥着左轮手枪，踩得枯枝咔嚓作响；老手却能安安稳稳地睡到破晓前才起。漫漫黑夜里，印第安斥候像蛇一样在草中蜿蜒爬行，一片草叶也不惊动。他们身后的灌木丛悄然合拢，仿佛鼹鼠一头钻进沙里，细沙随即淹过洞口。听不见一点声息，除非他们忽然把郊狼在荒野里的孤嚎学得惟妙惟肖。别的勇士也发出叫声来回答。有的人学得甚至比郊狼还像，郊狼自己倒不太在行。寒冷的时辰就这么过去了。对于头一回得在这种情形下熬夜的白脸人，久久悬着的一颗心实在难熬；对有经验的老手来说，那些阴森的叫声，还有叫声之间更阴森的沉寂，不过是在告诉他，夜晚又往前走了多少。
虎克对这套惯常的程序熟悉得很。因此，对于他此次置之不理的行为，不能用“不知情”来开脱。

至于皮卡尼尼人，他们一心相信虎克会讲信用。整晚他们所做的事，跟他的行径恰成鲜明对照。凡是符合部落声誉的事情，他们没有一样没做。他们的感官敏锐到叫文明人既惊叹又绝望。海盗之中头一个人一脚踩在枯枝上，他们就知道海盗上岸了；短短一会儿，郊狼叫已经传开。虎克带人登陆的地点与树下的家之间，每一尺土地都被穿着软皮鞋、把鞋跟倒转向前的勇士悄无声息地查探过。坡脚有溪流的高地只有一处。虎克别无选择，非得在这里扎营，等到破晓前才成。一切都算计得如此周密，简直是神鬼莫测。印第安人的主力裹好毯子，蹲在孩子们的家上方，神色泰然。在他们看来，男子汉最珍贵的品格就在这份镇定；如今他们只等寒冷的时刻一到，再把苍白的死亡送给敌人。

这些轻信对手守信的勇士们，个个睁着眼，却正做着好梦，想着天一亮要给他领教哪些精巧的酷刑。背信弃义的虎克就在这里找到了他们。据后来侥幸逃出这场屠杀的斥候们讲，他似乎连那片高地都没停一停；那片灰白的光线里，他肯定已经看见它了。从头到尾，这颗城府极深的脑袋仿佛连一瞬间也没想过，要老老实实等人来进攻。他甚至不肯再等上小半夜，径直往前猛冲，整套谋略不过就两个字：开打。那些目瞪口呆的斥候怎么办呢？战争的一切诡计他们都会，偏偏不懂这一种。他们只能束手无策地跟在他的脚后小跑，一边可怜巴巴地发出郊狼叫，一边把自己的所在暴露无遗，给自己招来了杀身之祸。

勇敢的虎莲公主身边聚着十二名最坚强的勇士。他们猛地望见，背信的海盗正扑面而来。先前罩在眼前、让他们只看得见胜利的那层薄膜脱落了。他们不会再把敌人绑到刑柱上行刑了。如今等在他们面前的是幸福猎场。他们知道这一点，却仍无愧于先辈们的子孙。即使到了那时，他们也还有工夫聚成方阵；倘若立即起身迎敌，方阵仍很难攻破。可部落的传统不许他们这样做。有规矩写着，高贵的勇士永不在白人面前露出惊讶。因此，海盗猝然出现，不管在他们心里引起多大震动，他们还是静坐了片刻，纹丝不动，仿佛敌人是应邀前来。然后，英勇地守住了传统，他们才一把抓起武器，战呼声撕裂了夜空。可到这时，已经太迟了。
这与其说是一场交战，不如说是一场屠杀，我们无意把它描画出来。皮卡尼尼部落多少出色的勇士就此丧生。他们也并非全然没有报仇：瘦狼倒下的同时，阿尔夫·梅森也倒下了，再不能去西属美洲海岸作恶。同样命丧尘土的，还有乔治·斯考里、查尔斯·特利，以及来自阿尔萨斯的福格蒂。特利死在可怕的花豹勇士的战斧下。最后，花豹勇士跟虎莲公主一道，领着残存的少数族人，从海盗中间杀开了一条血路。

这次用的战术，虎克到底该受几分责难，该由历史学家裁断。倘若他在高地上规规矩矩等到应当交手的时候，他和他的人多半会落得被人宰杀的下场。评断他时，把这个情形也算进去才公平。他或许本该先通知对手，自己打算改用一种新办法。可另一方面，一旦事先通报，就失了出其不意之效，他的计谋也就白搭了。整件事因此处处为难。不过，无论情不情愿，人总免不了对他生出一点佩服：想得出如此大胆的一着，是他的机智；干起来如此凶狠利落，又是他的一种天才。
在那个获胜的时刻，他对自己究竟是什么感受呢？他的那群走狗很想知道。他们喘着粗气，擦着弯刀，跟他的铁钩保持谨慎的距离，围在一边，眯起雪貂似的小眼，斜斜打量着这个非同寻常的人。他心里一定很得意，脸上却没显出半点来。他永远是个阴暗而孤独的谜，跟随从们隔着一段距离独自站立。他们精神上的距离，同样远。
这一夜的事还没办完。他出动要消灭的原就不是印第安人。他们不过是要先用烟熏走的一群蜂，赶开以后，他好伸手取蜜。他要的是潘，是潘、温蒂和他们那一伙人，但头一个要的，还是潘。
彼得不过是那么小一个男孩，不免叫人好奇，一个大男人为什么恨他至此。诚然，他曾把虎克的胳膊扔给鳄鱼。那鳄鱼锲而不舍，从此虎克的性命自然也就更没有保障。可就连这些，也很难解释这股如此不屈不挠、恶毒如斯的复仇心。其实，彼得身上有样东西，足以把海盗船长逼得发狂。不是他的勇气，不是他那惹人喜爱的模样，不是——不必再绕圈子，我们明明知道是什么，也必须说出来。是彼得那股神气活现的劲儿。
这股劲儿叫虎克神经都要发作，叫他的铁爪也开始抽搐，到了夜里还像只虫子似的，扰得他不得安宁。彼得只要还活着，这个备受折磨的人就觉得，自己是一头关在笼子里的狮子，而笼子里偏飞进了一只麻雀。
眼下的问题，是怎样从树洞钻下去；或者说，是怎样让他的走狗们钻下去。他用贪婪的目光在他们身上扫过，挑拣最瘦的那些。海盗们不自在地扭动起来。他们知道，只要有根杆子，船长绝不会介意拿它把他们硬捅下去。
孩子们呢？我们头先看见他们在第一阵兵器相撞声中仿佛变成了石像，一个个嘴张着，胳膊直伸向彼得，向他求救。现在回到他们身边，恰是他们把嘴合上、胳膊垂回身侧的时候。头顶上那阵地狱般的喧嚣，来得突然，止得几乎同样突然，像一股猛烈的阵风刮了过去。可他们知道，它刮过去的这一趟，已经决定了他们的命运。
哪一边赢了？
海盗们在树洞口急切地把耳朵贴紧，听见每个男孩都这样问。唉，也听见了彼得的回答。
“如果印第安人赢了，”他说，“他们就会敲鼓。他们一向用鼓声报捷。”
斯密恰巧已找着那面鼓，此时就坐在鼓上。“你们可再也听不着这面鼓啦。”他咕哝道。当然，是没有发出让人听得见的声音的，船长严令谁也不许出声。大出斯密意料的是，虎克竟打个手势，叫他敲鼓。斯密这才慢慢领悟，这道命令里藏着何等可怕的恶意。这个头脑简单的人，大约从来没有这么佩服过虎克。
斯密在鼓上敲了两下，便停住手，得意洋洋地侧耳听。
“鼓声！”坏蛋们听见彼得叫道，“印第安人赢啦！”
大难临头的孩子们齐声欢呼。对躲在上头的那一颗颗黑心而言，这欢呼真是再好听不过的乐曲。几乎紧接着，孩子们又一个接一个向彼得道别。海盗们虽然不明白这是怎么回事，其余的心思却都叫卑鄙的喜悦给淹没了：敌人就要从树洞里爬上来了。他们互相挤眉弄眼地笑，搓着双手。虎克迅速而无声地下了命令：每棵树派一个人，其余的列成一排，两人之间隔两码。

sections.title_zh: 第13章　你相信有仙子吗？
sections.title_en: CHAPTER XIII — DO YOU BELIEVE IN FAIRIES?
source_paragraphs: The more quickly this horror is disposed of the better. The first to emerge from his tree was Curly. He rose out of it into the arms of Cecco, who flung him to Smee, who flung him to Starkey, who flung him to Bill Jukes, who flung him to Noodler, and so he was tossed from one to another till he fell at the feet of the black pirate. All the boys were plucked from their trees in this ruthless manner; and several of them were in the air at a time, like bales of goods flung from hand to hand.

A different treatment was accorded to Wendy, who came last. With ironical politeness Hook raised his hat to her, and, offering her his arm, escorted her to the spot where the others were being gagged. He did it with such an air, he was so frightfully _distingue_, that she was too fascinated to cry out. She was only a little girl.

Perhaps it is tell-tale to divulge that for a moment Hook entranced her, and we tell on her only because her slip led to strange results. Had she haughtily unhanded him (and we should have loved to write it of her), she would have been hurled through the air like the others, and then Hook would probably not have been present at the tying of the children; and had he not been at the tying he would not have discovered Slightly's secret, and without the secret he could not presently have made his foul attempt on Peter's life.

They were tied to prevent their flying away, doubled up with their knees close to their ears; and for the trussing of them the black pirate had cut a rope into nine equal pieces. All went well until Slightly's turn came, when he was found to be like those irritating parcels that use up all the string in going round and leave no tags with which to tie a knot. The pirates kicked him in their rage, just as you kick the parcel (though in fairness you should kick the string); and strange to say it was Hook who told them to belay their violence. His lip was curled with malicious triumph. While his dogs were merely sweating because every time they tried to pack the unhappy lad tight in one part he bulged out in another, Hook's master mind had gone far beneath Slightly's surface, probing not for effects but for causes; and his exultation showed that he had found them. Slightly, white to the gills, knew that Hook had surprised his secret, which was this, that no boy so blown out could use a tree wherein an average man need stick. Poor Slightly, most wretched of all the children now, for he was in a panic about Peter, bitterly regretted what he had done. Madly addicted to the drinking of water when he was hot, he had swelled in consequence to his present girth, and instead of reducing himself to fit his tree he had, unknown to the others, whittled his tree to make it fit him.

Sufficient of this Hook guessed to persuade him that Peter at last lay at his mercy; but no word of the dark design that now formed in the subterranean caverns of his mind crossed his lips; he merely signed that the captives were to be conveyed to the ship, and that he would be alone.

How to convey them? Hunched up in their ropes they might indeed be rolled down hill like barrels, but most of the way lay through a morass. Again Hook's genius surmounted difficulties. He indicated that the little house must be used as a conveyance. The children were flung into it, four stout pirates raised it on their shoulders, the others fell in behind, and singing the hateful pirate chorus the strange procession set off through the wood. I don't know whether any of the children were crying; if so, the singing drowned the sound; but as the little house disappeared in the forest, a brave though tiny jet of smoke issued from its chimney as if defying Hook.
Hook saw it, and it did Peter a bad service. It dried up any trickle of pity for him that may have remained in the pirate's infuriated breast.
