The first thing he did on finding himself alone in the fast falling night was to tiptoe to Slightly's tree, and make sure that it provided him with a passage. Then for long he remained brooding; his hat of ill omen on the sward, so that a gentle breeze which had arisen might play refreshingly through his hair. Dark as were his thoughts his blue eyes were as soft as the periwinkle. Intently he listened for any sound from the nether world, but all was as silent below as above; the house under the ground seemed to be but one more empty tenement in the void. Was that boy asleep, or did he stand waiting at the foot of Slightly's tree, with his dagger in his hand?

There was no way of knowing, save by going down. Hook let his cloak slip softly to the ground, and then biting his lips till a lewd blood stood on them, he stepped into the tree. He was a brave man; but for a moment he had to stop there and wipe his brow, which was dripping like a candle. Then silently he let himself go into the unknown.

He arrived unmolested at the foot of the shaft, and stood still again, biting at his breath, which had almost left him. As his eyes became accustomed to the dim light various objects in the home under the trees took shape; but the only one on which his greedy gaze rested, long sought for and found at last, was the great bed. On the bed lay Peter fast asleep.

Unaware of the tragedy being enacted above, Peter had continued, for a little time after the children left, to play gaily on his pipes: no doubt rather a forlorn attempt to prove to himself that he did not care. Then he decided not to take his medicine, so as to grieve Wendy. Then he lay down on the bed outside the coverlet, to vex her still more; for she had always tucked them inside it, because you never know that you may not grow chilly at the turn of the night. Then he nearly cried; but it struck him how indignant she would be if he laughed instead; so he laughed a haughty laugh and fell asleep in the middle of it.

Sometimes, though not often, he had dreams, and they were more painful than the dreams of other boys. For hours he could not be separated from these dreams, though he wailed piteously in them. They had to do, I think, with the riddle of his existence. At such times it had been Wendy's custom to take him out of bed and sit with him on her lap, soothing him in dear ways of her own invention, and when he grew calmer to put him back to bed before he quite woke up, so that he should not know of the indignity to which she had subjected him. But on this occasion he had fallen at once into a dreamless sleep. One arm dropped over the edge of the bed, one leg was arched, and the unfinished part of his laugh was stranded on his mouth, which was open, showing the little pearls.

Thus defenceless Hook found him. He stood silent at the foot of the tree looking across the chamber at his enemy. Did no feeling of compassion disturb his sombre breast? The man was not wholly evil; he loved flowers (I have been told) and sweet music (he was himself no mean performer on the harpsichord); and, let it be frankly admitted, the idyllic nature of the scene stirred him profoundly. Mastered by his better self he would have returned reluctantly up the tree, but for one thing.

What stayed him was Peter's impertinent appearance as he slept. The open mouth, the drooping arm, the arched knee: they were such a personification of cockiness as, taken together, will never again one may hope be presented to eyes so sensitive to their offensiveness. They steeled Hook's heart. If his rage had broken him into a hundred pieces every one of them would have disregarded the incident, and leapt at the sleeper.

Though a light from the one lamp shone dimly on the bed Hook stood in darkness himself, and at the first stealthy step forward he discovered an obstacle, the door of Slightly's tree. It did not entirely fill the aperture, and he had been looking over it. Feeling for the catch, he found to his fury that it was low down, beyond his reach. To his disordered brain it seemed then that the irritating quality in Peter's face and figure visibly increased, and he rattled the door and flung himself against it. Was his enemy to escape him after all.

But what was that? The red in his eye had caught sight of Peter's medicine standing on a ledge within easy reach. He fathomed what it was straightway, and immediately he knew that the sleeper was in his power.

Lest he should be taken alive, Hook always carried about his person a dreadful drug, blended by himself of all the death-dealing rings that had come into his possession. These he had boiled down into a yellow liquid quite unknown to science, which was probably the most virulent poison in existence.

Five drops of this he now added to Peter's cup. His hand shook, but it was in exultation rather than in shame. As he did it he avoided glancing at the sleeper, but not lest pity should unnerve him; merely to avoid spilling. Then one long gloating look he cast upon his victim, and turning, wormed his way with difficulty up the tree. As he emerged at the top he looked the very spirit of evil breaking from its hole. Donning his hat at its most rakish angle, he wound his cloak around him, holding one end in front as if to conceal his person from the night, of which it was the blackest part, and muttering strangely to himself stole away through the trees.

Peter slept on. The light guttered and went out, leaving the tenement in darkness; but still he slept. It must have been not less than ten o'clock by the crocodile, when he suddenly sat up in his bed, wakened by he knew not what. It was a soft cautious tapping on the door of his tree.
Soft and cautious, but in that stillness it was sinister. Peter felt for his dagger till his hand gripped it. Then he spoke.
'Who is that?'
For long there was no answer: then again the knock.
'Who are you?'
No answer.

He was thrilled, and he loved being thrilled. In two strides he reached his door. Unlike Slightly's door it filled the aperture, so that he could not see beyond it, nor could the one knocking see him.
'I won't open unless you speak,' Peter cried.
Then at last the visitor spoke, in a lovely bell-like voice.
'Let me in, Peter.'
It was Tink, and quickly he unbarred to her. She flew in excitedly, her face flushed and her dress stained with mud.
'What is it?'

'Oh, you could never guess,' she cried, and offered him three guesses. 'Out with it!' he shouted; and in one ungrammatical sentence, as long as the ribbons conjurers pull from their mouths, she told of the capture of Wendy and the boys.
Peter's heart bobbed up and down as he listened. Wendy bound, and on the pirate ship; she who loved everything to be just so!
'I'll rescue her,' he cried, leaping at his weapons. As he leapt he thought of something he could do to please her. He could take his medicine.
His hand closed on the fatal draught.
'No!' shrieked Tinker Bell, who had heard Hook muttering about his deed as he sped through the forest.
'Why not?'
'It is poisoned.'
'Poisoned? Who could have poisoned it?'
'Hook.'
'Don't be silly. How could Hook have got down here?'
Alas, Tinker Bell could not explain this, for even she did not know the dark secret of Slightly's tree. Nevertheless Hook's words had left no room for doubt. The cup was poisoned.
'Besides,' said Peter, quite believing himself, 'I never fell asleep.'
He raised the cup. No time for words now; time for deeds; and with one of her lightning movements Tink got between his lips and the draught, and drained it to the dregs.
'Why, Tink, how dare you drink my medicine?'
But she did not answer. Already she was reeling in the air.
'What is the matter with you?' cried Peter, suddenly afraid.
'It was poisoned, Peter,' she told him softly; 'and now I am going to be dead.'
'O Tink, did you drink it to save me?'
'Yes.'
'But why, Tink?'

Her wings would scarcely carry her now, but in reply she alighted on his shoulder and gave his chin a loving bite. She whispered in his ear 'You silly ass'; and then, tottering to her chamber, lay down on the bed.

His head almost filled the fourth wall of her little room as he knelt near her in distress. Every moment her light was growing fainter; and he knew that if it went out she would be no more. She liked his tears so much that she put out her beautiful finger and let them run over it.
Her voice was so low that at first he could not make out what she said. Then he made it out. She was saying that she thought she could get well again if children believed in fairies.

Peter flung out his arms. There were no children there, and it was night-time; but he addressed all who might be dreaming of the Neverland, and who were therefore nearer to him than you think: boys and girls in their nighties, and naked papooses in their baskets hung from trees.
'Do you believe?' he cried.
Tink sat up in bed almost briskly to listen to her fate.
She fancied she heard answers in the affirmative, and then again she wasn't sure.
'What do you think?' she asked Peter.
'If you believe,' he shouted to them, 'clap your hands; don't let Tink die.'
Many clapped.
Some didn't.
A few little beasts hissed.

The clapping stopped suddenly; as if countless mothers had rushed to their nurseries to see what on earth was happening; but already Tink was saved. First her voice grew strong; then she popped out of bed; then she was flashing through the room more merry and impudent than ever. She never thought of thanking those who believed, but she would have liked to get at the ones who had hissed.
'And now to rescue Wendy.'

The moon was riding in a cloudy heaven when Peter rose from his tree, begirt with weapons and wearing little else, to set out upon his perilous quest. It was not such a night as he would have chosen. He had hoped to fly, keeping not far from the ground so that nothing unwonted should escape his eyes; but in that fitful light to have flown low would have meant trailing his shadow through the trees, thus disturbing the birds and acquainting a watchful foe that he was astir.
He regretted now that he had given the birds of the island such strange names that they are very wild and difficult of approach.

There was no other course but to press forward in redskin fashion, at which happily he was an adept. But in what direction, for he could not be sure that the children had been taken to the ship? A slight fall of snow had obliterated all footmarks; and a deathly silence pervaded the island, as if for a space Nature stood still in horror of the recent carnage. He had taught the children something of the forest lore that he had himself learned from Tiger Lily and Tinker Bell, and knew that in their dire hour they were not likely to forget it. Slightly, if he had an opportunity, would blaze the trees, for instance, Curly would drop seeds, and Wendy would leave her handkerchief at some important place. But morning was needed to search for such guidance, and he could not wait. The upper world had called him, but would give no help.
The crocodile passed him, but not another living thing, not a sound, not a movement; and yet he knew well that sudden death might be at the next tree, or stalking him from behind.
He swore this terrible oath: 'Hook or me this time.'
Now he crawled forward like a snake; and again, erect, he darted across a space on which the moonlight played: one finger on his lip and his dagger at the ready. He was frightfully happy.
translated_paragraphs: 这桩惨事还是越快讲过去越好。第一个从树洞冒出来的是卷毛；一抬头，正落在切科怀里。切科把他扔给斯密，斯密扔给斯塔基，斯塔基扔给比尔·朱克斯，朱克斯又扔给努德勒。他就这么给一个传一个，直到跌在那个黑人海盗脚前。所有男孩都是这样被人毫不留情地从树洞里薅出来的。有时半空里一下抛过好几个孩子，活像一包包货物在众人手中传递。
最后出来的温蒂，却受到了另一番礼遇。虎克彬彬有礼地向她掀帽致意，那礼貌里带着嘲弄；随后他伸出臂膀，请她挽着，一路陪她到那伙正在被堵上嘴的孩子跟前。他的派头那么足，显得那样卓尔不群，她一时被迷住，连喊叫也忘了。她毕竟还只是个小女孩。
说出温蒂一度曾被虎克迷住，也许有打小报告之嫌。我们之所以告她这一状，只因为这一念之差，带来了非同寻常的后果。假如她昂然甩开了他的手——我们多愿意写她真这么做啊——她一定也会像其余的孩子一样，给人抛到半空中。那样一来，虎克大概就不会在捆绑孩子时在场；他若不在场，又怎么会发现斯莱特利的秘密？不知道那个秘密，他随后便不可能对彼得下那种毒手了。

怕孩子们飞掉，海盗把他们的身子折过来，膝盖顶着耳朵捆起来了。为了绑他们，那个黑人海盗把一根绳子截成等长的九段。起先都很顺利，直到轮到斯莱特利。这个男孩活像那种恼人的包裹，你拿绳子绕上一圈，整根绳子就用完了，连一小截打结的头也没给你留。海盗们气得拿脚踢他，就跟你生起气来踢包裹一样——讲句公道话，你该踢的是绳子。说也奇怪，喝令他们住手的，恰是虎克。他嘴角一翘，带着恶意的得色。他手下那群走狗只是急得冒汗，因为这孩子只要一头给捆得紧些，另一头就要鼓出来。虎克那颗非凡的脑袋却已看透了斯莱特利的表面，追究的不是结果，而是原因。他脸上的喜色，正说明原因已被他找着。斯莱特利连腮帮都白了。他知道虎克已看穿他的秘密：鼓胀成这么个样子的男孩还能钻得过的树洞，断不会卡住一个普通大人。这会儿孩子们中最苦恼的是斯莱特利。他替彼得担惊受怕，后悔得要命。他一热就没命地灌水，有瘾似的，这才胀成如今这么个腰围。可是他没有把自己收一收去迁就树，却瞒着伙伴们把树洞削大了，叫树来迁就他。
虎克猜出来的已经够多，足以叫他相信，彼得终于落到他手里，任凭他怎么处置了。至于他脑袋深处的地下洞窟里正在成形的那个黑暗计划，嘴上一个字也没吐露。他只打个手势，叫他们把俘虏送上船去，给他留下独处的工夫。
可要怎么送呢？孩子们缩在绳子里，确实可以像桶一样滚下山坡，可这一路大半是沼泽。虎克的天才再一次克服了难题。他示意他们把小屋拿来当车。孩子们给扔进小屋，四个壮实的海盗把屋子抬上肩头，其他人在后头列队。这支奇怪的队伍唱着那首令人憎恶的海盗歌，穿过树林出发了。孩子们中间有人在哭吗？我不知道。就算有，也给歌声盖住了。可就在小屋将要消失在林间时，一小股烟从烟囱里英勇地直冒上来，像是还在向虎克叫板。
虎克看见了。这反而害了彼得。海盗那颗怒火中烧的心里，原先要还留着一丝一缕对彼得的怜悯，这下也全给烤干了。

夜色正迅速加深。当四周只剩下虎克自己时，他做的第一件事，就是踮着脚尖走到斯莱特利的树前，先确认自己果然能够通过这条通道。随后，他又沉思了好一阵子，那顶不祥的帽子搁在草地上，好让新起的一阵和风轻轻吹过头发，给他一点清凉。他的心思尽管这样黑暗，蓝眼睛却像蔓长春花一样柔和。他凝神细听，地下的世界里可有什么响动，上面一片寂静，底下也一样。地下的家仿佛只是虚空里又一处空空无人居住的房子。那男孩是睡着了，还是正拿着匕首，等在斯莱特利的树洞底下？
不下去看看，谁也不可能知道。虎克让斗篷轻柔地滑落在草地上，咬着嘴唇，直到唇上渗出一层令人不安的血色，才踏进树洞。他是个勇敢的人。可他仍得站在那里停上一瞬，擦擦额头，那上头的汗正像蜡烛上的油一样滴下来。随后他悄无声息地松开手，任由自己滑进未知的深处。
他没有遇见任何阻拦，到了竖洞底部，又站定，紧咬着那几乎已经离他而去的一口气。等双眼适应了微光，树底下的家里各种东西渐渐现出了形状。可他贪婪的目光只在一样东西上停住了，那是他寻找许久、终于找到的那张大床。彼得就躺在那里，睡得正熟。
彼得对上头正在发生的惨事毫不知情。孩子们刚走以后，他仍快活地吹了一阵排箫。那多半是个多少有些可怜的尝试，想让自己相信，自己其实并不在乎。接着他决定不吃药，叫温蒂伤伤心。然后他躺到床上，偏不往被单里钻，好再惹她生生气：她向来总把他们塞进被子里包好，因为谁也说不准，过了半夜会不会受凉。接下来，他差点儿哭了。可他猛然想到，若自己偏偏笑起来，她又该多生气。于是，他傲气十足地笑了一声，笑到一半便睡着了。

偶尔，但不是常常，他也会做梦。他的梦比别的男孩做的更让人痛苦。他一连几个钟头都没法从那些梦中挣脱出来，尽管在梦里他哀哀哭叫，十分可怜。我想，那些梦多少跟他的身世之谜有关。每当这种时候，温蒂总把他抱下床，放在自己膝头，用些她自己想出来的亲昵办法安抚他。等他渐渐安静了，还没完全醒，就把他放回床上，免得他知道自己被她弄得这样有失体面。可这一回，他一下便落进了无梦的睡眠。一只胳膊垂到床沿外，一条腿弓着；那个没笑完的笑还挂在他张开的嘴上，露出了里头的小珍珠。
虎克发现他时，他就是这样毫无防备。海盗静静站在树洞底部，隔着房间凝望自己的仇敌。莫非他阴暗的心中真没动过一点恻隐？这个人并非全然无可救药。据我听说，他喜欢花，也喜欢优美的音乐，自己羽管键琴弹得还颇有两下子。得坦白承认，这幅田园诗一样的景象深深触动了他。原本，心中较为美好的那一面已经占了上风，他就要满怀不甘地沿树洞原路爬回去，只是有一样东西拦住了他。
拦住虎克的是彼得睡着时的那副目中无人相。张开的嘴，垂下的胳膊，弓起的膝盖：这几样合在一处，简直就是活生生的神气活现。但愿往后再也别让这么一双视其为冒犯的、敏感的眼睛，撞上这样一幅景象了。这景象叫虎克的心肠又硬了起来。他的怒火要是把他炸成一百块，那么每一块都会把自己炸碎这桩小事抛到一边，扑向那熟睡的孩子。
屋里唯一一盏灯的微光照着床，虎克自己却站在暗中。他才悄悄向前迈一步，便发现遇到了阻碍：斯莱特利树洞底下的门。门没把洞口整个遮住，他方才就是从上沿往里看的。他摸索门闩，却气得发现，门闩在低处，手伸不到。在他混乱的脑海里，这时候，彼得脸上和身上那股令人发恼的神气，简直以肉眼可见的速度越来越足。他把门摇得咔啦啦响，又把身子朝门上猛撞。难道他的仇敌竟还是要逃出他的掌心？
可那是什么？他那闪着红光的眼睛看见了彼得的药。杯子正搁在一道凸台上，随手就能摸到。他马上明白那是什么，也立即知道，那个睡着的孩子现在由他摆布了。
为了不叫人活捉，虎克总随身带着一种可怖的药，是他亲手用落到他手里的那些致命毒戒调成的。他把它们煎熬成了一种黄色液体，科学至今对它一无所知。那可能是世上最狠毒的毒药。

此刻他往彼得的杯子里加了五滴。手在颤抖，不是因为羞耻，而是太得意了。他动手时没有看那熟睡的孩子，并不是怕自己心软到下不去手，不过是免得手上洒出来。然后，他用志得意满的一眼久久打量自己的受害者，转过身，艰难地沿着树洞一扭一扭爬了上去。他从树顶冒出来的模样，简直就像恶灵钻出了自己的坑穴。他把帽子歪歪地扣回头上，要多放肆有多放肆，把斗篷往身上一卷，一手将一角挡在身前，仿佛是要躲着夜色，不教它看见自己。可他自己原是这夜色里最黑暗的一部分。他一路古怪地自言自语，悄悄穿过树林走远了。
彼得还在睡。灯芯暗淡地闪了几闪，熄了，整个住处落入黑暗。他仍旧没醒。照那条鳄鱼的钟来算，想必已不下十点。这时，他忽然在床上坐直，不知道是什么吵醒了他。原来是有人在他的树洞门上，轻轻地、小心翼翼地叩门。
叩得又轻又小心，可在那片寂静里，倒透出点不祥来。彼得摸索自己的匕首，直到手掌握紧它，才开了口。
“是谁？”
半天没人回答。接着，又是一阵敲门声。
“你是谁？”
没有回答。
他浑身一阵激动；他就爱这种激动。只用两大步，他便到了自己门前。跟斯莱特利的门两样，这扇门恰好把洞口堵得严严实实。他看不见另一边，敲门的自然也看不见他。
“你不开口，我就不开门！”彼得喊道。
这时来客总算开了口，声音甜美得像清脆的铃响。
“彼得，让我进来。”
原来是叮当。他赶紧替她拉开门闩。她激动地飞进来，脸蛋通红，裙子上尽是泥点。
“出了什么事？”
“哦，你怎么也猜不到！”她叫着，让他猜三次。“快说！”他大喊。于是，她把温蒂和男孩们被俘的经过，统统塞进一个不讲文法的长句子里讲给他听。那句话拉出来的长短，简直像魔术师从嘴里往外扯的彩带。
彼得听着，一颗心忽上忽下。温蒂竟被人捆绑，押上海盗船了；她那么喜欢一切齐齐整整、恰到好处的人！
“我去救她！”他大喊，纵身朝自己的兵器扑去。跳到一半，他想起一件能讨她欢喜的事。他可以先把药吃了。
他的手掌握住了那杯要命的药水。
“别！”小叮当尖声叫道。虎克匆匆穿过树林时，曾自言自语地嘀咕着自己干下的事，她听见了。
“为什么不能喝？”
“里头有毒。”
“有毒？谁能在这里头下毒？”
“虎克。”
“别傻了。虎克怎么可能钻到底下这儿来？”
唉，小叮当偏偏解释不了，因为连她也不知道斯莱特利的树洞里那个阴暗的秘密。尽管如此，虎克的话不容半点怀疑。杯里已经下了毒。
“再说，”彼得说得连自己都信了，“我根本就没睡着过。”
他举起杯子。这时来不及说话，该动手了。叮当使出她那闪电般的身法，一下插进他的嘴唇和药杯之间，把药水喝了个底朝天，连药渣也没剩。
“哎，叮当！你怎么敢喝我的药？”
她没回答。她已在半空中摇摇晃晃。
“你怎么了？”彼得忽然害怕了，叫道。
“它有毒，彼得，”她轻轻告诉他，“我现在就要死掉了。”
“哦，叮当，你喝下它，是为了救我吗？”
“是呀。”
“可为什么呀，叮当？”
她的翅膀几乎已经托不住身体了。为了回答，她飞落到他的肩膀上，亲亲热热地咬了他的下巴一口。“你这傻驴。”她贴着他的耳朵悄悄说。随后她摇摇晃晃地回到自己的房间，躺上了床。
他忧心如焚地跪在她身边，脑袋几乎占满了她的小屋朝外敞开的整整一面。她的光一刻暗似一刻，他知道，等光熄灭，她也就再也不在了。她那么喜欢他的眼泪，便伸出她漂亮的小手指，让泪珠流过指头。
她的声音那么轻，起先他没能听清她在说些什么。随后他明白了。她在说，她想，倘若孩子们相信世上有仙子，她也许就能重新好起来。
彼得张开了双臂。这里没有别的孩子，时辰也是夜里。他却开口唤那些也许正在梦见永无岛的人。因为做着这样的梦，其实他们离他比你想象的更近。穿着睡衣的男孩和女孩，光着身子睡在树上吊篮里的印第安小宝宝，他都唤到了。
“你们相信吗？”他大叫。
叮当几乎是利利索索地从床上坐起来，等着听自己的命运。
她恍惚听见有人答“相信”，可紧接着又不敢肯定。
“你觉得呢？”她问彼得。
“如果你们相信，”他向他们大喊，“就拍拍手！别让叮当死去！”
许多孩子拍起手来。
有些没有拍。
还有几个小坏蛋发出嘘声。
掌声忽然停了，仿佛有无数位妈妈都奔进了儿童室，想瞧瞧到底发生了什么。可是叮当已经获救了。先是她的声音响亮起来；接着她从床上一跃而下；随后，她就已在屋子里闪来闪去，比以前更加快活，更加冒冒失失。她一点也没想到要感谢那些相信她的孩子，倒很想把那几个发出嘘声的揪出来收拾一顿。
“好了，现在去救温蒂。”
彼得从自己的树洞里冒出来，踏上这趟凶险的征程时，月亮正在多云的天际巡行。他身上佩满兵器，除此之外几乎没怎么穿衣服。这不是他本想挑的夜晚。他原打算贴近地面飞行，好不放过任何反常的迹象。可是月光这么忽明忽暗，挨着地飞，就免不了拖着自己的影子扫过树丛，惊动林鸟，叫警觉的敌人知道他已经出动。
他现在有些后悔，当初给岛上的鸟起了那么多古怪的名字，弄得它们野性难驯，见了人就跑。

除此以外，只剩下学印第安人的方式，贴地往前赶。幸好，这是他的拿手好戏。可该往哪个方向走呢？孩子们已经给送上船去，这一点他可不能确定。一阵小雪把所有的脚印都盖没了。整座岛安静得像死了一样，仿佛大自然为刚才那场屠杀惊骇得停住了片刻。彼得曾经向虎莲公主和小叮当学来一些林间行走的本领，又把它们教给了孩子们。他知道，越在危急的关头，孩子们越不会忘记。譬如，斯莱特利若有机会，会在树上削个记号；卷毛会一路丢下种子；到了要紧的地方，温蒂会留下她的手帕。可是要搜寻这些指引，得等到天亮，而他不能等。地面上的世界把他唤了出来，却不肯伸手帮忙。
鳄鱼从他身旁经过。除此以外，见不到一个活物，听不见一丝声响，不见一点动静。可他清清楚楚地知道，暴死也许就等在下一棵树边，也许正在身后蹑足追来。
他发了一个可怕的誓：“这一回，不是虎克，就是我。”
一会儿，他像蛇那样贴地潜行；一会儿，他又站直，穿过月光流动的空地，疾掠而过。一根手指竖在唇边，匕首随时可以出手。他快活得不得了。

source_paragraphs: One green light squinting over Kidd's Creek, which is near the mouth of the pirate river, marked where the brig, the _Jolly Roger_, lay, low in the water; a rakish-looking craft foul to the hull, every beam in her detestable like ground strewn with mangled feathers. She was the cannibal of the seas, and scarce needed that watchful eye, for she floated immune in the horror of her name.

She was wrapped in the blanket of night, through which no sound from her could have reached the shore. There was little sound, and none agreeable save the whir of the ship's sewing machine at which Smee sat, ever industrious and obliging, the essence of the commonplace, pathetic Smee. I know not why he was so infinitely pathetic, unless it were because he was so pathetically unaware of it; but even strong men had to turn hastily from looking at him, and more than once on summer evenings he had touched the fount of Hook's tears and made it flow. Of this, as of almost everything else, Smee was quite unconscious.

A few of the pirates leant over the bulwarks drinking in the miasma of the night; others sprawled by barrels over games of dice and cards; and the exhausted four who had carried the little house lay prone on the deck, where even in their sleep they rolled skilfully to this side or that out of Hook's reach, lest he should claw them mechanically in passing.

Hook trod the deck in thought. O man unfathomable. It was his hour of triumph. Peter had been removed for ever from his path, and all the other boys were on the brig, about to walk the plank. It was his grimmest deed since the days when he had brought Barbecue to heel; and knowing as we do how vain a tabernacle is man, could we be surprised had he now paced the deck unsteadily, bellied out by the winds of his success?
But there was no elation in his gait, which kept pace with the action of his sombre mind. Hook was profoundly dejected.

He was often thus when communing with himself on board ship in the quietude of the night. It was because he was so terribly alone. This inscrutable man never felt more alone than when surrounded by his dogs. They were socially so inferior to him.

Hook was not his true name. To reveal who he really was would even at this date set the country in a blaze; but as those who read between the lines must already have guessed, he had been at a famous public school; and its traditions still clung to him like garments, with which indeed they are largely concerned. Thus it was offensive to him even now to board a ship in the same dress in which he grappled her; and he still adhered in his walk to the school's distinguished slouch. But above all he retained the passion for good form.
Good form! However much he may have degenerated, he still knew that this is all that really matters.

From far within him he heard a creaking as of rusty portals, and through them came a stern tap-tap-tap, like hammering in the night when one cannot sleep. 'Have you been good form to-day?' was their eternal question.
'Fame, fame, that glittering bauble, it is mine,' he cried.
'Is it quite good form to be distinguished at anything?' the tap-tap from his school replied.
'I am the only man whom Barbecue feared,' he urged; 'and Flint himself feared Barbecue.'
'Barbecue, Flint--what house?' came the cutting retort.
Most disquieting reflection of all, was it not bad form to think about good form?

His vitals were tortured by this problem. It was a claw within him sharper than the iron one; and as it tore him, the perspiration dripped down his tallow countenance and streaked his doublet. Ofttimes he drew his sleeve across his face, but there was no damming that trickle.
Ah, envy not Hook.

There came to him a presentiment of his early dissolution. It was as if Peter's terrible oath had boarded the ship. Hook felt a gloomy desire to make his dying speech, lest presently there should be no time for it.
'Better for Hook,' he cried, 'if he had had less ambition.' It was in his darkest hours only that he referred to himself in the third person.
'No little children love me.'

Strange that he should think of this, which had never troubled him before; perhaps the sewing machine brought it to his mind. For long he muttered to himself, staring at Smee, who was hemming placidly, under the conviction that all children feared him.

Feared him! Feared Smee! There was not a child on board the brig that night who did not already love him. He had said horrid things to them and hit them with the palm of his hand, because he could not hit with his fist; but they had only clung to him the more. Michael had tried on his spectacles.

To tell poor Smee that they thought him lovable! Hook itched to do it, but it seemed too brutal. Instead, he revolved this mystery in his mind: why do they find Smee lovable? He pursued the problem like the sleuth-hound that he was. If Smee was lovable, what was it that made him so? A terrible answer suddenly presented itself: 'Good form?'
Had the bo'sun good form without knowing it, which is the best form of all?
He remembered that you have to prove you don't know you have it before you are eligible for Pop.
With a cry of rage he raised his iron hand over Smee's head; but he did not tear. What arrested him was this reflection:
'To claw a man because he is good form, what would that be?'
'Bad form!'
The unhappy Hook was as impotent as he was damp, and he fell forward like a cut flower.

His dogs thinking him out of the way for a time, discipline instantly relaxed; and they broke into a bacchanalian dance, which brought him to his feet at once; all traces of human weakness gone, as if a bucket of water had passed over him.
'Quiet, you scugs,' he cried, 'or I'll cast anchor in you'; and at once the din was hushed. 'Are all the children chained, so that they cannot fly away?'
'Ay, ay.'
'Then hoist them up.'

The wretched prisoners were dragged from the hold, all except Wendy, and ranged in line in front of him. For a time he seemed unconscious of their presence. He lolled at his ease, humming, not unmelodiously, snatches of a rude song, and fingering a pack of cards. Ever and anon the light from his cigar gave a touch of colour to his face.
'Now then, bullies,' he said briskly, 'six of you walk the plank to-night, but I have room for two cabin boys. Which of you is it to be?'

'Don't irritate him unnecessarily,' had been Wendy's instructions in the hold; so Tootles stepped forward politely. Tootles hated the idea of signing under such a man, but an instinct told him that it would be prudent to lay the responsibility on an absent person; and though a somewhat silly boy, he knew that mothers alone are always willing to be the buffer. All children know this about mothers, and despise them for it, but make constant use of it.
So Tootles explained prudently, 'You see, sir, I don't think my mother would like me to be a pirate. Would your mother like you to be a pirate, Slightly?'
He winked at Slightly, who said mournfully, 'I don't think so,' as if he wished things had been otherwise. 'Would your mother like you to be a pirate, Twin?'
'I don't think so,' said the first twin, as clever as the others. 'Nibs, would----'
'Stow this gab,' roared Hook, and the spokesmen were dragged back. 'You, boy,' he said, addressing John, 'you look as if you had a little pluck in you. Didst never want to be a pirate, my hearty?'
Now John had sometimes experienced this hankering at maths. prep.; and he was struck by Hook's picking him out.
'I once thought of calling myself Red-handed Jack,' he said diffidently.
'And a good name too. We'll call you that here, bully, if you join.'
'What do you think, Michael?' asked John.
'What would you call me if I join?' Michael demanded.
'Blackbeard Joe.'
Michael was naturally impressed. 'What do you think, John?' He wanted John to decide, and John wanted him to decide.
'Shall we still be respectful subjects of the King?' John inquired.
Through Hook's teeth came the answer: 'You would have to swear, "Down with the King."'
Perhaps John had not behaved very well so far, but he shone out now.
'Then I refuse,' he cried, banging the barrel in front of Hook.
'And I refuse,' cried Michael.
'Rule Britannia!' squeaked Curly.
The infuriated pirates buffeted them in the mouth; and Hook roared out, 'That seals your doom. Bring up their mother. Get the plank ready.'
They were only boys, and they went white as they saw Jukes and Cecco preparing the fatal plank. But they tried to look brave when Wendy was brought up.

No words of mine can tell you how Wendy despised those pirates. To the boys there was at least some glamour in the pirate calling; but all that she saw was that the ship had not been scrubbed for years. There was not a porthole, on the grimy glass of which you might not have written with your finger 'Dirty pig'; and she had already written it on several. But as the boys gathered round her she had no thought, of course, save for them.
'So, my beauty,' said Hook, as if he spoke in syrup, 'you are to see your children walk the plank.'
Fine gentleman though he was, the intensity of his communings had soiled his ruff, and suddenly he knew that she was gazing at it. With a hasty gesture he tried to hide it, but he was too late.
'Are they to die?' asked Wendy, with a look of such frightful contempt that he nearly fainted.
'They are,' he snarled. 'Silence all,' he called gloatingly, 'for a mother's last words to her children.'

At this moment Wendy was grand. 'These are my last words, dear boys,' she said firmly. 'I feel that I have a message to you from your real mothers, and it is this: "We hope our sons will die like English gentlemen."'
Even the pirates were awed; and Tootles cried out hysterically, 'I am going to do what my mother hopes. What are you to do, Nibs?'
'What my mother hopes. What are you to do, Twin?'
'What my mother hopes. John, what are----'
But Hook had found his voice again.
'Tie her up,' he shouted.
It was Smee who tied her to the mast. 'See here, honey,' he whispered, 'I'll save you if you promise to be my mother.'
But not even for Smee would she make such a promise. 'I would almost rather have no children at all,' she said disdainfully.

It is sad to know that not a boy was looking at her as Smee tied her to the mast; the eyes of all were on the plank: that last little walk they were about to take. They were no longer able to hope that they would walk it manfully, for the capacity to think had gone from them; they could stare and shiver only.

Hook smiled on them with his teeth closed, and took a step toward Wendy. His intention was to turn her face so that she should see the boys walking the plank one by one. But he never reached her, he never heard the cry of anguish he hoped to wring from her. He heard something else instead.
It was the terrible tick-tick of the crocodile.

They all heard it--pirates, boys, Wendy; and immediately every head was blown in one direction; not to the water whence the sound proceeded, but toward Hook. All knew that what was about to happen concerned him alone, and that from being actors they were suddenly become spectators.
Very frightful was it to see the change that came over him. It was as if he had been clipped at every joint. He fell in a little heap.
The sound came steadily nearer; and in advance of it came this ghastly thought, 'The crocodile is about to board the ship.'

Even the iron claw hung inactive; as if knowing that it was no intrinsic part of what the attacking force wanted. Left so fearfully alone, any other man would have lain with his eyes shut where he fell: but the gigantic brain of Hook was still working, and under its guidance he crawled on his knees along the deck as far from the sound as he could go. The pirates respectfully cleared a passage for him, and it was only when he brought up against the bulwarks that he spoke.
'Hide me,' he cried hoarsely.
They gathered round him; all eyes averted from the thing that was coming aboard. They had no thought of fighting it. It was Fate.

Only when Hook was hidden from them did curiosity loosen the limbs of the boys so that they could rush to the ship's side to see the crocodile climbing it. Then they got the strangest surprise of this Night of Nights; for it was no crocodile that was coming to their aid. It was Peter.
He signed to them not to give vent to any cry of admiration that might rouse suspicion. Then he went on ticking.
translated_paragraphs: 海盗河的河口附近有一道基德湾，一盏绿灯正歪着眼睛俯视海湾。灯光标出了那艘双桅横帆船的位置，“快乐罗杰号”就低低地卧在水里。这是艘模样放荡不羁的船，从里到外，脏到船壳底，每一根横梁都叫人憎恶，活像一片散落着撕烂羽毛的土地。它是海上的食人魔，其实根本用不着那只警醒的眼睛守卫；只消叫人听见它的名字，便足以让它安然漂行，无人敢犯。

夜色像一床毯子把它包住，船上即使有什么声音，也穿不过去，传不到岸上。其实声音很少。能让人听着顺耳的，只有船上那部缝纫机的嗡嗡声，斯密正坐在机前。手脚总是那么勤快，人又总是那么乐意帮忙，平平凡凡到了家，叫人说不出地怜悯的斯密。我也猜不透，他为什么竟能叫人无限怜惜；除非是因为，他对这份可怜毫无察觉，而这又格外可怜。就连壮汉看见他，也得赶紧把脸转开。有好几回夏日黄昏，虎克眼泪的泉源都被他触动，竟然涌流起来。对于这一切，斯密跟对几乎所有的事一样，浑然不觉。
几个海盗趴在船舷上，大口吸着夜里的瘴气。另一些横七竖八靠在木桶旁边，掷骰子，打纸牌。抬小屋的那四个人累坏了，趴在甲板上。就是在睡梦里，他们也会很有技巧地往这边一滚、往那边一滚，避开虎克够得到的地方，免得他经过时顺手钩上他们一爪。
虎克在甲板上踱步沉思。哦，这个难以测度的人！这是他获胜的时刻。彼得已经永远从他的道路上清除，其余所有男孩都在船上，眼看就要一个个踏上跳板。这是他当年降服“烤肉架”大厨以来干下的最阴狠的一桩事。我们都知道，人的躯壳是多么虚荣的一个容器。即使他这会儿叫胜利的风吹胀了肚子，在甲板上走得歪歪斜斜，我们又有什么可惊讶的呢？
可是他的步态里没有半分得意。他的脚步，与他阴郁的心思合着拍子。虎克十分沮丧。
在寂静的夜里独自在船上和自己交谈时，他常常就是这样。只因为他太孤独了。这个叫人猜不透的人，偏在自己养的狗们团团围住他的时候，感到最为孤独。他们的出身地位，比他可低得太远了。

虎克并不是他的真名。倘若透露他究竟是谁，哪怕到了今日，也会把全国搅得像着了火。不过，善于从字里行间读出意思的人想必早已猜到：他曾经上过一所有名的公学。母校的传统至今仍像衣服一样穿在他身上；事实上，那些传统中好大一部分讲的也恰恰是穿衣。因此，就是到现在，若身上还穿着刚用钩索勾住敌船时的那身衣服，便直接登上那艘船，在他看来也是失礼的。他走起路来，依然保留着那所学校特有的、高贵而略带懒散的步态。可他最放不下的，还是对“风度”的一片痴心。
风度！他不管堕落成了什么样的人，仍旧明白，世上真正要紧的就只有这个。
在内心最深处，他听见了生锈的大门开启似的一声吱呀。从门里传出严厉的笃、笃、笃，像失眠时听见深夜里有人敲锤子。“今天你可有风度？”那永远是他们问的问题。
“名声，名声，那个亮闪闪的玩意儿，我已经有了！”他喊道。
“有哪桩事特别出风头，果真合乎风度吗？”母校的敲击声这样回敬他。
“那个‘烤肉架’大厨只怕我一个，”他力陈理由，“就连弗林特本人都怕那位大厨。”
“烤肉架？弗林特？哪个宿舍出身的？”传来的反问刻薄极了。
最叫他无法安宁的还数这个念头：一心琢磨风度，这本身难道不是有失风度吗？
这问题折磨着他的五脏六腑，像一只藏在体内的利爪，比他手上的铁钩还尖锐。它一爪爪撕扯着他，汗从他蜡黄的脸上往下滴，在紧身上衣上淌出一道道痕迹。他一遍遍用袖子抹脸，可那涓涓细流怎么也截不住。
啊，别羡慕虎克。
他忽然预感到，自己的末日不远了。简直仿佛彼得发过的那个可怕的誓，已经登上了他的船。虎克心里阴郁地萌发出一个愿望，想先说好临终的遗言，免得待会儿没有工夫说。
“虎克呀，”他叫道，“当初的野心倘若能小一点，虎克本该过得好些。”他只有在心里最黑暗的时候，才用第三人称说自己。
“没有一个小孩子爱我。”
他此刻竟想起这个，真是奇怪。往昔他从没为此烦恼过。也许是缝纫机的声音叫他想到这件事。他长久地望着斯密，喃喃自语。斯密却正平心静气地缝衣边，深信天底下所有孩子见了他都害怕。
怕他！会怕斯密！那天晚上，整艘船上没有一个孩子不是早就喜欢上了他。他也曾对他们说凶狠的话，用巴掌打他们，因为他不会抡拳头。可他们反倒更亲热地簇着他了。迈克尔还试戴过他的眼镜。
要是告诉可怜的斯密，他们觉得他可爱呢！虎克心里痒痒的，真想这样说，可又觉得太残忍。他便在心中反复推敲这桩谜：他们为什么会觉得斯密可爱呢？他原是条追踪的猎犬，一咬住问题便穷追不舍。如果斯密真的可爱，是什么叫他这样可爱？猛然间，一个可怕的答案冒了出来：“风度？”
难道这水手长竟有风度，自己却不知道？恰恰这才是风度的最高一层。
他想起了，若要进学校里那个叫“波普”的社团，得先证明自己不知道自己有风度，才够资格。
他怒吼一声，把铁手高举到斯密头顶。可他没有抓下去。拦住他的，是这个念头：
“一个人有风度，你因此钩他一爪，这叫什么？”
“有失风度！”
可怜的虎克，汗淋淋的，也一样软绵绵的，使不出一点力气。他像一朵从茎上剪下的花，一头向前栽倒。
他的狗们以为这下有一阵子用不着怕他，纪律立刻松了。他们狂饮乱舞起来，闹腾得他马上又站起身，刚才那一点人类共有的软弱也随之一扫而空，好像有人兜头给他泼了一桶水。
“安静，你们这些杂种，”他喊道，“不然我把锚抛进你们肚子里！”喧嚣顿时平息。“孩子们都拿链子拴好，飞不走了，是不是？”
“是，长官。”
“那就把他们吊上来。”
除了温蒂，可怜的俘虏们全给拖出船舱，在他面前排成一列。有一阵子，他仿佛尚未察觉他们在场，懒洋洋地歪着身子，摆弄一副纸牌，哼着几句粗俗小调，倒也不算难听。隔上一会儿，雪茄的火光替他的脸照出一点血色。
“好了，伙计们，”他精神十足地说，“今晚，你们中有六个人得走跳板。可我还缺两个舱房勤杂童。你们当中，是哪两个来做？”
在船舱里的时候，温蒂曾吩咐：“别无缘无故地惹恼他。”于是图图彬彬有礼地站出来一步。他厌恶投到这种人手下当差的念头，却本能地觉得，最好把责任推到某个不在场的人身上。图图固然有点傻，却也知道，只有妈妈总是愿意站出来替人挡一下。孩子们都知道妈妈有这一点。他们为这一点有些瞧不起她们，却又时时刻刻用得着她们。
因此，图图谨慎地解释：“先生，事情是这样，我想我妈妈不会喜欢我当海盗的。斯莱特利，你妈妈喜欢你当海盗吗？”
他朝斯莱特利挤了一下眼。斯莱特利满脸悲戚，答道：“我想不会。”活像自己可巴不得情形不是这样。“双胞胎，你妈妈会喜欢你当海盗吗？”
“我想不会。”双胞胎中的老大答得和旁人一样机灵。“尼布斯，你的妈——”
“把你们的废话收起来！”虎克一吼，几个发言人便给拖了回去。“你，小子，”他对约翰说，“看着倒有那么一点胆量。你这好汉，就没想过要当个海盗？”
约翰有时候预习数学，确实犯过这种心痒的毛病。这时虎克单单挑中他，也颇叫他动心。
“我有一回想过，管自己叫血手杰克。”他不很有把握地说。
“还是个好名字呢。伙计，你要入伙，我们在船上就这么叫你。”
“你怎么想，迈克尔？”约翰问。
“我要入伙，你给我起个什么名儿？”迈克尔追问。
“黑胡子乔。”
迈克尔自然大受打动。“约翰，你怎么想？”他盼着约翰拿主意，约翰又盼着他拿主意。
“那我们还能当忠于国王的臣民吗？”约翰问。
虎克从牙缝间挤出回答：“你们得起誓说，‘打倒国王。’”
说起来，约翰此前的表现也许不大好，此刻他却真正发出了光彩。
“那我不干！”他一拳砸在虎克面前的木桶上，大喊道。
“我也不干！”迈克尔叫道。
“不列颠，统治吧！”卷毛尖声喊道。
海盗们恼羞成怒，抡手就打他们的嘴。虎克放声吼道：“这下你们死定了！把他们的妈妈带上来。预备跳板。”
他们毕竟只是些男孩，看见朱克斯和切科摆弄那块要命的木板，一个个嘴唇都白了。可是温蒂被带上来的时候，他们都使劲装出勇敢的模样。
温蒂有多瞧不起那些海盗，我实在说不出来。男孩们眼里，干海盗这一行多少有几分光彩；她看到的只是，那条船至少有好几年没好好刷洗过了。每一扇舷窗的玻璃都脏成那样，你随便挑哪个都可以拿手指头在上面写“脏猪”。有几扇她已经写过了。可当男孩们围拢在她身边，她心里自然而然只剩下他们。
“好啦，我的小美人，”虎克说，声音像泡在糖浆里，“你可要亲眼瞧瞧，你的孩子们怎样去走跳板啦。”
他尽管是位体面的绅士，方才跟自己较劲实在过于激烈，弄脏了褶皱领口。他突然明白，她正盯着那里。赶忙抬手要遮，却已经迟了。
“他们要死吗？”温蒂问。她望着他的那股轻蔑那么厉害，叫他差点儿当场昏过去。
“他们要死。”他咆哮道。接着他得意洋洋地喊：“全体肃静，听一位妈妈对她的孩子说最后几句话！”
这一刻的温蒂了不起极了。“亲爱的男孩们，我最后要说的话是这些，”她坚定地说，“我觉得，你们真正的妈妈托我带了口信。她们说：‘我们希望，我们的儿子死也要像英格兰的绅士。’”
就连海盗们也给震住了。图图歇斯底里地喊道：“我要照我妈妈的希望去做！尼布斯，你打算怎么做？”
“照我妈妈的希望去做。双胞胎，你打算怎么做？”
“照我妈妈的希望去做。约翰，你打算——”
可虎克这时又找回了自己的嗓音。
“把她绑起来！”他大声命令。
把她绑到桅杆上的是斯密。“宝贝，听我说，”他悄声道，“只要你答应当我妈妈，我就救你。”
可就算为了斯密，她也不肯许下这种诺言。“我差不多宁可一个孩子也不要。”她不屑地说。
说来叫人难过，斯密把她绑在桅杆上的时候，竟没一个男孩朝她这边看。他们的眼睛全盯着跳板：不久以后，他们就得在上面走一段短短的、最后的路了。他们甚至已不能指望自己走得像个大丈夫，因为连思考的能力都没有了，只剩下瞪眼，只剩下发抖。
虎克咬着牙朝他们微微一笑，抬脚朝温蒂走去。他想把她的脸转过来，好教她亲眼看见男孩们一个个走完跳板。可他没走到她身前，也没听见他原希望从她心底逼出的那一声惨叫。他听到了别的声音。
是鳄鱼那令人胆寒的滴答，滴答。
海盗们、男孩们、温蒂，全都听见了。立刻，每颗脑袋都像被风吹得齐齐转向一个方向。不是发出声音的水面，而是虎克。谁都知道，接下来发生的事只和他一个人有关。他们刚才还是戏里的人，这时忽然全成了看戏的。
看着他竟发生那样的变化，实在叫人害怕。仿佛每一个关节都挨了剪刀一下，他整个缩成小小一堆，瘫了下去。
那声音稳稳地越来越近。抢在它前面来的，是这个毛骨悚然的念头：“鳄鱼要上船了。”
就连铁爪也软垂着，一动不动，仿佛知道来袭的东西并没把它当作自己想要的那个人身上真正的一部分。如此可怕地给单独留下，换作旁人，早闭紧眼睛，跌在哪里就躺在哪里了。可虎克那颗非凡的脑袋还在运转。在它的指引下，他跪着沿甲板爬，能离那声音多远就多远。海盗们恭恭敬敬给他让出一条路。一直爬到船舷跟前，无路再爬，他才开口。
“把我藏起来。”他嘶声喊道。
他们在他四周围拢，谁也不肯往正在上船的东西那边看一眼。他们连抵抗的念头也没有。来的是命运。
直到再也看不见虎克，男孩们僵住的手脚才被好奇心松开。他们一齐奔到船舷边，要看鳄鱼是怎样往上爬的。就在那儿，他们遇见了这整个“夜晚中的夜晚”最出人意料的一桩奇事。爬上来救他们的，根本不是什么鳄鱼。是彼得。
他打手势示意他们，别发出钦佩的喊叫，那会惹人疑心。接着他又滴答滴答地响了下去。

sections.title_zh: 第15章　“这一次，不是虎克就是我”
sections.title_en: CHAPTER XV — 'HOOK OR ME THIS TIME'
source_paragraphs: Odd things happen to all of us on our way through life without our noticing for a time that they have happened. Thus, to take an instance, we suddenly discover that we have been deaf in one ear for we don't know how long, but, say, half an hour. Now such an experience had come that night to Peter. When last we saw him he was stealing across the island with one finger to his lips and his dagger at the ready. He had seen the crocodile pass by without noticing anything peculiar about it, but by and by he remembered that it had not been ticking. At first he thought this eerie, but soon he concluded rightly that the clock had run down.

Without giving a thought to what might be the feelings of a fellow-creature thus abruptly deprived of its closest companion, Peter at once considered how he could turn the catastrophe to his own use; and he decided to tick, so that wild beasts should believe he was the crocodile and let him pass unmolested. He ticked superbly, but with one unforeseen result. The crocodile was among those who heard the sound, and it followed him, though whether with the purpose of regaining what it had lost, or merely as a friend under the belief that it was again ticking itself, will never be certainly known, for, like all slaves to a fixed idea, it was a stupid beast.

Peter reached the shore without mishap, and went straight on; his legs encountering the water as if quite unaware that they had entered a new element. Thus many animals pass from land to water, but no other human of whom I know. As he swam he had but one thought: 'Hook or me this time.' He had ticked so long that he now went on ticking without knowing that he was doing it. Had he known he would have stopped, for to board the brig by the help of the tick, though an ingenious idea, had not occurred to him.

On the contrary, he thought he had scaled her side as noiseless as a mouse; and he was amazed to see the pirates cowering from him, with Hook in their midst as abject as if he had heard the crocodile.

The crocodile! No sooner did Peter remember it than he heard the ticking. At first he thought the sound did come from the crocodile, and he looked behind him swiftly. Then he realised that he was doing it himself, and in a flash he understood the situation. 'How clever of me,' he thought at once, and signed to the boys not to burst into applause.

It was at this moment that Ed Teynte the quartermaster emerged from the forecastle and came along the deck. Now, reader, time what happened by your watch. Peter struck true and deep. John clapped his hands on the ill-fated pirate's mouth to stifle the dying groan. He fell forward. Four boys caught him to prevent the thud. Peter gave the signal, and the carrion was cast overboard. There was a splash, and then silence. How long has it taken?
'One!' (Slightly had begun to count.)

None too soon, Peter, every inch of him on tiptoe, vanished into the cabin; for more than one pirate was screwing up his courage to look round. They could hear each other's distressed breathing now, which showed them that the more terrible sound had passed.
'It's gone, captain,' Smee said, wiping his spectacles. 'All's still again.'
Slowly Hook let his head emerge from his ruff, and listened so intently that he could have caught the echo of the tick. There was not a sound, and he drew himself up firmly to his full height.
'Then here's to Johnny Plank,' he cried brazenly, hating the boys more than ever because they had seen him unbend. He broke into the villainous ditty:

'Yo ho, yo ho, the frisky plank,
You walks along it so,
Till it goes down and you goes down
To Davy Jones below!'

To terrorise the prisoners the more, though with a certain loss of dignity, he danced along an imaginary plank, grimacing at them as he sang; and when he finished he cried, 'Do you want a touch of the cat before you walk the plank?'
At that they fell on their knees. 'No, no,' they cried so piteously that every pirate smiled.
'Fetch the cat, Jukes,' said Hook; 'it's in the cabin.'
The cabin! Peter was in the cabin! The children gazed at each other.
'Ay, ay,' said Jukes blithely, and he strode into the cabin. They followed him with their eyes; they scarce knew that Hook had resumed his song, his dogs joining in with him:

'Yo ho, yo ho, the scratching cat,
Its tails are nine, you know,
And when they're writ upon your back--

What was the last line will never be known, for of a sudden the song was stayed by a dreadful screech from the cabin. It wailed through the ship, and died away. Then was heard a crowing sound which was well understood by the boys, but to the pirates was almost more eerie than the screech.
'What was that?' cried Hook.
'Two,' said Slightly solemnly.
The Italian Cecco hesitated for a moment and then swung into the cabin. He tottered out, haggard.
'What's the matter with Bill Jukes, you dog?' hissed Hook, towering over him.
'The matter wi' him is he's dead, stabbed,' replied Cecco in a hollow Voice.
'Bill Jukes dead!' cried the startled pirates.
'The cabin's as black as a pit,' Cecco said, almost gibbering, 'but there is something terrible in there: the thing you heard crowing.'
The exultation of the boys, the lowering looks of the pirates, both were seen by Hook.
'Cecco,' he said in his most steely voice, 'go back and fetch me out that doodle-doo.'
Cecco, bravest of the brave, cowered before his captain, crying 'No, no'; but Hook was purring to his claw.
'Did you say you would go, Cecco?' he said musingly.
Cecco went, first flinging up his arms despairingly. There was no more singing, all listened now; and again came a death-screech and again a crow.
No one spoke except Slightly. 'Three,' he said.
Hook rallied his dogs with a gesture. ''Sdeath and odds fish,' he thundered, 'who is to bring me that doodle-doo?'
'Wait till Cecco comes out,' growled Starkey, and the others took up the cry.
'I think I heard you volunteer, Starkey,' said Hook, purring again.
'No, by thunder!' Starkey cried.
'My hook thinks you did,' said Hook, crossing to him. 'I wonder if it would not be advisable, Starkey, to humour the hook?'
'I'll swing before I go in there,' replied Starkey doggedly, and again he had the support of the crew.
'Is it mutiny?' asked Hook more pleasantly than ever. 'Starkey's ringleader.'
'Captain, mercy,' Starkey whimpered, all of a tremble now.
'Shake hands, Starkey,' said Hook, proffering his claw.

Starkey looked round for help, but all deserted him. As he backed Hook advanced, and now the red spark was in his eye. With a despairing scream the pirate leapt upon Long Tom and precipitated himself into the sea.
'Four,' said Slightly.

'And now,' Hook asked courteously, 'did any other gentleman say mutiny?' Seizing a lantern and raising his claw with a menacing gesture, 'I'll bring out that doodle-doo myself,' he said, and sped into the cabin.
'Five.' How Slightly longed to say it. He wetted his lips to be ready, but Hook came staggering out, without his lantern.
'Something blew out the light,' he said a little unsteadily.
'Something!' echoed Mullins.
'What of Cecco?' demanded Noodler.
'He's as dead as Jukes,' said Hook shortly.

His reluctance to return to the cabin impressed them all unfavourably, and the mutinous sounds again broke forth. All pirates are superstitious; and Cookson cried, 'They do say the surest sign a ship's accurst is when there's one on board more than can be accounted for.'
'I've heard,' muttered Mullins, 'he always boards the pirate craft at last. Had he a tail, captain?'
'They say,' said another, looking viciously at Hook, 'that when he comes it's in the likeness of the wickedest man aboard.'

'Had he a hook, captain?' asked Cookson insolently; and one after another took up the cry, 'The ship's doomed.' At this the children could not resist raising a cheer. Hook had well-nigh forgotten his prisoners, but as he swung round on them now his face lit up again.

'Lads,' he cried to his crew, 'here's a notion. Open the cabin door and drive them in. Let them fight the doodle-doo for their lives. If they kill him, we're so much the better; if he kills them, we're none the worse.'
For the last time his dogs admired Hook, and devotedly they did his bidding. The boys, pretending to struggle, were pushed into the cabin and the door was closed on them.

'Now, listen,' cried Hook, and all listened. But not one dared to face the door. Yes, one, Wendy, who all this time had been bound to the mast. It was for neither a scream nor a crow that she was watching; it was for the reappearance of Peter.

She had not long to wait. In the cabin he had found the thing for which he had gone in search: the key that would free the children of their manacles; and now they all stole forth, armed with such weapons as they could find. First signing to them to hide, Peter cut Wendy's bonds, and then nothing could have been easier than for them all to fly off together; but one thing barred the way, an oath, 'Hook or me this time.' So when he had freed Wendy, he whispered to her to conceal herself with the others, and himself took her place by the mast, her cloak around him so that he should pass for her. Then he took a great breath and crowed.

To the pirates it was a voice crying that all the boys lay slain in the cabin; and they were panic-stricken. Hook tried to hearten them; but like the dogs he had made them they showed him their fangs, and he knew that if he took his eyes off them now they would leap at him.
'Lads,' he said, ready to cajole or strike as need be, but never quailing for an instant, 'I've thought it out. There's a Jonah abroad.'
'Ay,' they snarled, 'a man wi' a hook.'
'No, lads, no, it's the girl. Never was luck on a pirate ship wi' a woman on board. We'll right the ship when she's gone.'
Some of them remembered that this had been a saying of Flint's. 'It's worth trying,' they said doubtfully.
'Fling the girl overboard,' cried Hook; and they made a rush at the figure in the cloak.
'There's none can save you now, missy,' Mullins hissed jeeringly.
'There's one,' replied the figure.
'Who's that?'

'Peter Pan the avenger!' came the terrible answer; and as he spoke Peter flung off his cloak. Then they all knew who 'twas that had been undoing them in the cabin, and twice Hook essayed to speak and twice he failed. In that frightful moment I think his fierce heart broke.
At last he cried, 'Cleave him to the brisket,' but without conviction.

'Down, boys, and at them,' Peter's voice rang out; and in another moment the clash of arms was resounding through the ship. Had the pirates kept together it is certain that they would have won; but the onset came when they were all unstrung, and they ran hither and thither, striking wildly, each thinking himself the last survivor of the crew. Man to man they were the stronger; but they fought on the defensive only, which enabled the boys to hunt in pairs and choose their quarry. Some of the miscreants leapt into the sea; others hid in dark recesses, where they were found by Slightly, who did not fight, but ran about with a lantern which he flashed in their faces, so that they were half blinded and fell an easy prey to the reeking swords of the other boys. There was little sound to be heard but the clang of weapons, an occasional screech or splash, and Slightly monotonously counting--five--six--seven--eight-- nine--ten--eleven.

I think all were gone when a group of savage boys surrounded Hook, who seemed to have a charmed life, as he kept them at bay in that circle of fire. They had done for his dogs, but this man alone seemed to be a match for them all. Again and again they closed upon him, and again and again he hewed a clear space. He had lifted up one boy with his hook, and was using him as a buckler, when another, who had just passed his sword through Mullins, sprang into the fray.
'Put up your swords, boys,' cried the newcomer, 'this man is mine.'
Thus suddenly Hook found himself face to face with Peter. The others drew back and formed a ring round them.
For long the two enemies looked at one another; Hook shuddering slightly, and Peter with the strange smile upon his face.
'So, Pan,' said Hook at last, 'this is all your doing.'
'Ay, James Hook,' came the stern answer, 'it is all my doing.'
'Proud and insolent youth,' said Hook, 'prepare to meet thy doom.'
'Dark and sinister man,' Peter answered, 'have at thee.'

Without more words they fell to, and for a space there was no advantage to either blade. Peter was a superb swordsman, and parried with dazzling rapidity; ever and anon he followed up a feint with a lunge that got past his foe's defence, but his shorter reach stood him in ill stead, and he could not drive the steel home. Hook, scarcely his inferior in brilliancy, but not quite so nimble in wrist play, forced him back by the weight of his onset, hoping suddenly to end all with a favourite thrust, taught him long ago by Barbecue at Rio; but to his astonishment he found this thrust turned aside again and again. Then he sought to close and give the quietus with his iron hook, which all this time had been pawing the air; but Peter doubled under it and, lunging fiercely, pierced him in the ribs. At sight of his own blood, whose peculiar colour, you remember, was offensive to him, the sword fell from Hook's hand, and he was at Peter's mercy.
'Now!' cried all the boys; but with a magnificent gesture Peter invited his opponent to pick up his sword. Hook did so instantly, but with a tragic feeling that Peter was showing good form.
Hitherto he had thought it was some fiend fighting him, but darker suspicions assailed him now.
'Pan, who and what art thou?' he cried huskily.
'I'm youth, I'm joy,' Peter answered at a venture, 'I'm a little bird that has broken out of the egg.'
This, of course, was nonsense; but it was proof to the unhappy Hook that Peter did not know in the least who or what he was, which is the very pinnacle of good form.
'To 't again,' he cried despairingly.

He fought now like a human flail, and every sweep of that terrible sword would have severed in twain any man or boy who obstructed it; but Peter fluttered round him as if the very wind it made blew him out of the danger zone. And again and again he darted in and pricked.
Hook was fighting now without hope. That passionate breast no longer asked for life; but for one boon it craved: to see Peter bad form before it was cold for ever.
Abandoning the fight he rushed into the powder magazine and fired it.
'In two minutes,' he cried, 'the ship will be blown to pieces.'
Now, now, he thought, true form will show.
But Peter issued from the powder magazine with the shell in his hands, and calmly flung it overboard.

What sort of form was Hook himself showing? Misguided man though he was, we may be glad, without sympathising with him, that in the end he was true to the traditions of his race. The other boys were flying around him now, flouting, scornful; and as he staggered about the deck striking up at them impotently, his mind was no longer with them; it was slouching in the playing fields of long ago, or being sent up for good, or watching the wall-game from a famous wall. And his shoes were right, and his waistcoat was right, and his tie was right, and his socks were right.
James Hook, thou not wholly unheroic figure, farewell.
For we have come to his last moment.

Seeing Peter slowly advancing upon him through the air with dagger poised, he sprang upon the bulwarks to cast himself into the sea. He did not know that the crocodile was waiting for him; for we purposely stopped the clock that this knowledge might be spared him: a little mark of respect from us at the end.

He had one last triumph, which I think we need not grudge him. As he stood on the bulwark looking over his shoulder at Peter gliding through the air, he invited him with a gesture to use his foot. It made Peter kick instead of stab.
At last Hook had got the boon for which he craved.
'Bad form,' he cried jeeringly, and went content to the crocodile.
Thus perished James Hook.

'Seventeen,' Slightly sang out; but he was not quite correct in his figures. Fifteen paid the penalty for their crimes that night; but two reached the shore: Starkey to be captured by the redskins, who made him nurse for all their papooses, a melancholy come-down for a pirate; and Smee, who henceforth wandered about the world in his spectacles, making a precarious living by saying he was the only man that Jas. Hook had feared.

Wendy, of course, had stood by taking no part in the fight, though watching Peter with glistening eyes; but now that all was over she became prominent again. She praised them equally, and shuddered delightfully when Michael showed her the place where he had killed one; and then she took them into Hook's cabin and pointed to his watch which was hanging on a nail. It said 'half-past one'!

The lateness of the hour was almost the biggest thing of all. She got them to bed in the pirates' bunks pretty quickly, you may be sure; all but Peter, who strutted up and down on deck, until at last he fell asleep by the side of Long Tom. He had one of his dreams that night, and cried in his sleep for a long time, and Wendy held him tight.
translated_paragraphs: 人活在世上，总会遇上些奇怪的事。事情已经发生了，有一阵子自己还不曾察觉。譬如，会突然发觉一只耳朵听不见声音已经有些时候了，究竟多久说不好，就算半个钟头吧。那天晚上，彼得便有了一场类似的经历。上回看见他时，他正悄悄穿行在岛上，指头竖在嘴边，匕首随时可以出手。他看见鳄鱼从身边经过，没觉得有什么奇怪。隔了好一阵，才想起来，它刚才怎么没滴答响呢？起初他觉得有些诡异，随后很快就猜对了。钟的发条走完了。

一只活物忽然失去了与自己形影不离的伙伴，心里会是什么滋味？彼得一丝半毫也没往那上头想。他立刻盘算的是，自己怎样利用这场灾祸才好。他决定学那滴答声，让野兽们相信他是鳄鱼，好不来找他的麻烦。他滴答得妙极了，却有一个没料到的结果：听见声音的野兽中，也有鳄鱼自己。它便跟在他身后。它是想找回失去的东西呢，还是以为自己又响起来了，只当跟朋友顺路？谁也永远没法确切知道。因为和一切脑子里只有一个死念头的生灵一样，它是只笨野兽。
彼得平安走到了岸边，脚下不停，径直往前。两条腿碰进水里，仿佛丝毫不曾察觉，身边已换了一种天地。好多动物都能这样从陆地走进水里，不过就我所知，旁的人没有这本事。他游着泳，心里只剩一个念头：“这回不是虎克，就是我。”滴答了太久，他如今还在接着响，自己却压根儿没觉着。他要是知道，反倒会停下来。仗着滴答声上船，固然是个聪明主意，他可从没想到过。
正相反，他以为自己像耗子一样没声没息地爬过了船舷。他惊讶地望见，海盗们竟全给他吓得缩成一团，中间的虎克烂泥似的瘫着，简直活像听见了鳄鱼。
鳄鱼！彼得刚想到它，便也听见了滴答声。起先他还以为声响真是从鳄鱼那儿来的，倏地回过头望。接着他才意识到，是他自己在响。一瞬间，事情全明白了。“我可真聪明！”他头一个念头就是这个，同时给男孩们打了个手势，叫他们可别鼓掌。
就在这时，舵手长埃德·泰恩特从船首的水手舱走出来，沿甲板走近。读者呀，请你看一眼表，给接下来的事计个时。彼得准确地刺了下去，刀扎得很深。约翰双手捂住那倒霉海盗的嘴，把临死的呻吟堵在里面。他一头往前栽。四个孩子接住了，没让他落地砰的一响。彼得一打信号，尸首便给扔下船舷。扑通一声，随即寂静。用了多久？
“一个！”（斯莱特利开始数了。）
彼得浑身上下从头到脚都像踮起了脚尖，一闪便没入了船舱里。真是一刻也不早，因为正有不止一个海盗鼓足勇气，打算回头去瞧。他们总算听得见彼此急促不安的呼吸，这就说明，那个更可怕的声响已经过去了。
“它走啦，船长，”斯密一边擦眼镜一边说，“一切又安静下来了。”
虎克慢慢把脑袋从褶皱领口里探出来，听得那么仔细，便是那滴答声留下的一点回音，怕也逃不过他的耳朵。一点声音都没有了。他这才坚定地把腰一挺，恢复了十足的身量。
“那好，为约翰尼跳板干杯！”他厚着脸皮大喝。男孩们看见了他方才丢脸的样子，所以他比先前更恨他们。他开口唱起那首恶棍的小调：

“哟嗬，哟嗬，跳板直颤悠，
照这样子往前走；
板子落下你也落，
海底找戴维·琼斯做朋友！”
为了把俘虏吓得更厉害些，他连风度也多少顾不得了，挤眉弄眼地朝他们唱着，沿一块看不见的跳板跳起舞来。唱完了，他大声问：“走跳板以前，想不想先尝一尝九尾猫的滋味？”
他们立刻跪了下来。“不要，不要！”他们叫得那么可怜，每个海盗都笑了。
“朱克斯，去拿九尾猫。”虎克说，“在船舱里。”
船舱！彼得就在船舱里呀！孩子们互相望着。
“遵命，长官！”朱克斯快快活活地答应，迈开大步进了船舱。孩子们的眼睛一直跟着他走，虎克已经接着唱起歌来，他的狗们也随声合唱，他们几乎没有注意：

“哟嗬，哟嗬，这只猫会挠，
它呀，尾巴共有九条；
九道字印写上你的背——”
最后一句是什么，永远没法知道了。一声骇人的尖叫突然从舱里传来，打断了歌。那叫声凄厉地穿过整条船，渐渐消失。接着响起一声雄鸡啼。男孩们明白它是什么意思，可海盗们听来，这声音几乎比刚才那声惨叫更加阴森。
“那是什么？”虎克喊道。
“两个。”斯莱特利庄严地数道。
意大利人切科犹豫片刻，才大步跨进舱去。转眼又踉踉跄跄地出来了，神色憔悴不堪。
“狗东西，比尔·朱克斯怎么了？”虎克居高临下，从齿缝里嘶声问。
“他怎么了？他死了。给刀捅死了。”切科的声音空洞洞的。
“比尔·朱克斯死了！”海盗们惊呼。
“舱里黑得像个深坑，”切科说，吓得几乎语无伦次，“可里头有个可怕的东西，就是你们听见学鸡叫的那个东西。”
男孩们喜形于色，海盗们各个阴沉着脸，这两样都逃不过虎克的眼睛。
“切科，”他用最冷冰冰的声音说，“回去，把那个喔喔叫的给我弄出来。”
切科是勇士中的勇士，到了船长跟前却畏缩起来，直喊“不，不”。虎克正对着他的钩子咕噜咕噜地说着亲切话。
“切科，我听见你说愿意去，是不是？”他若有所思地问。
切科去了。临去先绝望地把两手往上一举。没人再唱歌了。大家都侧着耳朵听。又是一声临死的惨叫，又是一声雄鸡啼。
除了斯莱特利，没人说话。“三个。”他数道。
虎克挥手招拢他的狗。“见鬼，要命的怪鱼！”他雷鸣般地吼道，“谁去把那个喔喔叫的给我拿来？”
“等切科出来再说。”斯塔基咆哮道。旁人也跟着叫起来。
“斯塔基，我好像听见你说，你自愿去。”虎克又和和气气地咕噜起来。
“天打雷劈，我可没有！”斯塔基喊道。
“我的钩子觉得你有。”虎克朝他走过去，“斯塔基，我在想，顺一顺这只钩子的心意，会不会更明智些？”
“我宁肯上绞架，也不肯进那里面去。”斯塔基执拗地回答。船员们又都站在他一边。
“这是哗变吗？”虎克问得比任何时候都愉快，“斯塔基是首领。”
“船长，饶命。”斯塔基哀求道，这时他浑身上下全抖了起来。
“握个手吧，斯塔基。”虎克说着，把铁爪递过去。
斯塔基四下一望，希望有人帮他一把，却没人肯帮。他一步步退，虎克一步步进，眼里已燃起那点红色的火花。海盗绝望地惨叫一声，跃上“长汤姆”大炮，一头扎进了海里。
“四个。”斯莱特利说。
“现在呢，”虎克温文尔雅地问，“还有哪位绅士提过哗变吗？”他抓起一盏灯，带着威胁一抬铁爪，说：“我自己去把那喔喔叫的给带出来。”说完飞身进了船舱。
“五个。”斯莱特利多想这样说啊。他先舔了舔嘴唇，预备开口。可虎克又踉跄着出来了，灯却不见了。
“有样东西吹灭了灯。”他说，声音不大稳。
“有样东西！”马林斯重复道。
“切科呢？”努德勒追问。
“跟朱克斯一样死透了。”虎克简短地说。
看他不肯再进船舱，一个个都对船长失了信心，哗变的声音再度响起。海盗无不迷信。库克森喊道：“听人说，船上要是多出一个讲不清来历的人，那就是这艘船遭了诅咒最灵验的征兆。”
“我听说，”马林斯咕哝道，“他最后总会登上海盗船。船长，他是不是长着尾巴？”
“人家说，”另一个恶狠狠盯着虎克，开了口，“他一来，就会化作这条船上最坏的那个人的模样。”
“船长，他也有只钩子吗？”库克森无礼地问。接下来，一个又一个跟着叫：“这船完了！”听到这里，孩子们忍不住欢呼了一声。虎克几乎把俘虏忘了。如今猛一转身瞧着他们，他的脸上又亮了起来。
“伙计们，”他对船员喊道，“我有个主意。把舱门打开，把他们全赶进去。让他们为了自己的命去跟那个喔喔叫的打。要是他们杀了它，对我们更好；要是它把他们都杀了，我们也没有损失。”
这是他那些狗最后一回佩服虎克。他们忠心耿耿地奉命办事。男孩们假装挣扎着，给推入舱内，门随即在身后关闭。
“听着！”虎克大喝一声。所有人都侧耳听，却没有一个人敢正面朝向那扇门。不对，有一个人敢，那就是温蒂。她一直被绑在桅杆上。她等着看的既不是惨叫，也不是鸡啼，她在等彼得重新出现。

她并没有等多久。彼得在船舱里找到了他进去要找的东西：一把能替孩子们打开镣铐的钥匙。此刻，男孩们各自找来兵器，悄悄溜出了舱。他先示意他们藏好，随即割断温蒂身上的绳子。这下大家要一块儿飞走，简直是再容易不过。只有一样东西挡着去路，是一个誓言：“这回不是虎克，就是我。”所以，替温蒂松了绑，他便悄声叫她也跟其余的人一道隐蔽，自己披上她的斗篷，站到她原先靠着桅杆的地方，假冒是她。然后他深深吸一口气，放声啼叫。
在海盗们听来，那声啼叫等于宣告，男孩们已全部倒毙在舱里。他们心胆俱裂。虎克试着给他们打气，可他一手调教出来的狗们却把獠牙冲向了他。他知道，只要自己此刻稍稍移开目光，他们就会朝他扑来。
“伙计们，”他说，要哄要打，都随时有所准备，却连一瞬也没有胆怯，“我已经想通了。咱们船上有个带来厄运的约拿。”
“不错，”他们龇牙咧嘴地说，“是个长钩子的家伙。”
“不，伙计们，不，是那姑娘！一条海盗船上只要有了女人，事情准不顺当。赶走了她，船就会时来运转。”
有几个想起来，弗林特从前是说过这样的话。“倒值得试一试。”他们将信将疑地说。
“把那姑娘扔下海！”虎克大喊。于是那一伙人都朝披斗篷的身影扑去。
“小姑娘，这回没谁能救你了。”马林斯嘶声嘲弄道。
“还有一位。”那个身影答道。
“是谁？”
“报仇者彼得·潘！”回答令他们魂飞魄散。彼得说着，一把掀开了斗篷。他们这才全明白，在舱里收拾他们的究竟是谁。虎克两次想开口，两次都说不出话来。我想，在那可怕的一瞬间，他那颗凶烈的心碎了。
他终于喊出一声：“把他从头劈到胸口！”可这话他自己也没把握。

“下来，男孩们，上！”彼得的声音响彻全船。转眼间，兵器碰撞的声音就在船上四处回荡。要是海盗们能聚在一起，打赢的准会是他们。可男孩们动手的时候，他们已经人人慌了神，像没头苍蝇一样乱跑乱砍，个个以为自己是全船最后一个活着的人。若是一对一，他们的力气本来更强。可他们只顾招架，男孩们便能成双结对，自己拣选猎物。有几个恶棍跳下了海；另一些藏到黑暗的角落里，却让斯莱特利找着了。他没有动刀，只举着灯到处跑，一寻着人，就把光直晃到那人脸上，晃得海盗一时眼花，轻易就落入其余男孩犹带热血的刀剑之下。船上几乎没有别的声音，只有兵刃铿然，偶尔一声尖叫或一声落水响，还有斯莱特利用一个腔调不停地数：五，六，七，八，九，十，十一。
我想，等一群打红了眼的男孩把虎克围起来的时候，旁的人都已经给解决了。独有虎克的命仿佛受了魔法庇护，在那道火圈里兀自挡得住众人。他的狗们全被收拾了，这一个人却似乎足以匹敌他们所有人。男孩们一次又一次近身围攻，他一次又一次杀出一片空地。他用钩子提起一个男孩，拿他当盾牌。正在这时，又有一人跃入战团，他刚刚才用剑刺穿了马林斯。
“收剑，男孩们，”新来的人喊道，“这个人是我的。”
如此突然，虎克便同彼得正面相对。其余的人都退开去，在两人身边围起一个圈子。
这对仇敌久久对视。虎克微微发抖，彼得脸上又挂着那种奇异的笑。
“这么说来，潘，”虎克终于开口，“这一切都是你干的。”
“不错，詹姆斯·虎克，”回答庄严冷峻，“都是我干的。”
“狂妄无礼的少年，”虎克说，“预备迎接你的末日吧。”
“阴险狠毒的男人，”彼得答道，“接我的剑！”

两人不再多说，动起手来。一时两把剑谁也占不到上风。彼得的剑术出神入化，招架得快到叫人眼花。时不时，他先假作攻势，紧跟一记直刺，便能越过对方的防守。可他胳膊终究短了一截，钢刃不能刺到实处。虎克剑术的华美几乎不输给他，运腕却不如他灵活。他凭沉重的攻势把彼得步步往后逼，一心想用最爱的一招直刺出其不意地结果他。那是很久以前在里约，海上大厨教给他的绝活。可令他大吃一惊的是，这一招竟一次次被挑开了。他便设法贴身，要用始终在空中抓挠的铁钩给彼得致命一击。彼得俯身从钩子下钻过去，一记凶狠的突刺，正扎进他肋间。你记得，他讨厌自己那种颜色古怪的血。他一看见这血，剑就从手里掉了。此刻，彼得要怎样处置他都可以。
“就是现在！”男孩们齐声叫喊。彼得却作了个极有气派的手势，请对手拾起剑来。虎克立刻照办，心里却感到一种悲哀：彼得正在显出极好的风度。
到这会儿为止，他还以为跟自己交手的是个什么魔鬼；现在，更阴沉的疑虑向他袭来。
“潘，你是谁？你究竟是什么？”他嘶哑地叫道。
“我是青春，我是快乐，”彼得顺口猜着回答，“我是只刚啄破蛋壳的小鸟。”
这话当然没有道理。可在不幸的虎克眼里，这说明彼得自己根本不知道他是谁，更不知道他究竟是什么。而这，恰恰是风度的顶峰。
“再来！”他绝望地叫道。
此刻他挥剑作战，简直像一架人形的连枷。那把可怕的剑每一横扫，任何拦在面前的男人或男孩，都会给劈作两半。可彼得在他身边轻巧翻飞，仿佛剑上刮起的风恰好把他吹出了险地。他一次次倏地扑进来，扎上一剑，又飘开。
虎克这时候已不抱胜利的希望。那颗满怀激情的心不再奢求活命，只渴望得到最后一点恩典：在它永远冷却以前，亲眼看见彼得失一次风度。
他弃战转身，冲进火药舱，点起火来。
“两分钟后，”他喊道，“这条船就要炸得粉碎。”
这下，这下总该露出真风度来了吧！他想。
彼得却从火药舱走出来，手里拿着那颗炮弹，镇定自若地把它扔过了船舷。

虎克自己又显出了什么风度呢？他尽管误入歧途，我们虽不同情他，却也可以为一件事高兴：直到最后，他都忠实于自己那一班人的传统。其余男孩此时正在他四周翻飞，起哄嘲弄，满脸轻蔑。他踉跄着走过甲板，力不从心地朝他们头顶挥击。可他的心思已不在孩子们身上。它正迈着懒懒的步子，走在久远以前的学校运动场上；或者想起佳作送呈校长称许的荣誉，想起倚在那堵名墙上观看校里的墙球赛。那时他的鞋穿得合规矩，背心穿得合规矩，领带系得合规矩，连袜子也穿得合规矩。
詹姆斯·虎克呀，你毕竟还称不上是一个全无英雄气概的人。永别了。
因为我们已经来到了他生命的最后一刻。
他看见彼得举着匕首从空中慢慢向自己逼近，纵身跳上船舷，打算投海。他不知道，那条鳄鱼正在等着他。我们特意让那只钟停住，为的就是叫他不必知道。临了，这是我们向他致上的一点敬意。
他还有最后一桩胜利。我想，这点胜利我们不必吝于给他。他站在船舷上，回头越过肩膀望着在半空滑来的彼得，做个手势，请他动脚。这一下，彼得果然踢了一脚，没有使刀去刺。
虎克苦求的那点恩典，终于得到了。
“有失风度！”他嘲笑着喊了一声，心满意足地投向了鳄鱼。
詹姆斯·虎克就这样丧了命。
“十七个！”斯莱特利唱念般地高喊。可是他的数字不完全对。那一夜，为自己的罪行付出代价的是十五个。另有两人到达了岸上：斯塔基被印第安人俘虏，派去给他们族里所有的小宝宝当保姆。这副境地，对海盗来说可是够凄凉的。斯密则戴着眼镜，打这以后四海流浪，逢人就说自己是詹姆斯·虎克唯一害怕的人，靠这句话勉强糊口。
温蒂自然一直站在一边，没有参战，虽说她亮晶晶的眼睛始终跟着彼得。可如今仗打完了，她又站到了大家中间。每个人她都一样地夸奖；迈克尔指给她看，自己是在哪里杀了一个海盗的，她便快快活活地打了个寒战。然后她领着他们进了虎克的船舱，指着挂在一枚钉子上的怀表。表针指的是：一点半！
已经这么晚了，差不多比所有的事都了不得。你尽可信她马上就把他们全送上海盗的铺位去睡了。只剩彼得，还趾高气扬地在甲板上走来走去，直到最后在“长汤姆”旁边睡着。那一夜他又做了那种梦，在梦里哭了好久。温蒂把他紧紧抱在怀里。

source_paragraphs: By two bells that morning they were all stirring their stumps; for there was a big sea running; and Tootles, the bo'sun, was among them, with a rope's end in his hand and chewing tobacco. They all donned pirate clothes cut off at the knee, shaved smartly, and tumbled up, with the true nautical roll and hitching their trousers.

It need not be said who was the captain. Nibs and John were first and second mate. There was a woman aboard. The rest were tars before the mast, and lived in the fo'c'sle. Peter had already lashed himself to the wheel; but he piped all hands and delivered a short address to them; said he hoped they would do their duty like gallant hearties, but that he knew they were the scum of Rio and the Gold Coast, and if they snapped at him he would tear them. His bluff strident words struck the note sailors understand, and they cheered him lustily. Then a few sharp orders were given, and they turned the ship round, and nosed her for the mainland.
Captain Pan calculated, after consulting the ship's chart, that if this weather lasted they should strike the Azores about the 21st of June, after which it would save time to fly.

Some of them wanted it to be an honest ship and others were in favour of keeping it a pirate; but the captain treated them as dogs, and they dared not express their wishes to him even in a round robin. Instant obedience was the only safe thing. Slightly got a dozen for looking perplexed when told to take soundings. The general feeling was that Peter was honest just now to lull Wendy's suspicions, but that there might be a change when the new suit was ready, which, against her will, she was making for him out of some of Hook's wickedest garments. It was afterwards whispered among them that on the first night he wore this suit he sat long in the cabin with Hook's cigar-holder in his mouth and one hand clenched, all but the forefinger, which he bent and held threateningly aloft like a hook.

Instead of watching the ship, however, we must now return to that desolate home from which three of our characters had taken heartless flight so long ago. It seems a shame to have neglected No. 14 all this time; and yet we may be sure that Mrs. Darling does not blame us. If we had returned sooner to look with sorrowful sympathy at her, she would probably have cried, 'Don't be silly; what do I matter? Do go back and keep an eye on the children.' So long as mothers are like this their children will take advantage of them; and they may lay to that.

Even now we venture into that familiar nursery only because its lawful occupants are on their way home; we are merely hurrying on in advance of them to see that their beds are properly aired and that Mr. and Mrs. Darling do not go out for the evening. We are no more than servants. Why on earth should their beds be properly aired, seeing that they left them in such a thankless hurry? Would it not serve them jolly well right if they came back and found that their parents were spending the week-end in the country? It would be the moral lesson they have been in need of ever since we met them; but if we contrived things in this way Mrs. Darling would never forgive us.

One thing I should like to do immensely, and that is to tell her, in the way authors have, that the children are coming back, that indeed they will be here on Thursday week. This would spoil so completely the surprise to which Wendy and John and Michael are looking forward. They have been planning it out on the ship: mother's rapture, father's shout of joy, Nana's leap through the air to embrace them first, when what they ought to be preparing for is a good hiding. How delicious to spoil it all by breaking the news in advance; so that when they enter grandly Mrs. Darling may not even offer Wendy her mouth, and Mr. Darling may exclaim pettishly, 'Dash it all, here are those boys again.' However, we should get no thanks even for this. We are beginning to know Mrs. Darling by this time, and may be sure that she would upbraid us for depriving the children of their little pleasure.
'But, my dear madam, it is ten days till Thursday week; so that by telling you what's what, we can save you ten days of unhappiness.'
'Yes, but at what a cost! By depriving the children of ten minutes of delight.'
'Oh, if you look at it in that way.'
'What other way is there in which to look at it?'

You see, the woman had no proper spirit. I had meant to say extraordinarily nice things about her; but I despise her, and not one of them will I say now. She does not really need to be told to have things ready, for they are ready. All the beds are aired, and she never leaves the house, and observe, the window is open. For all the use we are to her, we might go back to the ship. However, as we are here we may as well stay and look on. That is all we are, lookers-on. Nobody really wants us. So let us watch and say jaggy things, in the hope that some of them will hurt.

The only change to be seen in the night-nursery is that between nine and six the kennel is no longer there. When the children flew away, Mr. Darling felt in his bones that all the blame was his for having chained Nana up, and that from first to last she had been wiser than he. Of course, as we have seen, he was quite a simple man; indeed he might have passed for a boy again if he had been able to take his baldness off; but he had also a noble sense of justice and a lion courage to do what seemed right to him; and having thought the matter out with anxious care after the flight of the children, he went down on all fours and crawled into the kennel. To all Mrs. Darling's dear invitations to him to come out he replied sadly but firmly:
'No, my own one, this is the place for me.'

In the bitterness of his remorse he swore that he would never leave the kennel until his children came back. Of course this was a pity; but whatever Mr. Darling did he had to do in excess; otherwise he soon gave up doing it. And there never was a more humble man than the once proud George Darling, as he sat in the kennel of an evening talking with his wife of their children and all their pretty ways.
Very touching was his deference to Nana. He would not let her come into the kennel, but on all other matters he followed her wishes implicitly.

Every morning the kennel was carried with Mr. Darling in it to a cab, which conveyed him to his office, and he returned home in the same way at six. Something of the strength of character of the man will be seen if we remember how sensitive he was to the opinion of neighbours: this man whose every movement now attracted surprised attention. Inwardly he must have suffered torture; but he preserved a calm exterior even when the young criticised his little home, and he always lifted his hat courteously to any lady who looked inside.

It may have been quixotic, but it was magnificent. Soon the inward meaning of it leaked out, and the great heart of the public was touched. Crowds followed the cab, cheering it lustily; charming girls scaled it to get his autograph; interviews appeared in the better class of papers, and society invited him to dinner and added, 'Do come in the kennel.'

On that eventful Thursday week Mrs. Darling was in the night-nursery awaiting George's return home: a very sad-eyed woman. Now that we look at her closely and remember the gaiety of her in the old days, all gone now just because she has lost her babes, I find I won't be able to say nasty things about her after all. If she was too fond of her rubbishy children she couldn't help it. Look at her in her chair, where she has fallen asleep. The corner of her mouth, where one looks first, is almost withered up. Her hand moves restlessly on her breast as if she had a pain there. Some like Peter best and some like Wendy best, but I like her best. Suppose, to make her happy, we whisper to her in her sleep that the brats are coming back. They are really within two miles of the window now, and flying strong, but all we need whisper is that they are on the way. Let's.
It is a pity we did it, for she has started up, calling their names; and there is no one in the room but Nana.
'O Nana, I dreamt my dear ones had come back.'

Nana had filmy eyes, but all she could do was to put her paw gently on her mistress's lap; and they were sitting together thus when the kennel was brought back. As Mr. Darling puts his head out at it to kiss his wife, we see that his face is more worn than of yore, but has a softer expression.

He gave his hat to Liza, who took it scornfully; for she had no imagination, and was quite incapable of understanding the motives of such a man. Outside, the crowd who had accompanied the cab home were still cheering, and he was naturally not unmoved.
'Listen to them,' he said; 'it is very gratifying.'
'Lot of little boys,' sneered Liza.

'There were several adults to-day,' he assured her with a faint flush; but when she tossed her head he had not a word of reproof for her. Social success had not spoilt him; it had made him sweeter. For some time he sat half out of the kennel, talking with Mrs. Darling of this success, and pressing her hand reassuringly when she said she hoped his head would not be turned by it.
'But if I had been a weak man,' he said. 'Good heavens, if I had been a weak man!'
'And, George,' she said timidly, 'you are as full of remorse as ever, aren't you?'
'Full of remorse as ever, dearest! See my punishment: living in a kennel.'
'But it is punishment, isn't it, George? You are sure you are not enjoying it?'
'My love!'
You may be sure she begged his pardon; and then, feeling drowsy, he curled round in the kennel.
'Won't you play me to sleep,' he asked, 'on the nursery piano?' and as she was crossing to the day nursery he added thoughtlessly, 'And shut that window. I feel a draught.'
'O George, never ask me to do that. The window must always be left open for them, always, always.'
Now it was his turn to beg her pardon; and she went into the day nursery and played, and soon he was asleep; and while he slept, Wendy and John and Michael flew into the room.

Oh no. We have written it so, because that was the charming arrangement planned by them before we left the ship; but something must have happened since then, for it is not they who have flown in, it is Peter and Tinker Bell.
Peter's first words tell all.

'Quick, Tink,' he whispered, 'close the window; bar it. That's right. Now you and I must get away by the door; and when Wendy comes she will think her mother has barred her out; and she will have to go back with me.'

Now I understand what had hitherto puzzled me, why when Peter had exterminated the pirates he did not return to the island and leave Tink to escort the children to the mainland. This trick had been in his head all the time.

Instead of feeling that he was behaving badly he danced with glee; then he peeped into the day-nursery to see who was playing. He whispered to Tink, 'It's Wendy's mother. She is a pretty lady, but not so pretty as my mother. Her mouth is full of thimbles, but not so full as my mother's was.'
Of course he knew nothing whatever about his mother; but he sometimes bragged about her.

He did not know the tune, which was 'Home, Sweet Home,' but he knew it was saying, 'Come back, Wendy, Wendy, Wendy'; and he cried exultantly, 'You will never see Wendy again, lady, for the window is barred.'
He peeped in again to see why the music had stopped; and now he saw that Mrs. Darling had laid her head on the box, and that two tears were sitting on her eyes.
'She wants me to unbar the window,' thought Peter, 'but I won't, not I.'
He peeped again, and the tears were still there, or another two had taken their place.
'She's awfully fond of Wendy,' he said to himself. He was angry with her now for not seeing why she could not have Wendy.
The reason was so simple: 'I'm fond of her too. We can't both have her, lady.'

But the lady would not make the best of it, and he was unhappy. He ceased to look at her, but even then she would not let go of him. He skipped about and made funny faces, but when he stopped it was just as if she were inside him, knocking.

'Oh, all right,' he said at last, and gulped. Then he unbarred the window. 'Come on, Tink,' he cried, with a frightful sneer at the laws of nature; 'we don't want any silly mothers'; and he flew away.

Thus Wendy and John and Michael found the window open for them after all, which of course was more than they deserved. They alighted on the floor, quite unashamed of themselves; and the youngest one had already forgotten his home.
'John,' he said, looking around him doubtfully, 'I think I have been here before.'
'Of course you have, you silly. There is your old bed.'
'So it is,' Michael said, but not with much conviction.
'I say,' cried John, 'the kennel!' and he dashed across to look into it.
'Perhaps Nana is inside it,' Wendy said.
But John whistled. 'Hullo,' he said, 'there's a man inside it.'
'It's father!' exclaimed Wendy.

'Let me see father,' Michael begged eagerly, and he took a good look. 'He is not so big as the pirate I killed,' he said with such frank disappointment that I am glad Mr. Darling was asleep; it would have been sad if those had been the first words he heard his little Michael say.
Wendy and John had been taken aback somewhat at finding their father in the kennel.
'Surely,' said John, like one who had lost faith in his memory, 'he used not to sleep in the kennel?'
'John,' Wendy said falteringly, 'perhaps we don't remember the old life as well as we thought we did.'
A chill fell upon them; and serve them right.
'It is very careless of mother,' said that young scoundrel John, 'not to be here when we come back.'
It was then that Mrs. Darling began playing again.
'It's mother!' cried Wendy, peeping.
'So it is!' said John.
'Then are you not really our mother, Wendy?' asked Michael, who was surely sleepy.
'Oh dear!' exclaimed Wendy, with her first real twinge of remorse, 'it was quite time we came back.'
'Let us creep in,' John suggested, 'and put our hands over her eyes.'
But Wendy, who saw that they must break the joyous news more gently, had a better plan.
'Let us all slip into our beds, and be there when she comes in, just as if we had never been away.'

And so when Mrs. Darling went back to the night-nursery to see if her husband was asleep, all the beds were occupied. The children waited for her cry of joy, but it did not come. She saw them, but she did not believe they were there. You see, she saw them in their beds so often in her dreams that she thought this was just the dream hanging around her still.
She sat down in the chair by the fire, where in the old days she had nursed them.
They could not understand this, and a cold fear fell upon all the three of them.
'Mother!' Wendy cried.
'That's Wendy,' she said, but still she was sure it was the dream.
'Mother!'
'That's John,' she said.
'Mother!' cried Michael. He knew her now.

'That's Michael,' she said, and she stretched out her arms for the three little selfish children they would never envelop again. Yes, they did, they went round Wendy and John and Michael, who had slipped out of bed and run to her.

'George, George,' she cried when she could speak; and Mr. Darling woke to share her bliss, and Nana came rushing in. There could not have been a lovelier sight; but there was none to see it except a strange boy who was staring in at the window. He had ecstasies innumerable that other children can never know; but he was looking through the window at the one joy from which he must be for ever barred.
translated_paragraphs: 那天早上，船钟敲了两下，他们就已一个个手脚麻利地忙开了。海上浪很大，水手长图图在他们中间巡视，一手拎着绳头，嘴里嚼着烟叶。大家套上海盗的衣裳，把裤管截到膝头，利利落落刮过脸，一窝蜂涌上甲板：走起路来两边晃，时不时提提裤腰，那是货真价实的水手步子。
船长是谁，不用说你也知道。尼布斯当大副，约翰当二副。船上还有个女人。其余的人是桅杆前听令的水手，睡在船艏舱里。彼得已经把自己绑在舵轮前，却仍吹哨召集全体船员，给他们作了一番简短的训话。他希望他们拿出勇敢好汉的样子尽自己的本分，但他知道，他们是里约和黄金海岸的渣滓。有谁敢向他龇牙，他就把谁撕开。他这番粗豪响亮的话正对水手们的胃口，大伙儿扯着嗓子为他喝彩。几道干脆的命令发下，船掉了头，船首转向大陆。
潘船长参看海图，作了一番推算。倘若这种天气持续下去，他们大约六月二十一号可以抵达亚速尔群岛。到了那里，接下来飞行会比较省时。

有些人想把这条船变成正派船，还有些人赞成继续让它当海盗船。可是船长把他们当狗一样驱使，他们不敢向他表达自己的愿望，连不分谁先谁后的联名信也不敢写。接到命令当即服从，才是惟一安全的办法。斯莱特利听见叫他测水深，脸上露了点困惑，就挨了十二鞭。大伙儿都觉得，眼下彼得规规矩矩，无非是想打消温蒂的疑心；等他的新衣裳做好，情形说不准就会改变。那身衣裳，温蒂本不情愿，却正在拿虎克几件邪气最重的衣服替他改。后来男孩们私下传说，彼得头一夜穿上新衣，曾长久坐在船舱中，嘴里衔着虎克的雪茄烟嘴，一只手握成拳头，唯独食指弯曲着，像只钩子似的高举，带着威胁的意味。
不过，船要先不看了。现在得回到那所寂寞的家去，好久以前，我们故事里的三个人物就是从那里没心没肺地飞走的。这么久以来一直冷落十四号，想想真是惭愧。但有一点我们尽可放心：达林太太不会怪我们。要是我们早些回去，满怀伤感和同情地望着她，她多半会叫起来：“别犯傻！我有什么要紧的？快回去，替我留神看着孩子们。”做妈妈的只要一天这样，孩子们就一天有空子可钻。这事妈妈们可以打包票。

就是现在，我们敢踏进熟悉的儿童室，也不过因为它那些名正言顺的小主人正在回家的路上。我们赶到他们前头，无非为看看他们的被褥是不是晾透了，达林夫妇晚上是否会出门。我们也就是些跑腿的。凭什么要把他们的被子晾得舒舒服服的呢？他们当初溜得那么急，半点也不知感恩。要是他们回来，发现爸爸妈妈去了乡下过周末，这岂不是他们非常活该的报应？打我们头一回认识他们起，他们就欠这么一堂做人的课。不过，要是我们真这样安排，达林太太可永远不会原谅我们。

有一件事情我极想做：照作家的老习惯，告诉她孩子们就要回来了，说得再准一些，是下个星期四就到。那会把温蒂、约翰、迈克尔巴望的惊喜全都搅黄。他们在船上就盘算妥当啦：妈妈狂喜不已，爸爸欢呼雀跃，娜娜腾空而起，抢在头一个抱住他们。其实他们真正该预备的，是一顿打。要是先把消息透露出去，故意把场面全搅坏，该多有趣。这样他们神气十足地一进门，达林太太甚至不肯把嘴唇送给温蒂亲一口，达林先生还会懊恼地说：“真是见鬼，那几个男孩又回来啦。”可是，就连这样也休想得她一句谢。我们如今已有几分懂得达林太太，完全可以料到，她准会埋怨我们剥夺了孩子们小小的一份快乐。
“可是，亲爱的太太，离下个星期四还有十天。把实情告诉您，我们可以替您省下十天伤心的工夫呀。”
“不错，可得付出多大的代价！要夺去孩子们整整十分钟的欢喜呢。”
“哦，如果您一定要那么看。”
“不这么看，还有什么别的看法呢？”
你看，这个女人真是一点该有的骨气也没有。我原打算说些特别动听的话赞美她。可我瞧不起她，一句也不想说了。屋里的事情其实早已预备齐全，用不着谁再告诉她。床铺全都晾好了，她从不出门；你再瞧，那扇窗是开着的。我们对她根本也帮不上什么忙，不如回船上去。可既然已经到这儿，留下看看也无妨。我们不过是旁观的人罢了，并不真有人需要我们。那就一面旁观，一面说些带刺儿的话，但愿其中有几句能刺痛谁。

孩子们睡觉的那间房里，眼睛看得出的变化只有一处：每天九点到六点，狗窝不在原地了。孩子们飞走以后，达林先生骨子里明白，错处全在他。是他用链子拴起了娜娜，而她从头到尾都比他明智。当然，我们已经见过，他本来便是个心思单纯的人。要不是没法把自己的秃顶摘下来，他简直可以重新冒充个男孩。可他也有高尚的公道心，还有狮子般的勇气去做自己认为应当做的事。孩子们飞走后，他把这件事焦心地、仔细地想了个透，随即手脚着地，爬进了狗窝。达林太太好说歹说，亲热地请他出来，他却答得又悲伤又坚定：
“不，亲爱的，这才是我该待的地方。”
在深深的悔恨中，他起誓，在孩子们回来以前，绝不离开狗窝。这当然可惜；不过达林先生一旦要做一件事，总得做过了头；不那样，用不了多久他就会打退堂鼓。昔日骄傲的乔治·达林，夜里坐在狗窝里，同妻子谈起孩子们，谈起他们讨人喜欢的小举动，那时天下没有比他更谦卑的人。
他对娜娜的敬意，叫人看了十分感动。狗窝他不肯让她进去，可其余无论什么事，他对她的心愿都说一不二，从命到底。
每天早上，达林先生连同狗窝一块儿给人抬上马车，送往办公室；六点钟又照样送回家。要知道，他这人一向那么在意邻居的看法，如今一举一动却无不惹来惊诧的眼光。记得这一点，你就能看出，他的性格总还很有些力量。心里他准痛苦得很，不过他的外表始终平静，哪怕年轻人对他这小小的住处大发议论也一样。凡有女士往里张望，他总是彬彬有礼地掀帽致意。
这番举动也许多少有点堂吉诃德气，却实在了不起。不久，背后的缘由传了出去，感动了广大公众的心。人们成群跟在马车后头，扯着嗓子欢呼；迷人的姑娘爬上马车，向他讨签名；几家像样的报纸上都刊出了访谈。社交界的人邀他赴宴，还添一句：“务必请您连狗窝一起来。”

到了那个大事即将发生的星期四，达林太太坐在夜间儿童室，等待乔治回家。她是个眼神十分忧伤的女人。现在我们近近地望着她，记起她从前是那么快活，只因为失去了孩子，这一切就已不复存在。我发现，自己到底是没法说出她的坏话来的。她哪怕太爱那几个不争气的孩子了，也实在由不得自己。看她坐在那把椅子上，已经睡着了。人的目光头一个要去的地方——她的嘴角——几乎枯萎了。她一只手在胸前不安地摸索，像那里老有一处在疼。有人最爱彼得，有人最爱温蒂，我却最爱她。要不，为叫她快活起来，我们对那睡着的她轻轻说一声，那几个小淘气就要回来了？他们眼下离窗子其实已不到两英里，还飞得很有力气。我们只消悄悄说，他们在路上。说吧。
可惜，我们不该说的。她倏地挺身坐了起来，叫着他们的名字。屋里却除了娜娜，谁也没有。
“哦，娜娜，我梦见我亲爱的孩子们回来了。”
娜娜眼前也蒙上一层泪雾，可她能做的，只有把爪子轻轻放到女主人膝头。她们正这么相偎着坐在一起，狗窝抬回来了。达林先生从窝里探出头，去亲妻子。我们看见，他的脸较昔日疲惫多了，神情却柔和了些。
他把帽子递给莉莎。莉莎带着轻蔑接过去。她全无想象力，压根儿不能理解这样的一个人心里是为了什么。外头，随马车一路送他回家的人还在欢呼。他自然不会全无感触。
“听啊，”他说，“真叫人欣慰。”
“一大群小男孩呗。”莉莎嗤之以鼻。
“今天还有好几位大人呢。”他脸颊微微发红，向她作保。可她把脑袋一甩，他也没说半句责备的话。社交上的成功并没有惯坏他，反倒把他磨得更和气了。有一阵子，他半截身子探在狗窝外头坐着，同达林太太谈论自己新获得的成功。她说但愿他别给捧得昏了头，他便捏一捏她的手，请她宽心。
“可我要是个软弱的人呢，”他说，“天哪，我要是个软弱的人！”
“乔治，”她怯怯地问，“你心里的悔恨还跟原来一样深，是不是？”
“跟原来一样深，亲爱的！瞧瞧我是怎样受罚的：住在狗窝里。”
“可这确实是受罚，对不对，乔治？你拿得准，自己没有在享受这件事吧？”
“亲爱的！”
不用说，她一定向他赔了不是。接着，他有些困了，便在狗窝里蜷成一团。
“你能不能弹儿童室的钢琴，哄我睡着呢？”他问。在她往日间儿童室走去的时候，他又想也没想地添了一句：“把窗子关上吧。我觉得有风灌进来。”
“哦，乔治，千万别叫我做那件事。那扇窗必须一直替他们开着，一直，一直。”
这回轮到他向她赔不是。她走进日间儿童室，弹起琴来，没多久他就睡着了。他睡着的时候，温蒂、约翰和迈克尔飞进房间。
哦，不对。我们原来是这么写的，因为我们离开那艘船时，这就是三个孩子计划好的一出漂亮戏码。可那以后准发生了什么事，飞进来的并不是他们，而是彼得和小叮当。
彼得一开口，什么都明白了。
“快，叮当，”他悄声说，“关上窗子。把闩扣上。好，就是这样。现在咱俩得从房门溜出去。等温蒂来了，她就会以为是妈妈上了闩，不让她进屋。那样她就非跟我回去不可。”
我现在才弄明白先前一直不懂的一件事：彼得收拾完海盗以后，为什么没有回岛，把护送孩子们去大陆的事留给叮当一个人呢？原来他从一开始就揣着这套诡计。
他一点也不觉得自己这样做很坏，反倒兴高采烈地跳起舞来。然后，他朝日间儿童室探头一看，瞧是谁在弹琴。“是温蒂的妈妈，”他小声告诉叮当，“是位好看的太太，可没有我妈妈好看。她嘴里全是顶针，可也没我妈妈嘴里那么多。”
他当然对自己的妈妈一无所知，不过偶尔也爱拿她吹吹牛。
他不认得那支曲子，那是《家，甜蜜的家》。可他知道，那琴声在说：“回来吧，温蒂，温蒂，温蒂。”他得意地叫道：“太太，你再也见不到温蒂啦。窗子已经闩上了！”
音乐停住了，他又偷瞧一眼，看看是为什么。这回他看见达林太太把头搁在琴箱上，两滴眼泪正挂在她的眼睛上。
“她想要我替她拔掉窗闩，”彼得想，“可我偏不，我才不。”
他又看了一眼。泪珠还在，或者说，另两颗泪珠已经顶替了原来那两颗。
“她真是喜欢温蒂呀。”他独自说道。这会儿他生她的气，气她怎么不明白她为什么不能有温蒂。
道理明明很简单：“我也喜欢她呀。太太，我们两个人不能各有一个温蒂。”
可那位太太偏不肯认命，弄得他也不快活。他索性不再看她，可即便如此，她也不肯放过他。他跳来跳去，扮种种鬼脸。可一停住，便觉得她仿佛就在自己身体里面，轻轻地敲门。
“哦，好吧。”他终于说，喉咙里咕嘟一声。接着他拔开了窗闩。“叮当，走啊！”他冲着自然的法则报以一个极其不屑的冷笑，“我们才不要什么傻妈妈呢。”说完，飞走了。
这样一来，温蒂、约翰和迈克尔到底还是发现，窗子为他们开着。当然，凭他们先前那番表现，可配不上这份好运。他们落到了地板上，全不觉得惭愧。最小的那一个甚至已经把自己的家忘了。
“约翰，”他拿不准地朝四周望了望，说，“我觉得自己以前好像到过这里。”
“你当然到过，傻瓜。喏，你原来的床。”
“还真是呢。”迈克尔说得却没多少把握。
“哎！”约翰叫道，“狗窝！”他一个箭步跨过去，往里看。
“也许娜娜在里头。”温蒂说。
可约翰吹了声口哨。“嘿，”他说，“里头睡着个人。”
“是爸爸！”温蒂惊叫。
“让我看看爸爸。”迈克尔急切地央求。他仔仔细细看了一番，说：“也没有我杀的那个海盗高大嘛。”他失望得那么坦白，我真庆幸达林先生正在睡觉。要是他再听见小迈克尔开口，头一句竟是这句话，那该多叫人伤心。
看见爸爸在狗窝里，温蒂和约翰多少都吃了一惊。
“我记得，”约翰说，口气像一个已不敢相信自己记性的人，“他从前总不是睡在狗窝里的吧？”
“约翰，”温蒂迟疑着说，“也许，从前的生活究竟怎样，我们并不像自己以为的那样记得清楚。”
他们心里一凉。这也是他们活该。
“我们回来了，妈妈居然没在屋里，”约翰这个小坏蛋说，“她可真够粗心的。”
就是在这时候，达林太太重新弹起了琴。
“是妈妈！”温蒂往里一望，叫了出来。
“还真是！”约翰说。
“那你不真是我们的妈妈吗，温蒂？”迈克尔问。他一定是困糊涂了。
“哎呀！”温蒂叫道。平生头一回，一阵真正的悔意刺了她一下。“我们确实早该回来了。”
“咱们悄悄进去，”约翰提议，“伸手蒙住她的眼睛。”
温蒂却有个更好的办法。她看得出，这个天大的喜讯该让妈妈和缓一些知道。
“我们悄悄地各自上床。轮到她进来，就看见我们都在那儿，仿佛我们压根儿没离开过。”
因此，达林太太再回夜间儿童室，看看丈夫睡着了没有时，所有的小床上都有人了。孩子们等着她欢呼，可那一声终究没来。她瞧见了他们，却不相信他们真的在那里。你知道，她在梦里见过他们睡在床上的情景，已经见过太多次了，这会儿只当是那场梦还缠着她，没有消散。
她在火炉边那把椅子上坐了下来。从前她就是坐在那儿，把他们抱在怀里照料的。
三个孩子一点儿也不明白，一阵冰冷的恐惧一齐落到他们心头。
“妈妈！”温蒂叫道。
“那是温蒂。”她说。可她仍相信，那只是个梦。
“妈妈！”
“那是约翰。”她说。
“妈妈！”迈克尔叫道。这一回，他认得她了。
“那是迈克尔。”她说。她张开双臂，想去抱那三个任性的小孩子，那双胳膊再也不能抱住的小孩子。不，它们抱住了。温蒂、约翰和迈克尔早已溜下床，奔到她面前；她的双臂全把他们圈住了。
“乔治！乔治！”等终于能说得出话了，她高声喊道。达林先生醒来，同她一道分享这份幸福，娜娜也飞奔进来了。再没有比眼前更可爱的景象。然而目睹这一切的，只有一个正从窗外直直往里望的、奇异的男孩。他拥有数不清的狂喜，那些快乐是别的孩子永远不能知道的。可他隔着窗子所望的这一种快乐，偏偏是他永远被挡在门外、得不到的那一种。

sections.title_zh: 第17章　温蒂长大以后
sections.title_en: CHAPTER XVII — WHEN WENDY GREW UP
source_paragraphs: I hope you want to know what became of the other boys. They were waiting below to give Wendy time to explain about them; and when they had counted five hundred they went up. They went up by the stair, because they thought this would make a better impression. They stood in a row in front of Mrs. Darling, with their hats off, and wishing they were not wearing their pirate clothes. They said nothing, but their eyes asked her to have them. They ought to have looked at Mr. Darling also, but they forgot about him.
Of course Mrs. Darling said at once that she would have them; but Mr. Darling was curiously depressed, and they saw that he considered six a rather large number.
'I must say,' he said to Wendy, 'that you don't do things by halves,' a grudging remark which the twins thought was pointed at them.
The first twin was the proud one, and he asked, flushing, 'Do you think we should be too much of a handful, sir? Because if so we can go away.'
'Father!' Wendy cried, shocked; but still the cloud was on him. He knew he was behaving unworthily, but he could not help it.
'We could lie doubled up,' said Nibs.
'I always cut their hair myself,' said Wendy.
'George!' Mrs. Darling exclaimed, pained to see her dear one showing himself in such an unfavourable light.

Then he burst into tears, and the truth came out. He was as glad to have them as she was, he said, but he thought they should have asked his consent as well as hers, instead of treating him as a cypher in his own house.
'I don't think he is a cypher,' Tootles cried instantly. 'Do you think he is a cypher, Curly?'
'No, I don't. Do you think he is a cypher, Slightly?'
